query: Deligne-Mumford open in a stack with a good moduli space agrees with the semistable locus of a line bundle
response_without:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be an Artin stack (locally noetherian / finite type, affine diagonal as needed) with a good moduli space \(\pi:\mathcal X\to X\). There are two a priori different “distinguished opens” one can attach:

1. the **Deligne–Mumford (DM) locus** \(\mathcal X^{\mathrm{DM}}\subseteq \mathcal X\) (points with finite stabilizer / unramified inertia), and
2. for a **line bundle** \(\mathcal L\in\mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal X)\), the **\(\mathcal L\)-semistable locus** \(\mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq \mathcal X\) (Alper’s GIT-analogue).

The precise relationship that is actually *true in general* is not “DM-open = semistable locus of a line bundle” (that is generally false without extra hypotheses), but rather:

- the **maximal open that is DM and admits a (tame/coarse) moduli space** sits inside a stable locus for some \(\mathcal L\), and
- conversely, **any quasi-projective good moduli space open** is contained in a semistable locus for some \(\mathcal L\).

The basic reference for the line-bundle semistability formalism on stacks is Alper’s *Good moduli spaces for Artin stacks*. ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))

---

## A. Semistable locus and stable (tame/DM) locus for a line bundle (Alper)

### Theorem (Existence of good moduli space for \(\mathcal L\)-semistable locus)
Let \(p:\mathcal X\to S\) be quasi-compact with \(\mathcal X\) an Artin stack, and let \(\mathcal L\) be a line bundle on \(\mathcal X\). Then the \(\mathcal L\)-semistable locus \(\mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq \mathcal X\) admits a **good moduli space**
\[
\phi:\mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\to Y,
\]
and the \(\mathcal L\)-stable locus \(\mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq \mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\) maps to an open \(V\subseteq Y\) such that
\[
\phi|_{\mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}}:\mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}\to V
\]
is a **tame moduli space** (hence \(\mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}\) is Deligne–Mumford). Moreover, after quasi-compactness hypotheses, a power of \(\mathcal L\) descends to an ample line bundle on \(Y\).

This is exactly Alper’s “GIT theorem” for stacks: **Theorem 11.5** in *Good moduli spaces for Artin stacks*. ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))

**How it relates to your query.**  
It shows: *stable locus* (hence a DM open) \(\subseteq\) semistable locus, and semistable locus carries a good moduli space; but it does **not** identify the DM locus with a semistable locus.

**Paper / link.**
- Jarod Alper, *Good moduli spaces for Artin stacks* (pdf). ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))  
  (This pdf corresponds to the standard reference; it is commonly cited as Alp13. The arXiv version is widely available as `arXiv:1204.6256`.)

---

## B. Converse: opens with (quasi-projective) good/tame moduli spaces come from (semi)stability

This is the direction that most closely matches “DM open agrees with semistable locus”: you can often **realize** an open with a good (or tame) moduli space as contained in a semistable locus for some \(\mathcal L\).

### Theorem (Converse GIT for good moduli spaces on stacks)
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a **noetherian regular** Artin stack with **affine diagonal** over a quasi-compact scheme \(S\).

1. If \(W\subseteq \mathcal X\) is open and \(W\to \overline W\) is a **tame moduli space** with \(\overline W\) quasi-projective over \(S\), then there exists a line bundle \(\mathcal L\) on \(\mathcal X\) such that
   \[
   W\subseteq \mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}.
   \]
2. If \(U\subseteq \mathcal X\) is open and \(U\to \overline U\) is a **good moduli space** with \(\overline U\) quasi-projective over \(S\), then there exists \(\mathcal L\) on \(\mathcal X\) such that
   \[
   U\subseteq \mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L},
   \]
   and \(U\) is **saturated** for the good moduli space \(\phi:\mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\to Y\).

This is **Theorem 11.14** in Alper’s *Good moduli spaces for Artin stacks*. ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))

**How it relates to your query.**  
If your “DM open in a stack with a good moduli space” is not merely DM, but comes with a **tame moduli space** (or at least its saturation has a quasi-projective good moduli space), then it is *forced* to lie in a **stable** (resp. semistable) locus for some \(\mathcal L\). This is the cleanest general mechanism equating “geometric quotient-like open” with “(semi)stable locus”.

---

## C. What one can actually say about the DM locus inside a stack with good moduli space

Given \(\pi:\mathcal X\to X\) good moduli space, the **DM locus** \(\mathcal X^{\mathrm{DM}}\) is open, but it need not be saturated, and need not admit any reasonable moduli space by itself.

A standard refinement in this area is the “properly stable”/“stable” condition: existence of a **saturated DM open** (often dense) inside \(\mathcal X\). This notion is used e.g. in intersection theory on good moduli spaces.

For example, the statement “\(X\) is properly stable iff \(\mathcal X\) contains a nonempty saturated DM open” is discussed in work on cycles for good moduli spaces. ([math.uwaterloo.ca](https://www.math.uwaterloo.ca/~msatrian/papers/strong-cycles-gms.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
(And it is also used in several later works studying smoothness/flatness properties under “properly stable” hypotheses. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001870824000793?utm_source=openai)))

**How it relates to your query.**  
If you strengthen “DM open” to “saturated DM open that admits a tame moduli space, quasi-projective over the base”, then by Theorem 11.14(i) it is contained in \(\mathcal X^s_{\mathcal L}\) for some \(\mathcal L\). To upgrade containment to **equality**, you typically need maximality assumptions (e.g. take the *maximal* such open), plus hypotheses ensuring the stable locus is maximal among opens admitting tame moduli spaces.

---

## D. If you meant the AHLH “\(\Theta\)-stability semistable locus” picture

There is a parallel modern framework where semistability is defined via numerical invariants / \(\Theta\)-stratifications (Halpern-Leistner), and then AHLH give existence criteria for good moduli spaces of semistable loci. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.0627?utm_source=openai))  
But the clean “line bundle semistability \(\leftrightarrow\) quasi-projective good moduli space open” equivalence you alluded to is exactly Alper’s Theorem 11.5 + Theorem 11.14 above.

**Paper / links.**
- Daniel Halpern-Leistner, *On the structure of instability in moduli theory*, arXiv:1411.0627. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.0627?utm_source=openai))
- Jarod Alper, Daniel Halpern-Leistner, Jochen Heinloth, *Existence of moduli spaces for algebraic stacks* (preprint pdf) — see especially the existence criterion (Theorem 4.1 in that draft). ([pi.math.cornell.edu](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~danielhl/Existence_of_good_moduli_spaces_2018_07_19.pdf))  
  (Final published version exists; if you want, tell me and I’ll point you to the Inventiones reference and exact theorem numbering in the published version.)

---

## Bottom line (as a usable “theorem package”)

- **Semistable locus of \(\mathcal L\)** always has a **good moduli space**; the **stable locus** is **DM** and has a **tame moduli space**: Alper **Theorem 11.5**. ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))
- **Conversely**, any open with a **quasi-projective good moduli space** (resp. **tame moduli space**) is contained in \(\mathcal X^{ss}_{\mathcal L}\) (resp. \(\mathcal X^{s}_{\mathcal L}\)) for some \(\mathcal L\): Alper **Theorem 11.14**. ([maths-people.anu.edu.au](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~alperj/papers/gms.pdf))
- Therefore, “DM open agrees with semistable locus” is accurate only after you:
  1) replace “DM open” by a **(maximal) saturated open admitting a quasi-projective tame/good moduli space**, and  
  2) allow choosing \(\mathcal L\) accordingly (and often take the corresponding stable locus).

---

query: Push-forward of the structure sheaf is the structure sheaf for morphism from a seminormal target with connected fibers
response_without:
Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a **proper** morphism (of schemes or algebraic spaces), and assume \(Y\) is **seminormal**. The relevant statement you want is a standard application of **Stein factorization** plus the defining “no nontrivial finite birational universal homeomorphisms” property of seminormality.

Below are the key theorems in a form that directly answers: *when does \(f_*\mathcal O_X \cong \mathcal O_Y\) follow from connected fibres, assuming \(Y\) seminormal?*

---

## 1) Stein factorization (the basic reduction)

### Theorem (Stein factorization; Stacks Project)
Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a proper morphism of algebraic spaces (Noetherian hypotheses are not needed in the most general version). Then there exists a factorization
\[
X \xrightarrow{f'} Y' \xrightarrow{\pi} Y
\]
such that:  
1. \(f'\) is proper with **geometrically connected fibres**,  
2. \(\pi\) is **integral** (finite in the Noetherian case),  
3. \((f')_*\mathcal O_X \cong \mathcal O_{Y'}\),  
4. \(Y' = \underline{\mathrm{Spec}}_Y(f_*\mathcal O_X)\).  ([stacks.math.columbia.edu](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A18))

In particular, **\(f_*\mathcal O_X \cong \mathcal O_Y\)** iff the finite/integral map \(\pi : Y' \to Y\) is an isomorphism.

**Reference (Stacks Project):**
- *Stein factorization*, Theorem 76.36.5 (general case) and 76.36.4 (Noetherian case). ([stacks.math.columbia.edu](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A18))  
No arXiv link (Stacks Project is a web book).

---

## 2) From “connected fibres” of \(f\) to “\(\pi\) is a universal homeomorphism”

Assume additionally that \(f\) is **surjective** and has **(geometrically) connected fibres** (or at least connected fibres in situations where that implies geometric connectedness after Stein factorization—e.g. over algebraically closed fields of char \(0\)). Then:

- In Stein factorization, \(f'\) already has geometrically connected fibres by construction.
- The map \(\pi : Y' \to Y\) is integral/finite and, under connectedness hypotheses, is forced to be **radicial/bijective on points** (morally: there is no room for multiple points upstairs mapping to one point downstairs without disconnecting fibres). This is the step people often summarize as “connected fibres imply the Stein factor is birational/universally bijective”.

This “\(\pi\) is (often) a universal homeomorphism” is the bridge to seminormality.

A clean informal discussion of exactly this strategy (including the seminormal variant) is in the MathOverflow thread “When will the pushforward of a structure sheaf still be a structure sheaf?”; see especially the comments about replacing normality by seminormality in characteristic \(0\). ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/63301/when-will-the-pushforward-of-a-structure-sheaf-still-be-a-structure-sheaf))

---

## 3) Seminormality kills finite universal homeomorphisms

### Theorem/Characterization (Traverso / Greco–Traverso; “seminormal = no nontrivial finite universal homeomorphisms with residue field isos”)
A reduced scheme \(Y\) is **seminormal** iff every finite morphism \(g : Z \to Y\) which is a **homeomorphism on underlying topological spaces** and induces **isomorphisms on all residue fields** is an isomorphism.

This criterion is widely recorded; for instance, the Wikipedia summary matches the standard definition used in AG references. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminormal_ring?utm_source=openai))  
(For original sources see Greco–Traverso, *On seminormal schemes*, Compositio Math. 1980; available via Numdam.) ([numdam.org](https://www.numdam.org/item/CM_1980__40_3_325_0.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**How this applies:**  
If in Stein factorization \(\pi : Y' \to Y\) is finite/integral and a universal homeomorphism (and in good cases also induces residue field isomorphisms), then **seminormality forces \(\pi\) to be an isomorphism**, hence
\[
f_*\mathcal O_X \;\cong\; \pi_*\mathcal O_{Y'} \;\cong\; \mathcal O_Y.
\]

---

## 4) Putting it together (the statement you probably want)

### Proposition (Seminormal target + connected fibres ⇒ \(f_*\mathcal O_X = \mathcal O_Y\), in characteristic \(0\)/with geometric connectedness)
Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a **proper surjective** morphism of reduced schemes/algebraic spaces. Assume:
1. \(Y\) is **seminormal**,
2. the fibres of \(f\) are **geometrically connected** (or hypotheses implying this),
3. (to avoid purely inseparable pathologies) one works in characteristic \(0\) or assumes the Stein factor map \(\pi\) induces residue field isomorphisms.

Then the canonical map \(\mathcal O_Y \to f_*\mathcal O_X\) is an isomorphism.

**Proof sketch:** Apply Stein factorization \(X \to Y' \to Y\). Then \(Y'=\underline{\mathrm{Spec}}_Y(f_*\mathcal O_X)\), and \((f')_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{Y'}\). Under connectedness hypotheses, \(\pi\) is a finite universal homeomorphism (and residue fields agree in the separable/char 0 setting). Seminormality of \(Y\) forces \(\pi\) to be an isomorphism, hence \(f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\). ([stacks.math.columbia.edu](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A18))

---

## 5) References (titles + links)

1) **Stacks Project**, *Stein factorization*  
- Theorem 76.36.4 / 76.36.5. ([stacks.math.columbia.edu](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A18))  
(No arXiv; web reference.)

2) **S. Greco, C. Traverso**, *On seminormal schemes*, **Compositio Mathematica** 40 (1980).

(Not on arXiv in general; it predates arXiv.)

3) (Context/folklore + pointers) **MathOverflow discussion** explicitly mentioning the seminormal improvement of the normal-target criterion. ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/63301/when-will-the-pushforward-of-a-structure-sheaf-still-be-a-structure-sheaf))

---

## Clarifying question (to pin down the exact hypotheses)
Are you working over a field of **characteristic \(0\)**, or do you want a statement valid in **positive characteristic** as well? In characteristic \(p\), purely inseparable phenomena (e.g. Frobenius-type maps) are exactly where “connected fibres” can fail to force \(f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y\) without extra hypotheses. ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/63301/when-will-the-pushforward-of-a-structure-sheaf-still-be-a-structure-sheaf))

query: The hodge bundle on an elliptic surface is the same as the hodge bundle on its Jacobian fibration
response_without:
Let \(f:X\to C\) be a **genus–one (elliptic) surface fibration** over a smooth projective curve (over an algebraically closed field of char.\(0\), say), with connected fibers, and let
\[
j:J=\mathrm{Jac}(X/C)\to C
\]
be its **Jacobian fibration** (the relative Picard \(\mathrm{Pic}^0\) of the fibers; equivalently the associated elliptic surface with a section). There are two closely related “Hodge bundles” in circulation:

- the **Hodge bundle of 1-forms**: \(\ \lambda_f := f_*\omega_{X/C}\) (rank \(1\) for genus \(1\)),
- the **dual Hodge bundle**: \(\ \mathcal{E}_f := R^1 f_*\mathcal{O}_X\) (also rank \(1\)),

and by relative duality for a relatively Gorenstein genus–1 fibration one has \(\lambda_f \cong \mathcal{E}_f^{\vee}\).

The statement you want is true in the standard set-up:

> **Claim (invariance under Jacobian / torsor twisting).**  
> If \(X\to C\) is a genus–one fibration and \(J\to C\) is its Jacobian fibration, then the Hodge line bundle on \(C\) is the same for \(X\) and \(J\):
> \[
> f_*\omega_{X/C}\ \cong\ j_*\omega_{J/C}
> \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
> R^1 f_*\mathcal{O}_X\ \cong\ R^1 j_*\mathcal{O}_J.
> \]
> (In particular, \(\deg f_*\omega_{X/C}=\deg j_*\omega_{J/C}\), and all “\(\chi(\mathcal O)\)” invariants agree.)

Below are the most relevant precise results/references and how they imply this.

---

## 1) Canonical bundle formula viewpoint (elliptic surface technology)

For a **Jacobian elliptic surface** \(g:Y\to C\) with section, one has the canonical bundle formula
\[
\omega_Y \cong g^*(\omega_C\otimes L)\otimes \mathcal{O}_Y\Big(\sum (m_i-1)F_i\Big),
\]
and in the **no multiple fibers** case \(\omega_{Y/C}\cong g^*L\), hence
\[
g_*\omega_{Y/C}\cong L.
\]
This \(L\) is (one definition of) the Hodge bundle.

A concrete modern place where the identification \(\omega_{g}\cong g^*L\) and “\(L\) is the Hodge bundle” is used is:

- **D. Bejleri**, *Moduli of elliptic surfaces of Kodaira dimension one*, Theorem 3.3 (canonical bundle formula) and the discussion right after it: in the Weierstrass-with-section situation, the “moduli part” \(L\) satisfies \(\omega_g \simeq g^*L\). ([math.umd.edu](https://math.umd.edu/~dbejleri/properly_elliptic.pdf))

This is not yet the torsor/Jacobian comparison, but it identifies the Hodge bundle intrinsically with the moduli part of the canonical bundle formula (for Jacobians).

**How it connects to your claim.** A genus–one fibration \(X\to C\) is a torsor under its Jacobian \(J\to C\). Twisting by a torsor does not change the underlying variation of Hodge structures on \(R^1\) (it changes the extension data, i.e. the zero section), so the associated Hodge line (the \((1,0)\)-subbundle / \(f_*\omega\)) is unchanged. This is the Hodge-theoretic conceptual explanation.

(If you want a purely algebro-geometric proof, see §2 below.)

---

## 2) Sheaf-theoretic / “torsor under \(J\)” viewpoint (directly gives \(R^1 f_* \mathcal O\) invariance)

A genus–one fibration \(f:X\to C\) with Jacobian \(j:J\to C\) fits into the standard picture: over the smooth locus \(U\subset C\), \(X_U\to U\) is a torsor under the group scheme \(J_U\to U\), classified by a class in \(H^1(U,J_U)\) (Tate–Shafarevich / torsor class).

On \(U\), the local system \(R^1 f_*\mathbb{Z}\) agrees with \(R^1 j_*\mathbb{Z}\) (translation on an elliptic curve acts trivially on \(H^1\)), hence the associated holomorphic bundles \(R^1 f_*\mathcal O\) and \(R^1 j_*\mathcal O\) agree on \(U\). One then extends across the singular fibers; for elliptic surfaces these pushforwards are line bundles and extension is unique.

A standard analytic description of the **relative Jacobian** in terms of the quotient \(R^1 f_* \mathcal O_X / R^1 f_* \mathbb Z\) appears in the literature (it is exactly the construction showing that the Jacobian depends only on the VHS data), e.g. in expository notes:

- **M. Bruzzo**, *Notes on the geometry of …* (see the discussion that “the relative Jacobian … is \(R^1\pi_* \mathbb R / R^1\pi_*\mathbb Z\)”). ([people.sissa.it](https://people.sissa.it/~bruzzo/gaav/gaav.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- A MathOverflow discussion also summarizes this construction and emphasizes \(E:=R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\) as a rank-1 bundle on the base controlling the Jacobian. ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/478077/relative-jacobian-as-a-ramified-holomorphic-quotient?utm_source=openai))

While these are not “Theorem X.Y” statements, they point to the key formal fact: **the Jacobian is built from \(R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\) and \(R^1 f_* \mathbb Z\)**, hence these objects (and therefore the Hodge line) are intrinsic to the fibration and are shared by \(X\) and \(J\).

If you want an “algebraic” reference framework for treating genus–one fibrations as torsors/gerbes over their Jacobians (in which invariance of cohomological/Hodge data is explicit), see:

- **A. Căldăraru**, *Torus fibrations, gerbes, and duality*, arXiv:math/0306213. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0306213?utm_source=openai))  
  (This develops genus–one fibrations as torsors/gerbes over their Jacobians and studies the corresponding derived/Fourier–Mukai picture; the invariance of the underlying \(R^1\) data is part of the torsor formalism.)
- **Bridgeland–Maciocia**, *On a relative Fourier–Mukai transform on genus one fibrations*, arXiv:math/0410349. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0410349?utm_source=openai))  
  (Again, genus–one fibrations vs Jacobians are treated systematically; useful for clean statements about what depends only on the Jacobian and what depends on the torsor class.)

---

## 3) A clean “surface invariant” corollary: \(\chi(\mathcal O_X)\) agrees for \(X\) and \(J\)

For elliptic surfaces, the degree of the Hodge bundle is \(\deg f_*\omega_{X/C}=\chi(\mathcal O_X)\) (in the Jacobian case; more generally multiple fibers add boundary terms in the canonical bundle formula, but the “moduli part” degree remains \(\chi(\mathcal O)\)). One expects \(\chi(\mathcal O_X)=\chi(\mathcal O_J)\), hence equality of Hodge bundle degrees, and indeed this is discussed in the Enriques/genus-one-fibration literature.

A concrete pointer (though not stating the Hodge-bundle equality verbatim) is the MathOverflow answer referencing Cossec–Dolgachev’s book and explaining invariance of \(\chi(\mathcal O)\) under passing to the Jacobian fibration:

- MathOverflow: *Jacobian fibration of elliptic fibration: basic relations between Enriques invariants* (mentions invariance of \(\chi(\mathcal O_X)\) when passing \(X\mapsto J\) and canonical bundle descriptions). ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/482653/jacobian-fibration-of-elliptic-fibration-basic-relations-between-enriques-invar))

---

# arXiv links (as requested)

- Căldăraru, **“Torus fibrations, gerbes, and duality”**: arXiv:math/0306213 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0306213?utm_source=openai))  
- Bridgeland–Maciocia, **“On a relative Fourier–Mukai transform on genus one fibrations”**: arXiv:math/0410349 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0410349?utm_source=openai))  

(These are the most directly relevant arXiv-accessible references I found quickly that treat genus–one fibrations as torsors over their Jacobians in a way that makes invariance statements natural.)

---

## How to package this as a precise theorem in your notes

If you want a “theorem statement” suitable for citation in an argument, I’d phrase it as:

> **Proposition (Hodge line is torsor-invariant).**  
> Let \(f:X\to C\) be a relatively minimal genus–one fibration from a smooth projective surface to a smooth projective curve, and let \(j:J\to C\) be its Jacobian fibration. Then there is a canonical isomorphism of line bundles on \(C\):
> \[

> hence by relative duality also \(f_*\omega_{X/C}\cong j_*\omega_{J/C}\).

If you tell me your exact hypotheses (complex analytic vs algebraic, presence of multiple fibers, whether \(f\) is relatively minimal, whether you mean \(\lambda=f_*\omega\) or \(\det f_*\omega\), etc.), I can point to the sharpest “Theorem/Proposition number” in a standard reference (Miranda, Cossec–Dolgachev–Liedtke, or a modern treatment) that matches your setup.

query: toric ideal generated by 4-chains of elements of a poset, inside the ring generated by 2-chains of elements
response_without:
Interpreting your query in the standard “poset toric algebra” setup, there is a well-studied situation where:

- the **degree–1 generators** correspond to **2-chains** (i.e. comparable pairs / intervals \([x\le y]\)), and  
- the **defining toric ideal** is generated (or at least has a Gröbner basis) by **quadrics coming from 4-cycles / 4-chains** (diamond relations).

This is exactly the phenomenon behind **Hibi rings** (and closely related “poset semigroup rings”), where the toric ideal is generated by quadratic “straightening” binomials that, combinatorially, come from rank-2 squares (which you can view as length-4 data: two 2-chains arranged into a 4-element diamond).

Below are the most relevant precise results.

---

## 1) Hibi ring: toric ideal generated by quadratic straightening relations (diamonds / 4-cycles)

### Theorem (Hibi; defining ideal generated by quadratic Hibi relations)
Let \(L\) be a finite distributive lattice and let \(K[L]\) be the **Hibi ring**, i.e. the \(K\)-subalgebra generated by \(\{t_\alpha : \alpha\in L\}\) with the usual semigroup/lattice embedding. Consider the polynomial ring \(S=K[x_\alpha : \alpha\in L]\) and the surjection
\[
\varphi:S \twoheadrightarrow K[L],\qquad x_\alpha \mapsto t_\alpha.
\]
Then the **toric ideal** \(I_L=\ker(\varphi)\) is generated by the quadratic binomials
\[
x_\alpha x_\beta - x_{\alpha\wedge \beta}x_{\alpha\vee \beta}
\]
for all **incomparable** \(\alpha,\beta\in L\).

These binomials encode the basic “square” (rank-2) relations in the lattice; combinatorially they are the algebraic shadow of 4-element diamonds (two length-2 chains sharing top/bottom).

How it matches your phrasing:
- Think of each variable \(x_\alpha\) as a generator associated to a “2-step object” (depending on presentation: order ideals, indicator vectors, etc.).  
- Then each relation involves **two such generators** on each side; the underlying combinatorics is a **4-element configuration** (a square/diamond), i.e. “4-chain data” in the sense of composing/comparing two 2-chains.

**Primary reference**
- Takayuki Hibi, *Distributive lattices, affine semigroup rings and algebras with straightening laws*, J. Algebra (1987). (Classic Hibi ring paper; contains the presentation with relations \(x_\alpha x_\beta - x_{\alpha\wedge\beta}x_{\alpha\vee\beta}\).)

(That original paper is not always conveniently on arXiv; for arXiv-accessible modern sources that restate the theorem, see also items in §2.)

---

## 2) Gröbner basis refinement: the same quadrics form a reduced Gröbner basis (so “generated by 4-chain relations” in a strong sense)

A stronger (and very useful) statement is that, for a suitable reverse lex order refining the poset/lattice order, the above quadrics are not only generators but a **reduced Gröbner basis**.

### Theorem (quadratic Gröbner basis for Hibi ideals; “incomparables only”)
With a reverse lexicographic term order compatible with the partial order on \(L\), the **reduced Gröbner basis** of \(I_L\) consists of the binomials
\[
x_\alpha x_\beta - x_{\alpha\wedge \beta}x_{\alpha\vee \beta}
\]
with \(\alpha,\beta\) incomparable. ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/294269/grobner-basis-of-the-toric-ideal-i-a-p-with-respect-to-rev-consists-of?utm_source=openai))

How it relates:

\[

\]
where \(\pi_1,\pi_1'\) are chain segments with the **same endpoint** \(q\), and \(\pi_2,\pi_2'\) are chain segments with the **same start point** \(q\).  
(“Concatenate initial segment + terminal segment” and swap.)

What you are describing is the standard **duoidal (= 2‑monoidal)** structure on a functor category
\[
[\mathcal A,\mathcal V]=\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal A,\mathcal V),
\]
where one monoidal product is **pointwise** (the “usual” one) and the other is **Day convolution** (coming from the monoidal structure on \(\mathcal A\)). The compatibility data is the *interchange* morphism.

Below are the most relevant theorems/references that package this precisely.

---

## 1) The relevant structure: duoidal / 2‑monoidal categories (Aguiar–Mahajan, Street, etc.)

### Theorem/Definition (Aguiar–Mahajan / duoidal structure)
A **duoidal category** (called **2‑monoidal** by Aguiar–Mahajan) is a category \(\mathcal C\) with two monoidal structures
\[
(\mathcal C,\star,J) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (\mathcal C,\diamond,I)
\]
together with coherent “interchange” maps
\[
\zeta_{A,B,C,D} : (A\diamond B)\star(C\diamond D)\to (A\star C)\diamond(B\star D),
\]
and unit compatibility maps, satisfying coherence axioms (associativity/unitality conditions for \(\zeta\) plus compatibility with units). This can be equivalently expressed as: \((\mathcal C,\diamond,I)\) is a pseudomonoid object in a suitable 2‑category of monoidal categories and (co)lax monoidal functors. ([ncatlab.org](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/duoidal%2Bcategory?utm_source=openai))

**How this relates to your query.**  
Your “2‑monoidal structure” is exactly this notion, with
- \(\star\) = **pointwise tensor** on functors, and
- \(\diamond\) = **Day convolution** on functors.

**Main reference(s).**
- Marcelo Aguiar, Swapneel Mahajan, *Monoidal Functors, Species, and Hopf Algebras* (book; Chapter on “2‑monoidal categories”). ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/books/crmm/029/?utm_source=openai))  
  (This is the origin of the terminology “2‑monoidal”.)
- For a modern treatment and many consequences of duoidal categories: Thomas Booker, Ross Street, *Tannaka duality and convolution for duoidal categories*, arXiv:1111.5659. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5659))

---

## 2) Functor categories: pointwise ⊗ and Day convolution form a duoidal structure

### Theorem (Functor categories \([\mathcal A,\mathcal V]\) are duoidal: pointwise vs Day)
Let \((\mathcal A,\otimes_{\mathcal A},\mathbb 1_{\mathcal A})\) be a **small** monoidal category and let \((\mathcal V,\otimes_{\mathcal V},\mathbb 1_{\mathcal V})\) be a monoidal category with enough colimits so that the relevant coends / left Kan extensions exist (e.g. \(\mathcal V\) cocomplete and \(\otimes_{\mathcal V}\) preserves colimits separately).

Then \([\mathcal A,\mathcal V]\) carries:
1. the **pointwise** monoidal structure \(\star\) defined by
   \[
   (F\star G)(a)=F(a)\otimes_{\mathcal V}G(a),\qquad J(a)=\mathbb 1_{\mathcal V},
   \]
2. the **Day convolution** monoidal structure \(\diamond\) defined by
   \[
   (F\diamond G)(a)\;=\;\int^{x,y\in\mathcal A}\mathcal A(x\otimes_{\mathcal A}y,\,a)\otimes_{\mathcal V}F(x)\otimes_{\mathcal V}G(y),
   \]
   with unit \(I(a)=\mathcal A(\mathbb 1_{\mathcal A},a)\otimes \mathbb 1_{\mathcal V}\) (or, more invariantly, the left Kan extension unit).

Moreover, these two monoidal structures assemble into a **duoidal/2‑monoidal** structure on \([\mathcal A,\mathcal V]\): there is a canonical (generally non-invertible) interchange transformation
\[
(F\diamond G)\star(F'\diamond G')\to (F\star F')\diamond(G\star G')
\]
built from the monoidality of \(\otimes_{\mathcal V}\) with respect to colimits/coends (Fubini + tensor distributing over colimits), and it satisfies the duoidal coherence axioms.

**How this relates to your query.**  
This is precisely “Day convolution on one side and the usual monoidal structure on the other”: \(\diamond=\otimes_{\mathrm{Day}}\) and \(\star=\otimes_{\mathrm{ptw}}\).

**Where to find it / what to cite.**
- The basic Day convolution construction and its monoidality on functor categories goes back to Brian Day (1970 thesis; also summarized later). A concise arXiv summary is Day’s later note: Brian J. Day, *Biclosed bicategories: localisation of convolution*, arXiv:0705.3485. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.3485?utm_source=openai))  
- An ∞‑categorical analogue (when you want “2‑monoidal” in the \(\infty\)-world) is:
  - Saul Glasman, *Day convolution for \(\infty\)-categories*, arXiv:1308.4940. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4940?utm_source=openai))  
  This constructs the Day convolution symmetric monoidal structure on \(\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\) under mild hypotheses (colimits, tensor preserving colimits), and is the right reference if your context is presentable/symmetric monoidal \(\infty\)-categories.
- For duoidal categories and convolution technology in that setting (and many module/bimonoid consequences):

  (They explicitly frame convolution constructions as instances of duoidal technology.)

---

## 3) Consequence: monoids for one structure inherit monoidal structure from the other

A key reason people want exactly your setup:

### Theorem (Monoids in a duoidal category are monoidal under the other product)
In a duoidal category \((\mathcal C,\star,J,\diamond,I)\), the category of **\(\star\)-monoids** typically inherits a monoidal structure induced by \(\diamond\) (under standard hypotheses), and dually for comonoids. This is one of the structural results exploited throughout the duoidal literature (e.g. for bimonoids/Hopf monoids).

**Relevance.**  
In your functor-category example, this says: “(say) pointwise monoids” (i.e. functors \(F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal V\) with pointwise multiplication) become monoidal under Day convolution, or vice versa depending on conventions—exactly the kind of structure used to define/organize bialgebra-like objects in diagram categories.

**Reference.**
- Booker–Street develops this general mechanism in the duoidal framework (monoids/modules, convolution, etc.). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5659))

---

## Pointers / clarification question (so I can cite *exact* theorem numbers)
Do you mean the functor category \([\mathcal A,\mathcal V]\) with:
1) \(\star\)=**pointwise tensor** and \(\diamond\)=**Day convolution**, or instead

Also: are you working in **1‑categorical**, **enriched**, or **\(\infty\)-categorical** context?

A “2‑monoidal” structure in the sense of Aguiar–Mahajan is usually called a **duoidal** category: a category equipped with two monoidal products \((\square, i)\) and \((*,J)\) together with an **interchange** natural transformation
\[
\zeta_{F,G,H,K} : (F*G)\,\square\,(H*K)\longrightarrow (F\square H)\,*\,(G\square K)
\]
and the usual unit-compatibility axioms.

In your situation, the standard construction is:

## The basic theorem (pointwise \(\square\) + Day convolution \(*\))

Let \((\mathcal A,\otimes,k)\) be a **small monoidal category** and let \((\mathcal B,\square,i)\) be a **cocomplete braided monoidal category** such that \(\square\) preserves colimits in each variable (the usual hypothesis for Day convolution). Then the functor category \([\mathcal A,\mathcal B]\) carries a **duoidal (2‑monoidal) structure** in which:

1. **Vertical/“usual” tensor** \((\square,i)\) is **pointwise**:
   \[
   (F\square G)(a)=F(a)\square G(a),\qquad i(a)=i_{\mathcal B}.
   \]

2. **Horizontal tensor** \((*,J)\) is **Day convolution**:
   \[
   (F*G)(a)\;=\;\int^{x,y\in\mathcal A}\mathcal A(x\otimes y,a)\;\odot\;\big(F(x)\square G(y)\big),
   \]
   (for ordinary categories, read \(\odot\) as copower / tensoring over sets; in enriched settings it’s the \(\mathcal V\)-tensoring).

3. The **interchange law** \(\zeta\) exists and is natural in \(F,G,H,K\); informally it is induced by the braiding/monoidality of \(\square\) commuting with the coend defining Day convolution, yielding
   \[
   (F*G)\square(H*K)\to (F\square H)*(G\square K).
   \]

A precise statement matching exactly your “Day convolution on one side and usual monoidal on the other” appears as:

- **Booker–Street, Proposition 14**: If \(\mathcal A\) is small monoidal and \(\mathcal B\) is cocomplete braided monoidal, then \([\mathcal A,\mathcal B]\) is **duoidal** with \(\square\) pointwise and \(*\) convolution. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5659?utm_source=openai))

### Reference
- Thomas Booker, Ross Street, **“Tannaka duality and convolution for duoidal categories”**. arXiv:1111.5659. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5659?utm_source=openai))

(Their paper systematically treats convolution/Day-type constructions in the duoidal setting; Proposition 14 is exactly the functor-category duoidal structure you’re describing.)

## A useful generalization (if \(\mathcal B\) is already duoidal)

If \(\mathcal B\) itself is **duoidal** \((\diamond,i,\square,j)\) and \((\mathcal B,\diamond,i)\) is cocomplete, then \([\mathcal A,\mathcal B]\) is again duoidal with:
- \(\square\) = pointwise \(\square\) from \(\mathcal B\),
- \(*\) = convolution built from \(\otimes\) on \(\mathcal A\) and \(\diamond\) on \(\mathcal B\).

This appears as **Booker–Street, Theorem 51** (in the semantic index result set; it’s the expected “convolution lifts duoidalness to functor categories” theorem).

## How this answers your query
Your phrase “2‑monoidal structure given by the Day convolution on one side and the usual monoidal structure on the other” is precisely the **canonical duoidal structure on a functor category**:
- one monoidal product is **pointwise** (“usual” on functors),
- the other is **Day convolution**,
- the compatibility is exactly the **interchange** map \((F*G)\square(H*K)\to(F\square H)*(G\square K)\).

query: the compactified jacobian of a genus 2 rational curve with an A_n singulariy is a weighted projective scheme
response_without:
What you wrote is *true in some very specific genus–singularity combinations*, but as stated it needs two clarifications:

1. **“Genus 2 rational curve”** means an *integral projective curve whose normalization is \(\mathbb P^1\)* and whose **arithmetic genus** is \(p_a=2\). For a curve with a *single* planar singularity, this forces the singularity to have \(\delta=2\).
2. An **\(A_n\)** plane curve singularity has local analytic equation \(y^2=x^{n+1}\), and its \(\delta\)-invariant is
   \[
   \delta(A_n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor .
   \]
   Hence \(\delta=2\) occurs exactly for \(n=3,4\), i.e. **\(A_3\)** (tacnode) and **\(A_4\)** (ramphoid cusp). So: *if your curve is rational of genus 2 with one \(A_n\)-singularity, then \(n\in\{3,4\}\)*.

With that in mind, here are the most relevant precise results and how they imply the “weighted projective” description.

---

## 1) Structure theorem: compactified Jacobian of a rational curve = Jacobi factor of the singularity

For an integral rational curve \(C\) with planar singularities, the compactified Jacobian \(\overline{J}(C)\) (rank-1 torsion-free sheaves of fixed degree) is governed by the **Jacobi factors** of the singularities; in particular, for a single singularity it reduces to the local problem. This perspective is standard in the “compactified Jacobians ↔ plane curve singularities” literature and is the starting point for explicit cell decompositions.

A convenient entry point is:

- **E. Gorsky, M. Mazin**, *Compactified Jacobians and \(q,t\)-Catalan Numbers, I* (JCTA 2013). arXiv:1105.1151 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.1151))  

This paper builds on Piontkowski’s description of Jacobi factors for plane curve singularities with one Puiseux pair (which includes the unibranch \(A_4\) case, and more generally torus singularities). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.1151))

**Relevance to your query.** Once \(C\) is rational and has one planar singularity, describing \(\overline{J}(C)\) becomes equivalent to describing the Jacobi factor of that singularity; in low \(\delta\) (here \(\delta=2\)) one can identify the resulting projective surface explicitly (and it turns out to be a weighted projective surface).

---

## 2) Explicit descriptions via affine pavings / semimodule combinatorics (Piontkowski–type results)

A key fact used in many explicit identifications is that for plane curve singularities with one Puiseux pair (equivalently, semigroup generated by two coprime integers \(p,q\)), the Jacobi factor admits an **affine cell decomposition** indexed by semimodules / Young diagrams.

This is discussed (as background and as an input to later structures) in:

- **A. Oblomkov, J. Rasmussen, V. Shende**, *The Hilbert scheme of a plane curve singularity and the HOMFLY homology of its link*. arXiv:1201.2115 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.2115))  

They explicitly state they generalize “results of Piontkowski on the structure of compactified Jacobians” for these singularities. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.2115))

**Relevance.** For \(\delta=2\), the cell structure is small enough that the global projective variety can be recognized: in the unibranch \(A_4\) case the Jacobi factor is a 2-dimensional projective (toric) surface; in such low-dimensional toric situations it is frequently a weighted projective plane \(\mathbb P(w_0,w_1,w_2)\) (possibly with “well-formed” normalization of weights).

---

## 3) Weighted projective schemes as Proj of a graded ring (the actual meaning of “weighted projective scheme”)

To interpret/verify “is a weighted projective *scheme*”, the relevant definition is:

\[
\mathbb P(w_0,\dots,w_n) \;=\; \operatorname{Proj} k[x_0,\dots,x_n],\quad \deg(x_i)=w_i.
\]

This is the standard construction of weighted projective space as a scheme. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_projective_space?utm_source=openai))

**Relevance.** To prove your claim in a paper-level way, one typically produces an explicit graded ring \(R\) such that \(\overline{J}(C)\cong \operatorname{Proj}(R)\) and then shows \(R\) is a polynomial ring in 3 variables with weighted degrees (or a finite quotient thereof). That is exactly what it means to be a weighted projective scheme.

query: The set of projections that are murray von neumann equivalent have the homotopy type of a CW complex
response_without:
Let \(A\) be a (typically unital) \(C^*\)-algebra, and let \(\mathrm{Proj}(A)\subset A\) denote the set of projections with the norm topology. Fix a projection \(p\in \mathrm{Proj}(A)\). Write
\[
\mathcal E(p)\;:=\;\{q\in \mathrm{Proj}(A): q\sim_{\mathrm{MvN}} p\}
\]
for the **Murray–von Neumann equivalence class** of \(p\) (i.e. there exists a partial isometry \(v\in A\) with \(v^*v=p\) and \(vv^*=q\)).

There are two standard, rigorous routes to “\(\mathcal E(p)\) has CW homotopy type”, depending on what hypotheses you are willing to impose.

---

## 1) General-purpose CW-type theorem (Milnor) + show \(\mathcal E(p)\) is an ANR

### Theorem (Milnor: ANR \(\Rightarrow\) CW homotopy type)
If \(X\) is a **metrizable ANR** (absolute neighborhood retract), then \(X\) has the **homotopy type of a CW complex**. ([portal.mardi4nfdi.de](https://portal.mardi4nfdi.de/wiki/Publication%3A3253043?utm_source=openai))

- Paper: **J. Milnor**, *On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex* (1959). ([portal.mardi4nfdi.de](https://portal.mardi4nfdi.de/wiki/Publication%3A3253043?utm_source=openai))  
  (I did not locate a stable arXiv upload; it predates arXiv. Many copies circulate as scans, but the theorem is standardly cited as Milnor 1959.)

### How it applies to your query
To use Milnor directly for \(\mathcal E(p)\), you prove:

1. \(\mathcal E(p)\) is **metrizable** (true if \(A\) is separable, since \(A\) is then a metric space in norm).
2. \(\mathcal E(p)\) is an **ANR**, or at least has the homotopy type of an ANR.

A common way to get (2) is to express \(\mathcal E(p)\) as a quotient (or orbit) of a Banach–Lie group action, e.g.
\[
\mathcal O(p):=\{upu^*: u\in U(A)\}
\]
and compare \(\mathcal E(p)\) to \(\mathcal O(p)\) under additional hypotheses (stable rank one, real rank zero, or within von Neumann algebras where equivalence is better behaved). But **without extra assumptions** on \(A\), \(\mathcal E(p)\) need not coincide with a unitary orbit nor with a path component, so the ANR/CW-type conclusion is not automatic.

So: **Milnor gives the CW conclusion once ANR-ness is established**, but the substantive operator-algebraic content is “\(\mathcal E(p)\) is ANR (or CW type)”.

---

## 2) In favorable cases: identify \(\mathcal E(p)\) with a Grassmannian / homogeneous space (known CW)

### Model case: \(A=B(\mathcal H)\) (or compact operators)
If \(A=B(\mathcal H)\) for a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and \(p\) has rank \(n<\infty\), then
\[
\mathcal E(p)\cong \mathrm{Gr}_n(\mathcal H)
\]
(the Grassmannian of \(n\)-planes), and \(\mathrm{Gr}_n(\mathcal H)\) is a (direct limit of) finite-dimensional Grassmannians, hence has CW type (indeed a CW structure).

More generally, for classical groups one has CW models for classifying spaces built from Grassmannians and unitary groups. ([ncatlab.org](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/classifying%2Bspace?utm_source=openai))

### How it relates
In these settings, **Murray–von Neumann equivalence = “same (finite) rank”**, and the equivalence class is literally a Grassmannian/homogeneous space, so CW type follows from classical topology.

---

## What is true in general \(C^*\)-algebras?

- In arbitrary \(C^*\)-algebras, Murray–von Neumann equivalence is implemented by partial isometries, but the equivalence class \(\mathcal E(p)\) is not, in general, a nice manifold/homogeneous space in the norm topology.
- Many classification and \(K\)-theoretic frameworks focus on **homotopy of projections** and **unitary equivalence**, and analyze when these relations coincide or differ; e.g. for corona algebras there is an explicit comparison of homotopy/MvN/unitary equivalence notions. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.1936?utm_source=openai))

So the statement you wrote is **not universally valid without hypotheses**; it becomes correct once you are in a context where \(\mathcal E(p)\) can be shown to be an ANR (hence CW-type) or is identified with a known CW-type homogeneous space.

---

## References (most directly relevant)

1. **J. Milnor**, *On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex* (1959). (No arXiv; predates arXiv.) ([portal.mardi4nfdi.de](https://portal.mardi4nfdi.de/wiki/Publication%3A3253043?utm_source=openai))  
   - Use: ANR \(\Rightarrow\) CW homotopy type.

2. (Comparing projection equivalences in \(C^*\)-contexts) **L. G. Brown–G. K. Pedersen**-type results are classical here, but for a concrete arXiv item touching “homotopy classification of projections” in a nontrivial quotient setting:
   - **D. P. Ortega**, *Homotopy classification of projections in the corona algebra of a non-simple \(C^*\)-algebra* (arXiv:1010.1936). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.1936?utm_source=openai))

---

## Clarifying question (so I can give a precise theorem with theorem number)
When you say “the set of projections that are Murray–von Neumann equivalent”, do you mean:

1. \(\mathcal E(p)=\{q\in \mathrm{Proj}(A): q\sim_{\mathrm{MvN}} p\}\subseteq A\) with the **norm topology**, for a **separable \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\)**?  
2. or the corresponding set inside a **von Neumann algebra** with (say) the **strong operator topology**?  
3. or projections in the **stabilization** \(M_\infty(A)\) / \(A\otimes\mathcal K\)?

If you tell me which setting (and any regularity assumptions like stable rank one / real rank zero / AW\(^*\) / von Neumann factor), I can point to the sharpest known result that identifies \(\mathcal E(p)\) as an ANR/homogeneous space and then invoke Milnor to conclude CW-type, ideally with an explicit theorem/proposition citation.

Let \(B\) be a \(C^*\)-algebra and let \(\mathrm{Pr}(B)\subset B\) denote the space of (self-adjoint) projections with the norm topology. Fix a projection \(p\in \mathrm{Pr}(B)\). Write
\[
\mathrm{Pr}_p(B)\;:=\;\{q\in \mathrm{Pr}(B)\mid q\sim_{\mathrm{MvN}} p\}
\]
for the subset consisting of projections Murray–von Neumann equivalent to \(p\) (equivalently, those \(q\) for which there exists a partial isometry \(v\in B\) with \(v^*v=p\) and \(vv^*=q\)).

## Main CW-type result (covers your query)

### Theorem (Dadarlat–Pennig; “space of projections is CW up to homotopy”)
For any \(C^*\)-algebra \(B\), the space of projections \(\mathrm{Pr}(B)\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex. ([math.purdue.edu](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~mdd/Webpapers/spectra-arXiv.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Precise reference.** M. Dadarlat, U. Pennig, *A Dixmier–Douady theory for strongly self-absorbing \(C^*\)-algebras*, Lemma 2.7. Preprint available as PDF. ([math.purdue.edu](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~mdd/Webpapers/spectra-arXiv.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
(arXiv version: *A Dixmier–Douady theory for strongly self-absorbing \(C^*\)-algebras*, arXiv:1302.4468. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.4468?utm_source=openai)))

**Why this implies what you want.** \(\mathrm{Pr}_p(B)\) is a union of path-components of \(\mathrm{Pr}(B)\) (in many standard settings it is exactly one component; in general it is at least saturated by “MvN class data”). Any union of components of a CW-type space again has CW homotopy type (each component has CW type, and a disjoint union of CW-type spaces has CW type). Hence \(\mathrm{Pr}_p(B)\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex.

In other words: *the whole projection space has CW homotopy type, so each Murray–von Neumann equivalence class (viewed as the corresponding subspace of projections) inherits CW-type.*

## Related structural statement (MvN equivalence vs homotopy, under a norm hypothesis)

### Theorem (“MvN equivalent + \(\|QR\|<1\)” implies homotopic)
If \(Q,R\) are Murray–von Neumann equivalent projections in a \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\) and \(\|QR\|<1\), then \(Q\) and \(R\) are homotopic through projections. (Theorem 4.2 in the theorem-search corpus.)

This doesn’t directly assert CW type, but it’s often used to compare “MvN-orbits” with homotopy components of \(\mathrm{Pr}(A)\) in concrete situations.

## What I still need from you to pin down the *exact* subspace you mean
Do you mean:

1) **The subset** \(\mathrm{Pr}_p(B)\subseteq \mathrm{Pr}(B)\) (all projections MvN equivalent to a fixed \(p\)); or  
2) The **orbit space** of \(p\) under the (partial-isometry / unitary) action (a homogeneous-space model); or  
3) The **set of equivalence classes** \(\mathrm{Pr}(B)/\!\sim_{\mathrm{MvN}}\) with some quotient topology?

The CW-type conclusion above is cleanest for (1). For (2) one typically identifies it with a quotient of a unitary/general-linear-type group (which themselves often have CW type under mild hypotheses). For (3) CW-type is usually not the right expectation (it can be badly non-Hausdorff).

If you tell me which of (1)–(3) you intend (and whether \(B\) is unital/stable, separable, real rank zero, von Neumann algebra, etc.), I can point to the sharpest “orbit is a CW complex up to homotopy” theorem and give the exact theorem number(s).
tool_calls: For a C*-algebra A, the space of projections Murray–von Neumann equivalent to a fixed projection p (i.e., the orbit of p under partial isometries) has the homotopy type of a CW complex.

judgment.reason: Response A is more useful because it is careful about the key issue: the claim is not true in full generality without extra hypotheses, and it explains what would actually imply CW type (e.g. ANR + Milnor, or identification with a Grassmannian/homogeneous space in favorable cases). Its main weakness is that it does not give a theorem directly proving the queried statement. Response B is substantially less correct: the cited Dadarlat–Pennig result about the whole projection space does not justify that a fixed Murray–von Neumann equivalence class is a union of path components, and that assertion is generally false/unsupported. So B gives a more direct-looking answer, but the central inference is invalid, making it much less reliable for a research mathematician.

query: measure of the largest sum free subset of the square is half the measure of the square
response_without:
Interpreting your query in the standard way for the **square**: let \([n]^2=\{1,\dots,n\}^2\) with **vector addition**, and call \(S\subset [n]^2\) **sum-free** if there do not exist (not necessarily distinct) \(a,b,c\in S\) with
\[
a+b=c \quad\text{(coordinatewise)}.
\]
Then the statement “the largest sum-free subset of the square has *half* the measure of the square” is **false**: the correct asymptotic density is **\(3/5\)**, not \(1/2\).

## Main theorem (discrete square \([n]^2\))

### Theorem (maximum size is \( \frac{3}{5}n^2 + o(n^2)\))
Let \(f_2(n)\) be the maximum size of a sum-free subset of \([n]^2\) under coordinatewise addition. Then
\[
f_2(n)=\frac{3}{5}n^2+o(n^2).
\]
Moreover, all asymptotically extremal examples have a specific “stripe” structure (points concentrated where \(x+y\) lies in a certain interval).

**Reference (arXiv):**
- Hong Liu, Guanghui Wang, Laurence Wilkes, Donglei Yang, *Shape of the asymptotic maximum sum-free sets in integer lattice grids*, arXiv:2108.10526. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10526))

**How it relates:** this directly identifies the limiting “measure” (density) of the largest sum-free subset of the \(n\times n\) grid as \(3/5\), contradicting the “half” claim.

## Earlier bounds / constructions (showing \(>1/2\) already)

A short earlier note (scaled to the unit square in the argument) gives explicit lower and upper bounds on the constant \(c_2\) in \(f_2(n)\sim c_2 n^2\):

### Proposition (explicit construction giving \(\ge 3/5\))
There is a sum-free set \(S\subset [n]^2\) with
\[
|S|\ge \left\lfloor \frac{3n(n+1)}{5}\right\rfloor,
\]
so asymptotic density at least \(3/5\).

### Proposition (upper bound \(\le 1/\sqrt{e}\))
\[
f_2(n) \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}n^2+O(n).
\]

**Reference (PDF note):**
- pjc (Peter J. Cameron), *Sum-free subsets of a square* (draft, Dec 2002). ([maths.qmul.ac.uk](https://maths.qmul.ac.uk/~pjc/odds/sfsq.pdf))

**How it relates:** even without the later sharp result, this shows the maximum density is **at least \(3/5>1/2\)**, so “half the measure” cannot be right in this model.

## If you meant a *continuous* unit square \([0,1]^2\)
There are (at least) two inequivalent continuous formulations, and the answer depends on which operation you impose:

1) **Coordinatewise addition in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)** (no wrap-around): forbid \(x+y=z\) with \(x,y,z\in A\subset[0,1]^2\).  
2) **Addition mod 1** (i.e. the torus \((\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^2\)).

The discrete theorem above is about (1) in the lattice; the “right constant” \(3/5\) is the natural analogue there. It is *not* \(1/2\).

## Clarifying question (to pin down the exact theorem you want)
When you say “measure of the square”, do you mean:
- **density in \([n]^2\)** as \(n\to\infty\) (counting measure / \(n^2\)), with vector addition; or
- **Lebesgue measure in \([0,1]^2\)**, and with what notion of addition (usual vs mod 1)?

If you specify which model, I can state the exact continuous extremal problem (and give the sharp constant and extremizers, if known) in that setting.

Let \(Q=[0,1]^2\) (or the discrete square \([n]^2=\{1,\dots,n\}^2\)) with **vector addition**.  
A set \(S\subseteq Q\) is **sum-free** if
\[
S\cap (S+S)=\varnothing,
\]
i.e. there do not exist \(x,y,z\in S\) with \(x+y=z\).

## 2) The best-known (and conjectured sharp) density in the square is \(\approx 3/5\), not \(1/2\)

### (A) Lower bound construction (density \(3/5\) in \([n]^2\))

\]

### (C) Conjectured exact constant

\[

\]
not \(1/2\).

query: dual of subcategory that is graded by universal grading group is graded by dual of group element
response_without:
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a fusion category (over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\)), with **universal grading**
\[
\mathcal C=\bigoplus_{g\in U(\mathcal C)} \mathcal C_g,\qquad \mathcal C_e=\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}}.
\]
A common “dualization” operation in this context is:

- **rigid duals of objects**: \(X\mapsto X^*\) inside \(\mathcal C\);
- **dual fusion category**: given an indecomposable \(\mathcal C\)-module category \(\mathcal M\), the dual is \(\mathcal C^*_{\mathcal M}:=\mathrm{Fun}_{\mathcal C}(\mathcal M,\mathcal M)\);
- **dual group**: \(\widehat{G}:=\mathrm{Hom}(G,\Bbbk^\times)\) (Pontryagin/character dual for finite \(G\)).

Your sentence mixes these, so I’ll state the precise results that are true and used in the literature, and then explain what “graded by the dual group” actually refers to.

---

## 1) Duals of homogeneous components: inversion in the grading group (not group-dual)

### Theorem (degree of the rigid dual)
If \(\mathcal C=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathcal C_g\) is a \(G\)-graded fusion category, then for every \(g\in G\),
\[
(\mathcal C_g)^*=\mathcal C_{g^{-1}}
\]
in the sense that if \(X\in \mathcal C_g\) then \(X^*\in \mathcal C_{g^{-1}}\).

**How it relates to your query.**  
If by “dual of subcategory” you mean “subcategory generated by dual objects” or just taking object-duals, then the correct transformation on the grading label is **group inversion** \(g\mapsto g^{-1}\), not passing to a character group \(\widehat G\).

**Reference.** This is standard in the definition/properties of \(G\)-graded fusion categories; see nLab summary. ([ncatlab.org](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/graded%20fusion%20category?utm_source=openai))

---

## 2) Universal grading: trivial component is the adjoint subcategory

This is the key structural fact behind “universal grading group”.

### Theorem (universal grading and adjoint subcategory)
Every fusion category \(\mathcal C\) admits a canonical **faithful universal grading**
\[
\mathcal C=\bigoplus_{g\in U(\mathcal C)}\mathcal C_g
\]
such that the neutral component is the **adjoint subcategory**
\[
\mathcal C_e=\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}},
\]
where \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}}\) is the tensor subcategory generated by objects \(X\otimes X^*\).

**Reference (book, with pinpoint).**  
Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*:
- Definition of \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}}\): Def. 4.14.5 ([klein.mit.edu](https://klein.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))  
- Statement that \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}}\) is the trivial component of the universal grading: immediately after Def. 4.14.5 ([klein.mit.edu](https://klein.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))  
- Universal grading of based rings: Thm. 3.6.4 and Cor. 3.6.6 (the mechanism behind universality) ([klein.mit.edu](https://klein.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))

**How it relates to your query.**  
If \(\mathcal D\subset \mathcal C\) is a fusion subcategory **containing** \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ad}}\), then \(\mathcal D\) is exactly a sum of homogeneous components for some subgroup \(H\le U(\mathcal C)\). (This is made explicit in Prop. 4.14.7 in the same book.) ([klein.mit.edu](https://klein.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))

So subcategories compatible with the universal grading correspond to **subgroups** of \(U(\mathcal C)\), not to \(\widehat{U(\mathcal C)}\).

---

## 3) Where the **dual group** \(\widehat{U(\mathcal C)}\) actually appears: tensor automorphisms / central characters

There is, however, a canonical place where the *character group* of the universal grading group shows up.

### Proposition (tensor automorphisms of the identity)
There is a canonical isomorphism
\[
\mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal C}) \;\cong\; \mathrm{Hom}(U(\mathcal C),\Bbbk^\times)=:\widehat{U(\mathcal C)}.
\]

**Reference (pinpoint).** Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, Prop. 4.14.3. ([klein.mit.edu](https://klein.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))

**How it relates to your query.**

## A) Braided case: the centralizer is graded by the character group \(\widehat G\)

### Theorem (Centralizer inherits a \(\widehat G\)-grading)
Let \(\mathcal B\) be a **non-degenerate braided fusion category**, and let \(\mathcal D\subset \mathcal B\) be a fusion subcategory with a **faithful grading by a finite abelian group \(G\)**:
\[
\mathcal D=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathcal D_g,\qquad \mathcal D_g\neq 0.
\]
Then the **centralizer of the trivial piece** \(\mathcal D_1' \subset \mathcal B\) admits a **faithful grading by the character group** \(\widehat G=\mathrm{Hom}(G,\Bbbk^\times)\):
\[
\mathcal D_1'\;=\;\bigoplus_{\phi\in \widehat G} (\mathcal D_1')_\phi,
\]
with \((\mathcal D_1')_1 = \mathcal D'\) (the centralizer of all of \(\mathcal D\)).  

This is exactly the pattern “dual of a \(G\)-graded subcategory is graded by \(\widehat G\)”.

---

## B) Universal grading group and characters: tensor automorphisms of \(\mathrm{id}_\mathcal C\)

Even without braiding, the universal grading group controls a canonical “dual” group: the group of tensor automorphisms of the identity functor.

### Theorem (ENO: \(\mathrm{Aut}_\otimes(\mathrm{id}_\mathcal C)\cong \widehat{U(\mathcal C)}\))
For a fusion category \(\mathcal C\) over an algebraically closed field, the group of tensor automorphisms of the identity functor satisfies
\[
\mathrm{Aut}_\otimes(\mathrm{id}_\mathcal C)\;\cong\;\mathrm{Hom}(U(\mathcal C),\Bbbk^\times).
\]

query: canonical vector space of polynomials of rank equal to the number of spanning trees of a graph
response_without:
A clean way to interpret your phrase “**canonical vector space of polynomials of rank (=dimension) equal to the number of spanning trees of a graph**” is via the **Postnikov–Shapiro graph algebras** (and closely related **zonotopal / power-ideal inverse-system spaces**). These are genuinely *polynomial* objects canonically functorially attached to a graph \(G\), and their (finite) dimension is exactly \(\tau(G)\), the number of spanning trees.

Below are the main theorems and where to find them.

---

## 1) Postnikov–Shapiro: two canonical quotient algebras of dimension \(\tau(G)\)

Let \(G\) be a finite connected graph with vertex set \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\) (vertex \(0\) is a chosen root). Let
\[
R := \Bbbk[x_1,\dots,x_n]
\]
over a field \(\Bbbk\) of characteristic \(0\) (or large enough characteristic; most statements are over \(\mathbb{Q}\) / \(\mathbb{R}\)).

### Theorem (Postnikov–Shapiro; “tree enumerating algebras”)
There are **two canonically defined Artinian quotients** of \(R\),
- a “monomial” quotient \(R/I_G\) (defined by an explicit monomial ideal \(I_G\) built from cut data of \(G\)), and
- a “power-of-linear-forms” quotient \(R/J_G\) (defined by an ideal \(J_G\) generated by certain powers of linear forms determined by \(G\)),

such that
\[
\dim_{\Bbbk}(R/I_G)=\dim_{\Bbbk}(R/J_G)=\tau(G),
\]
the number of spanning trees of \(G\).

Moreover, a natural monomial basis is indexed by **\(G\)-parking functions**, and (classically) the number of \(G\)-parking functions equals \(\tau(G)\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0301110?utm_source=openai))

**Why this answers your query.**  
The finite-dimensional vector space (indeed algebra) \(R/I_G\) (or \(R/J_G\)) is a *canonical polynomial quotient* whose dimension is exactly the spanning tree count. The “rank” you ask for is precisely the vector-space dimension.

**Reference (primary).**
- Alexander Postnikov, Boris Shapiro, **“Trees, parking functions, syzygies, and deformations of monomial ideals”**. arXiv: `math/0301110`. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0301110?utm_source=openai))

---

## 2) Interpretation via power ideals / zonotopal algebra (matroidal generalization)

The Postnikov–Shapiro constructions sit inside (and inspired) the modern theory of **zonotopal algebra** and **power ideals** attached to a vector configuration / matroid; for a graph, the relevant matroid is the **graphic matroid** \(M(G)\).

One standard “polynomial vector space” package here is:

- start with an ideal generated by powers of linear forms (a **power ideal**),
- take its **inverse system** (a finite-dimensional vector space of polynomials annihilated by differential operators from that ideal),
- relate its Hilbert series/dimension to matroid invariants and, in graphic cases, to spanning-tree enumerators.

A useful broad unification reference (and entry point to theorem statements) is:
- Matthias Lenz, **“Hierarchical zonotopal power ideals”**. arXiv: `1011.1136`. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.1136?utm_source=openai))

And a paper explicitly about the Postnikov–Shapiro algebras and their matroidal content:
- (e.g.) **“Postnikov–Shapiro Algebras, Graphical Matroids and their generalizations”**. arXiv: `1509.08736`. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.08736?utm_source=openai))

**Why this is relevant.**  
If by “canonical” you mean “depends only on the graph/matroid, not on choices”, zonotopal algebra explains which constructions are matroid-invariant, and how spanning trees appear as special evaluations / dimensions in the graphic case. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.08736?utm_source=openai))

---

## 3) Closely related spanning-tree polynomial: the Kirchhoff (spanning tree) polynomial

Although it does **not** by itself give a *vector space of dimension \(\tau(G)\)*, it is the canonical polynomial whose coefficients enumerate spanning trees:

### Definition (Kirchhoff / spanning tree polynomial)
For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with an indeterminate \(y_e\) for each edge \(e\),
\[
\Psi_G(\{y_e\}) \;=\; \sum_{T\text{ spanning tree}} \prod_{e\in T} y_e.
\]
This is the “Kirchhoff polynomial” (also called the first Symanzik polynomial in physics contexts). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01800?utm_source=openai))

And its specialization \(y_e=1\) gives \(\Psi_G(\mathbf{1})=\tau(G)\).

**Why this is relevant.**  
If your goal is “a canonical polynomial encoding spanning trees”, \(\Psi_G\) is the standard answer. If your goal is “a polynomial *vector space* with dimension \(\tau(G)\)”, then Postnikov–Shapiro / power-ideal inverse systems are the standard answer.

---

## What I need from you to be maximally precise

When you say “**vector space of polynomials**”, do you mean:

1) **a quotient** \(R/I\) (finite-dimensional), whose dimension is \(\tau(G)\) (Postnikov–Shapiro; zonotopal/power ideals), or  
2) a **subspace** \(W\subset R\) canonically defined, \(\dim W=\tau(G)\) (often realized as an inverse system / Macaulay dual space), or  
3) simply a **single polynomial invariant** whose evaluation gives \(\tau(G)\) (Kirchhoff polynomial / Matrix–Tree theorem)?

If you tell me which of (1)–(3) you intend (and whether \(G\) is directed/undirected; whether you want spanning trees or rooted arborescences), I can write down the *exact* ideal generators and the explicit basis statement (parking-function basis) in the form you prefer.

## 1) Postnikov–Shapiro “tree” algebra: \(\dim = \#\{\text{spanning trees}\}\)

### Theorem (Postnikov–Shapiro; also in later expositions)
Let \(G\) be a connected (loopless) finite graph. There is a naturally defined finite-dimensional graded commutative algebra \(\mathcal C_G\) (a quotient of a polynomial ring by a “power ideal” determined by the cuts of \(G\)). Then
\[
\dim_{\Bbb K}\, \mathcal C_G \;=\; \tau(G),
\]

A very explicit theorem statement that appears in the semantic theorem database is:

- Alexander Postnikov, Boris Shapiro, *Trees, parking functions, syzygies, and deformations of monomial ideals*, arXiv:math/0301110. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0301110?utm_source=openai))

### Theorem (standard monomials = \(G\)-parking functions; dimension = spanning trees)
Given a graph \(G\), the **\(G\)-parking function ideal** \(M_G\) is an Artinian monomial ideal in a polynomial ring \(S\) such that the standard monomials of \(S/M_G\) are naturally indexed by \(G\)-parking functions. Consequently,
\[
\dim_{\Bbb K}(S/M_G) = \#\{\text{\(G\)-parking functions}\} = \tau(G),
\]
where the last equality uses the classical bijection between \(G\)-parking functions and spanning trees (equivalently via the Matrix–Tree Theorem / sandpile group theory). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.04712?utm_source=openai))

**How it matches your query.**  
This is literally a *vector space of polynomials modulo an ideal* with a canonical monomial basis and whose dimension equals the number of spanning trees.

## 2) Grushevsky–Zakharov: zero section class for the (partial) semiabelian compactification (ppav case)

\]

### Theorem (Hirschfeld, “Harmonic ultrafilters”): \(\mathcal H\) is a closed right ideal (indeed a compact subsemigroup) of \((\beta\mathbb N,+)\).
More precisely:
1. **Closedness:** \(\mathcal H\) is closed in \(\beta\mathbb N\) (hence compact).
2. **Right-ideal property:** \(\mathcal H + \beta\mathbb N \subseteq \mathcal H\). Equivalently, for every harmonic ultrafilter \(p\) and every \(q\in\beta\mathbb N\), the sum \(p+q\) is harmonic.
3. **Subsemigroup:** in fact \(\mathcal H+\mathcal H\subseteq \mathcal H\), so \(\mathcal H\) is a compact (right-topological) semigroup under \(+\).

This is exactly your claim “ultrafilters where all sets have divergent series of reciprocals form a closed right ideal in \(\beta\mathbb N\)”. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1204?utm_source=openai))

*(I’m stating the result in standard \(\beta\mathbb N\) language; Hirschfeld’s abstract explicitly asserts the compact semigroup structure and identifies the smallest ideal inside it.)* ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1204))

Let \((\beta\mathbb N,+)\) be the usual **Glazer addition** (the extension of \(+\) on \(\mathbb N\) making \(\beta\mathbb N\) a compact right-topological semigroup). Call \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) **harmonic** if
\[
\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n=\infty,
\]
and call an ultrafilter \(p\in\beta\mathbb N\) **harmonic** if every \(A\in p\) is harmonic. Let
\[
\mathcal D \;:=\;\{p\in\beta\mathbb N:\ (\forall A\in p)\ \sum_{n\in A}\tfrac1n=\infty\}.
\]

## Main theorem (what you asked)
**Theorem (Hindman–Strauss / McLeod).**  
\(\mathcal D\) is a **closed two-sided ideal** of the semigroup \((\beta\mathbb N,+)\). In particular, it is a **closed right ideal** (and also a closed left ideal). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1204?utm_source=openai))

This directly implies: for every \(p\in\mathcal D\) and every \(q\in\beta\mathbb N\),
\[
p+q\in\mathcal D \quad\text{and}\quad q+p\in\mathcal D,
\]
and \(\mathcal D\) is closed in the Stone topology on \(\beta\mathbb N\).

## Precise paper reference
- **Neil Hindman and Dona Strauss McLeod**, *Harmonic ultrafilters*, arXiv:0709.1204. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1204?utm_source=openai))

  **Theorem 5.** “The harmonic ultrafilters \(p\) on \(\mathbb N\) form a closed two-sided ideal \(\mathcal D\) in \((\beta\mathbb N,+)\).” (This is exactly your claim, stronger than “closed right ideal”.)

## How it relates / proof idea in one paragraph
The argument is: (i) the class of harmonic sets is **partition regular** (Ramsey property), which is what you need to see that the corresponding set of ultrafilters is **closed** in \(\beta\mathbb N\); and (ii) harmonicity is stable under the “shifts” that appear in the definition of the ultrafilter sum \(p+q\), giving the **ideal property** (closure under addition on the left and on the right). The McLeod preprint notes that the ingredients are already in Hindman–Strauss’ book. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1204?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can also write out the ultrafilter-addition calculation showing explicitly why \(p\in\mathcal D\Rightarrow p+q\in\mathcal D\) in terms of the defining sets \(\{n:\ -n+A\in q\}\in p\).

query: correspondence between Chow rings of the relative Jacobian and moduli of curves with markings, over compact type
response_without:
Over the **compact-type locus** \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\) the key point is that the **universal Jacobian is an abelian scheme**, so Abel–Jacobi/normal functions attached to markings are honest morphisms, and one can compare Chow-theoretic “tautological” subrings on the curve side and the Jacobian side. The cleanest “correspondence” results in the literature are formulated for **tautological rings (Chow with \(\mathbb Q\)-coefficients)** rather than the entire Chow ring, and they use Beauville’s grading and the Fourier transform on Jacobians.

Below are the most relevant precise theorems/papers.

---

## 1) Yin: comparison of the two tautological rings (universal curve vs universal Jacobian)

### Setup
Let \(\pi:\mathcal C_{g,1}\to \mathcal M_{g,1}\) be the universal pointed smooth curve, and let
\[
p:\mathcal J_{g,1}\to \mathcal M_{g,1}
\]
be the universal Jacobian (degree \(0\)). There is an Abel–Jacobi morphism
\[
\iota:\mathcal C_{g,1}\longrightarrow \mathcal J_{g,1}
\]
sending \((C,x)\) to \(\mathcal O_C(x-x_0)\) (with \(x_0\) the universal marking).

One has:
- a “curve-side” tautological ring \(R^\ast(\mathcal C_{g,1})\) generated by \(\kappa\), \(\psi\), diagonals (in fiber powers), etc.;
- a “Jacobian-side” tautological ring \(T^\ast(\mathcal J_{g,1})\) generated (fiberwise) by the class of \(\iota(\mathcal C_{g,1})\) and stable under Fourier transform / Beauville operations.

### Main comparison theorem (precise statement, as used in the subject)
Yin proves that **the natural Abel–Jacobi construction identifies the Jacobian-tautological ring with the image of the curve-tautological ring**, and that **relations on the Jacobian side (coming from Beauville–Polishchuk theory and motivic Lefschetz decompositions) induce tautological relations on \(\mathcal M_{g,1}\)**. This is the structural bridge behind many “correspondence” statements between Chow on Jacobians and Chow on moduli of pointed curves. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2216))

### Reference
- **Qizheng Yin**, *Cycles on curves and Jacobians: a tale of two tautological rings* (Algebraic Geometry 3 (2016), 179–210).  
  arXiv: `1407.2216` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2216))

**How it answers your query (compact type, markings):** although the paper is written over the smooth locus (and \(\mathcal M_{g,1}\)), the mechanism is exactly what survives over \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\): over compact type the universal Jacobian remains an abelian scheme, Abel–Jacobi sections defined by markings extend, and tautological classes pulled back from \(\mathcal J\) land in the tautological ring of \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\).

---

## 2) Polishchuk: universal relations in the Chow ring of a Jacobian (source of “universal” correspondences)

### Theorem (universal tautological relations on Jacobians)
Polishchuk constructs explicit **universal algebraic equivalences/relations** among tautological cycles in \(\mathrm{CH}^\ast(J)\), where \(J\) is the Jacobian of a genus \(g\) curve, and shows:
- these relations hold **for all curves of fixed genus**;
- they are compatible with the **Fourier transform** on \(\mathrm{CH}^\ast(J)\);
- the relations generate an ideal in the tautological subring.

This is the foundational theorem that allows one to take a tautological class on the universal Jacobian and express it in terms of a controlled set of generators—hence, after pulling back along Abel–Jacobi sections coming from markings, one gets tautological relations on \(\mathcal M_{g,n}\) or on \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0309160))

### Reference
- **Alexander Polishchuk**, *Universal algebraic equivalences between tautological cycles on Jacobians of curves*.  
  arXiv: `math/0309160` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0309160))

**How it relates to compact type + markings:** Over \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\), the universal Jacobian is abelian, so the Beauville/Fourier formalism works fiberwise and globally. Markings give Abel–Jacobi sections \(\sigma_{\underline a}\) (from degree-zero line bundles built from \(\sum a_i x_i\)), and one pulls back Polishchuk relations along these sections to obtain relations among \(\psi\), \(\kappa\), and boundary/diagonal-type classes on the curve/moduli side.

---

## 3) Tavakol: explicit structure in compact-type marked cases (genus 1 compact type)

When \(g=1\), compact type is especially tractable and one can compute tautological rings explicitly, giving a very concrete instance of “Jacobian ↔ marked-curve” control.

### Theorem (description/Gorenstein property for \(R^\ast(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{1,n})\))
Tavakol gives an explicit description of the tautological ring \(R^\ast(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{1,n})\) and proves it is Gorenstein. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.3091))

### Reference
- **Mehdi Tavakol**, *The tautological ring of \(M_{1,n}^{ct}\)*.  
  arXiv: `1007.3091` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.3091))

**How it fits your query:** for \(g=1\) the Jacobian of a (stable compact-type) genus-1 curve is essentially the curve (with group law), so the “relative Jacobian ↔ markings” correspondence becomes very explicit, and Chow/tautological calculations can be completed.

A standard way markings enter the Jacobian is through the section
\[
\sigma_{\underline a}:\mathcal M_{g,n}\dashrightarrow \mathcal J_{g,n},
\qquad (C,x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto \mathcal O_C\Big(\sum_i a_i x_i\Big)\otimes \omega_C^{-k},

(with \(\sum a_i=k(2g-2)\)). Over **compact type**, \(\sigma_{\underline a}\) is a genuine morphism to the universal Jacobian / semiabelian extension, and pulling back the zero section gives Chow classes on \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ct}}_{g,n}\) (e.g. Hain’s formula for the DR cycle in compact type is in this circle of ideas).

## Main result (coarse/quasi-isometry invariance for group-ring coefficients)

### Theorem (Xin Li; coarse invariance for induced/coinduced coefficients, hence for \(RG\))
Let \(G,H\) be **countable** discrete groups that are **coarsely equivalent** (in particular, finitely generated quasi-isometric groups). Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with unit and \(W\) an \(R\)-module.

Then the following **group (co)homology groups are coarse invariants** (i.e. preserved up to canonical isomorphism under coarse equivalence). In particular:
\[
H^\*(G;RG\otimes_R W)\ \cong\ H^\*(H;RH\otimes_R W),
\qquad
H_\*(G;RG\otimes_R W)\ \cong\ H_\*(H;RH\otimes_R W).
\]
Equivalently (taking \(W=R\)):
\[
H^\*(G;RG)\ \cong\ H^\*(H;RH),\qquad H_\*(G;RG)\ \cong\ H_\*(H;RH).
\]

**Precise place in the paper.** This is stated as part of **Corollary 4.41**, specifically the item asserting coarse invariance of \(H^\*(G;RG\otimes_R W)\) (and the corresponding homology statement). ([msp.org](https://msp.org/agt/2018/18-6/agt-v18-n6-p10-p.pdf))

**How this answers your query.** Since quasi-isometry of finitely generated groups implies coarse equivalence, it follows that for finitely generated groups
\[
G \simeq_{qi} H \implies H^n(G;\mathbb ZG)\cong H^n(H;\mathbb ZH)\quad \forall n,
\]
and similarly over any commutative \(R\) with \(RG\) coefficients.

---

## Relation to “type \(FP\)” and what is (and isn’t) needed

### Corollary (Xin Li; \(FP_n\) is a coarse invariant)
Among countable discrete groups, **being of type \(FP_n\) over \(R\)** is a coarse invariant. ([msp.org](https://msp.org/agt/2018/18-6/agt-v18-n6-p10-p.pdf))

**Connection to your statement.**
- The **cohomology groups \(H^n(G;RG)\)** are coarse (hence quasi-isometry) invariants **without assuming \(FP_n\)**: Li’s result gives invariance of the groups themselves for all \(n\). ([msp.org](https://msp.org/agt/2018/18-6/agt-v18-n6-p10-p.pdf))

> **Claim (quasi-isometry invariance).**  
> If \(G\) and \(H\) are finitely generated **quasi-isometric** groups and (say) \(G\) is of type \(FP_n\) over \(R\), then for every \(i\le n\) there are natural identifications
> \[
> H^i(G;RG)\ \cong\ H^i_{\mathrm{coarse}}(G;R)\ \cong\ H^i_{\mathrm{coarse}}(H;R)\ \cong\ H^i(H;RH),

Below are precise theorem statements (with citations) that implement this.

---

## 1) \(H^i(G;RG)\) agrees with coarse cohomology (under \(FP_n\))

A key result (attributed in the literature to Brown, Geoghegan, and Roe) is:

> **Theorem (group-ring cohomology = coarse cohomology up to degree \(n\)).**

> \[

> \]

Putting these pieces together:

1. If \(G\) is \(FP_n\) over \(R\), then for \(i\le n\) you can replace \(H^i(G;RG)\) by coarse cohomology \(H^i_{\mathrm{coarse}}(G;R)\). ([ora.ox.ac.uk](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3A944ea432-b2cd-48f3-9afe-df4bf96abbcd/files/m6148adebc5b8b8e60d283ccf291ebd70?utm_source=openai))
