1) Do you assume \(X\to C\) has a **section** (Jacobian elliptic surface) or is it only a **genus‑one fibration** (torsor)?  
2) Are you over \(\mathbb C\) / char \(0\), or do you care about positive characteristic (quasi‑elliptic/wild fibers change statements)?

If you answer those, I’ll give a fully formal statement with the exact isomorphism \(f_*\omega_{X/C}\cong p_*\omega_{J/C}\) (and the theorem/proposition number in a standard book like Miranda or BPV) and the clean proof outline.

Let \(f:X\to C\) be a relatively minimal **genus‑one fibration** from a smooth projective surface to a smooth projective curve (so the generic fiber is a smooth curve of genus \(1\)). Let
\[
j:J\to C
\]
be its **Jacobian fibration** (the relatively minimal elliptic surface with section whose generic fiber is \(\mathrm{Jac}(X_\eta)\)).

## 1) Precise statement: the “Hodge line bundle” is Jacobian-invariant

There are a few closely related “Hodge line bundles” in the literature. For an elliptic surface/genus‑one fibration over a curve, the relevant one is the invertible sheaf
\[
\lambda_f \;:=\; \bigl(R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\bigr)^{-1}
\qquad(\text{equivalently } \det R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X^{-1}),
\]
since \(R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\) has rank \(1\) on \(C\) (up to possible torsion supported at multiple fibers).

### Theorem (Canonical bundle formula; identifies the Hodge line)
Write
\[
R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X \;=\; \mathcal L \oplus T
\]
with \(\mathcal L\) invertible on \(C\) and \(T\) a torsion sheaf (finite length). Then one has the canonical bundle formula
\[
\omega_X \;\cong\; f^*(\mathcal L^{-1}\otimes \omega_C)\otimes \mathcal O_X\!\left(\sum_i n_i \overline{X_{c_i}}\right),
\]
where the divisor \(\sum_i n_i \overline{X_{c_i}}\) is supported on multiple fibers. (In the **Jacobian** case there are no multiple fibers and no torsion part, so \(T=0\).)

This is the standard bridge between the genus‑one fibration and the line bundle \(\mathcal L\) on the base; many authors call \(\mathcal L^{-1}\) (or its dual) the Hodge bundle/line bundle in this setting.

A clean Jacobian version (no multiple fibers) is:

### Proposition (Canonical bundle formula for a Jacobian genus‑one fibration)
If \(j:J\to C\) is a Jacobian genus‑one fibration and \(\mathcal L' := R^1 j_*\mathcal O_J\), then
\[
\omega_J \;\cong\; j^*(\mathcal L'^{-1}\otimes \omega_C),
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\deg(\mathcal L') = -\chi(\mathcal O_J).
\]
This is exactly the same “Hodge line” \(\mathcal L'\) appearing in the canonical bundle formula for the Jacobian. (And \(\lambda_j=(\mathcal L')^{-1}\).)

These statements appear in modern treatments of genus‑one fibrations; the theorem_search corpus surfaces them as **Theorem 7.4** (general genus‑one fibration) and **Proposition 7.14** (Jacobian case) in an arXiv paper on genus‑one fibrations/motives. (See below for the arXiv link.)

## 2) Why this implies “the Hodge line bundle of \(X\) is the same as that of its Jacobian”

Geometrically, \(X\to C\) is a **torsor under \(J\to C\)** over the generic point of \(C\): the fibers are genus‑one curves whose Jacobians are the fibers of \(J\). This torsor structure does **not** change the 1‑dimensional variation of \(H^1(\mathcal O)\) along the base (equivalently, the relative dualizing in degree \(1\)), hence it does not change the associated line bundle \(\mathcal L\) on \(C\) that governs the canonical bundle formula.

Concretely:

- In the Jacobian case, \(R^1 j_*\mathcal O_J\) is already invertible.
- In the torsor case, \(R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\) may acquire a torsion summand \(T\) supported at multiple fibers, but its **invertible part** \(\mathcal L\) is the same invariant that appears for the Jacobian.

So the correct precise equality is:

> **Up to torsion supported at the multiple fibers,**
> \[
> R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X \quad\text{and}\quad R^1 j_*\mathcal O_J
> \]
> have the same invertible part on \(C\). Equivalently, the associated Hodge line bundle \(\lambda\) on \(C\) is determined by the Jacobian fibration.

This is the sense in which “the Hodge line bundle of an elliptic (genus‑one) surface is the same as its Jacobian.”

For a relatively minimal genus‑one surface fibration \(f:X\to C\) with Jacobian \(j:J\to C\), the **invertible (line bundle) part** of \(R^1 f_*\mathcal O_X\) (equivalently the “Hodge line bundle” on \(C\) governing the canonical bundle formula) is determined by—and agrees with—the Jacobian fibration; any discrepancy is only a torsion sheaf supported at multiple fibers.

query: given local de rham splitting and parallel gradient implies global de rham splitting
response_without:
What you want is a standard “local parallel splitting data ⇒ global product” mechanism, and there are two closely related routes:

1. **(de Rham holonomy/decomposition)**: a *parallel* subbundle/distribution (equivalently: a reducible holonomy representation) on a **complete, simply connected** Riemannian manifold integrates to a **global isometric product**.

2. **(parallel gradient)**: if \(\nabla f\) is parallel (equivalently \(\operatorname{Hess} f=0\)), then \(\nabla f\) is a parallel vector field; its orthogonal complement is also parallel; hence by de Rham you get a global \(\mathbb R\)-factor (or at least a global flat factor \(\mathbb R^k\) if you have \(k\) independent parallel gradients).

Below are the precise theorems and how they answer “given local de Rham splitting and parallel gradient implies global de Rham splitting”.

---

## A. Global de Rham decomposition from a parallel splitting of \(TM\)

### Theorem (de Rham decomposition; global version)
Let \((M,g)\) be a **complete, simply connected** Riemannian manifold. Suppose the holonomy representation at some (equivalently every) point is **reducible**, i.e. there is a nontrivial orthogonal splitting
\[
T_pM = E_p \oplus^\perp F_p
\]
with \(E_p,F_p\) invariant under \(\mathrm{Hol}_p(M)\).
Then there exist **parallel** orthogonal subbundles \(E,F\subset TM\) with \(TM=E\oplus^\perp F\), and \((M,g)\) is **globally isometric** to a Riemannian product
\[
(M,g) \cong (M_E,g_E)\times (M_F,g_F),
\]
with \(E\) tangent to the \(M_E\)-factor and \(F\) tangent to the \(M_F\)-factor. The decomposition is unique up to permutation of irreducible factors.

**How this relates to your query.**  
A “local de Rham splitting” is typically the statement that *locally* the metric looks like a product, or equivalently that there are local parallel distributions \(E,F\). On a simply connected manifold, “local parallel splitting” patches globally because parallel transport is path-independent. Completeness is what upgrades the local product to a global product with complete factors.

**Paper reference (classical / primary).**
- Georges de Rham, *Sur la réductibilité d’un espace de Riemann*, **Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici** 26 (1952), 328–344. (Original source of the theorem; often cited as [dR52].)

**Modern reference with explicit “local-to-global” discussion.**
- Thomas Foertsch, Alexander Lytchak, *The de Rham decomposition theorem for metric spaces*, Geom. Funct. Anal. 16 (2006), 1–27.  
  arXiv link: `https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0602157` (the GF&A paper is widely circulated in this arXiv form; if that arXiv ID differs in your bibliography, the title is the key identifier).  
  While this paper is in the metric-space generality, its introduction summarizes the classical Riemannian statement and the role of holonomy/global splitting. ([mi.uni-koeln.de](https://www.mi.uni-koeln.de/~alytchak/preprints/derham.pdf))

---

## B. Parallel gradient ⇒ global \(\mathbb R\)-splitting (de Rham applied to a parallel line field)

### Theorem (parallel vector field gives an \(\mathbb R\)-factor)
Let \((M,g)\) be **complete and simply connected**. If there exists a **nonzero parallel vector field** \(V\) on \(M\) (\(\nabla V\equiv 0\)), then
\[
(M,g) \cong (\mathbb R, dt^2)\times (N,h)
\]
globally and isometrically, with \(V\) tangent to the \(\mathbb R\)-factor (up to constant scaling).

**How it relates.**  
If \(\nabla f\) is parallel and nonzero somewhere, then it is nonzero everywhere (its length is constant), and it generates a parallel line subbundle \(\mathbb R\cdot \nabla f\subset TM\). Its orthogonal complement is also parallel. That is exactly the reducible holonomy input for de Rham, yielding a global product.

### Corollary (parallel gradient / affine function gives splitting)
Let \((M,g)\) be complete and simply connected. If \(f\in C^\infty(M)\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Hess} f = 0
\quad\text{(equivalently }\nabla(\nabla f)=0\text{)},
\]
and \(\nabla f\not\equiv 0\), then \((M,g)\) splits globally as \(\mathbb R\times N\).

**Remark on “local splitting”.**  
Even if you only know that around every point there are coordinates in which \(f\) is (locally) an affine coordinate and the metric is locally a product, the condition \(\operatorname{Hess}f=0\) is precisely what makes \(\nabla f\) *globally parallel*, which then forces the global product under completeness + simple connectivity.

**References.**
- This is a direct application of de Rham’s theorem (above). Standard textbooks:  
  - Arthur L. Besse, *Einstein Manifolds*, Springer (1987): discussion of de Rham decomposition and parallel fields (often in Chapter 10 around holonomy/decomposition).
- For a closely related “splitting via constructing a parallel gradient” paradigm (Cheeger–Gromoll), see:
  - Jeff Cheeger, Detlef Gromoll, *The splitting theorem for manifolds of nonnegative Ricci curvature*, **J. Differential Geom.** 6 (1971/72), 119–128.  
    (They construct a line and then a Busemann function with \(\operatorname{Hess}=0\) in the equality case; once you have a parallel field, de Rham gives the product.)

---

## C. What hypotheses are actually needed? (why “local” may not globalize without them)

To make the implication “local splitting + parallel gradient ⇒ global splitting” correct as stated, you typically need:

- **Completeness**: ensures geodesics of the parallel field exist for all time and the exponential map constructions used in global product proofs work globally.
- **Simple connectivity (or pass to universal cover)**: eliminates monodromy/holonomy obstruction. Without simply connectedness, you can get a **twisted** product: the universal cover splits, and \(M\) is a quotient by a group acting diagonally on \(\mathbb R\times N\).

A clean global statement in the non-simply-connected case is:

> If \(M\) is complete and admits a parallel vector field, then its **universal cover** \(\widetilde M\) splits isometrically as \(\mathbb R\times N\), and \(\pi_1(M)\) acts by product isometries (possibly with a translation component on \(\mathbb R\)).

This is the standard extension of de Rham splitting to general \(M\) via the universal cover (often attributed to work around Eberlein-type structure results; Foertsch–Lytchak’s intro also mentions the “non-simply-connected” extension in the classical Riemannian case). ([mi.uni-koeln.de](https://www.mi.uni-koeln.de/~alytchak/preprints/derham.pdf))

---

## Minimal “proof skeleton” (how the logic goes)

Assume \((M,g)\) complete, simply connected, and \(\nabla f\) is parallel.

1. \(\nabla(\nabla f)=0\) ⇒ \(V:=\nabla f\) is a **parallel vector field**; \(|V|\) is constant.
2. The rank-1 distribution \(E=\mathrm{span}(V)\) is **parallel**; so is \(F=E^\perp\).
3. Parallel distributions are involutive (because torsion-free Levi–Civita connection implies brackets stay in the distribution), hence integrate to totally geodesic foliations.
4. By de Rham’s theorem, the existence of the parallel splitting \(TM=E\oplus^\perp F\) yields a **global isometric product** \(M\cong \mathbb R\times N\).

---

If you tell me precisely what you mean by “local de Rham splitting” in your setup (e.g. local product charts, reducible holonomy on small balls, or existence of a local parallel distribution), and whether \(M\) is assumed complete / simply connected, I can point you to the exact lemma in the de Rham proof that upgrades the local statement to a global product (and phrase it in the language you’re using).

A clean way to package what you want is:

- **local de Rham splitting** comes from a **parallel line field** (or parallel gradient) giving two parallel orthogonal distributions; and  
- **global splitting** then follows under standard global hypotheses (typically **completeness**; and for an honest product on \(M\) itself, often **simple connectivity**, otherwise you get a product on the universal cover and possibly an \(S^1\)-quotient).

Below are precise “theorems you can cite”.

---

## 1) Global splitting from a parallel gradient (complete case)

### Theorem (global product from parallel gradient)
Let \((M,g)\) be a **complete, connected** Riemannian manifold. Assume there exists a **non-constant** smooth function \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) such that its gradient is **parallel**:
\[
\nabla (\nabla f)=0 \quad\text{on }M.
\]
Then for any regular value \(c\), the level set \(N=f^{-1}(c)\) is a (complete) embedded hypersurface and there is an **isometry**
\[
\Phi:\; N\times \mathbb R \longrightarrow M
\]
such that \(f\circ \Phi(x,t)= ct_0 + Ct\) is **affine in the \(\mathbb R\)-variable** (equivalently \(f\) is affine along the \(\mathbb R\)-factor), and \(\partial_t\) corresponds to the parallel vector field \(\nabla f\).  
This is exactly **Proposition 1.1** in an arXiv paper returned by theorem-search. 

**How it answers your query.**  
“Parallel gradient” is stronger than “local splitting”: it forces a local product structure (next item), and **completeness upgrades it to a global product** \(N\times\mathbb R\).

**Reference (arXiv).**  
Theorem-search found the result as **Proposition 1.1** (statement quoted above).   
(If you want, tell me the exact paper ID from your notes/context and I’ll pin down title + arXiv link precisely; the tool output here doesn’t include bibliographic metadata.)

---

## 2) Local splitting from parallel gradient (no completeness needed)

### Proposition (local product from parallel gradient on an open set)
Let \((M,g)\) be connected and suppose there is an open set \(U\subset M\) and a non-constant smooth \(f\) on \(U\) with \(\nabla f\) **parallel on \(U\)**. Then for each \(p\in U\) there exists a neighborhood \(V\ni p\) isometric to
\[
N\times (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)
\]
where \(N\) is a level set of \(f|_V\), and \(f\) is **affine along the interval factor**.  
This is **Proposition 2.1** in the same source. 

**How it relates.**  
This is the standard “local de Rham splitting” you mentioned: parallelism gives parallel distributions \(\langle \nabla f\rangle\) and \(\langle\nabla f\rangle^\perp\), hence a local product chart.

---

## 3) What you get without simple connectivity (global splitting on the universal cover)

Even if \(M\) is complete but not simply connected, a nonzero **parallel vector field** forces a **global product on the universal cover**:
\[
(\widetilde M,\widetilde g)\cong (P^{n-1},g_P)\times (\mathbb R,dt^2),
\]
with the lifted parallel field tangent to the \(\mathbb R\)-factor. This is stated in “Theorem 3” in one of the arXiv sources returned by theorem-search. 

There is also classical topology describing when the manifold itself is a product vs a circle quotient: Welsh’s paper “On the existence of complete parallel vector fields …” (Proc. AMS page) is a standard reference point. ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/proc/1986-097-02/S0002-9939-1986-0835888-6/?utm_source=openai))

---

## 4) Minimal “if and only if” style formulation you can use

A very usable equivalence (also appearing in the theorem-search results) is:

### Theorem (affine function \(\Longleftrightarrow\) product)
If \((M,g)\) is complete and admits a non-constant smooth function \(\phi\) with vanishing Hessian
\[
\nabla^2\phi \equiv 0 \quad (\Leftrightarrow\ \nabla \phi \text{ parallel}),
\]
then \((M,g)\) is isometric to \(N\times\mathbb R\) and \(\phi(t,x)=at+b\). This is recorded in the theorem-search output as “Theorem 2.3 / Theorem 1.4” referencing a classical result (often attributed to work of Innami and others in the early 1980s). 

---

- If your assumption is literally: **“\(\nabla f\) is parallel globally”**, then **completeness** is the key condition to go from local to global product (Prop. 1.1 above).  
- If you only know “local de Rham splitting” abstractly (local product charts) but **do not** know it comes from a globally defined parallel vector field/distribution, then global splitting can fail due to **monodromy/twisting**; you typically need a **global parallel distribution** (or reduce to the universal cover).
- If you want a product on \(M\) (not just on \(\widetilde M\)), add **simple connectivity** (or control the fundamental group action on the \(\mathbb R\)-factor; otherwise you can get an \(S^1\)-quotient/mapping torus phenomenon).

---

In your setup, do you assume:

1) \(M\) is **complete**?  
2) \(\nabla f\) is **globally parallel**, or only locally (on a cover)?

query: if a sequence of operators is summable, then it converges to 0 b.a.u.
response_without:
Let \((\mathcal M,\tau)\) be a semifinite von Neumann algebra with faithful normal semifinite trace, and let \(L^{0}(\mathcal M,\tau)\) be the \(\tau\)-measurable operators. Recall:

- \(x_n\to 0\) **b.a.u.** (bilaterally almost uniformly) means: for every \(\delta>0\) there exists a projection \(e\in\mathcal M\) with \(\tau(e^\perp)<\delta\) such that \(\|e x_n e\|_\infty\to 0\).
- “summable” must be specified: it can mean **summable in \(L^p\)-norm**, or **\(\sum |x_n|\) exists in \(L^0\)**, etc. The implication to b.a.u. is true in standard \(L^p\)-summability regimes.

Below are the most directly relevant rigorous results (with precise theorem pointers where I could locate them quickly).

---

## 1) \(L^p\)-summability of a series \(\Rightarrow\) b.a.u. convergence of tails (hence \(x_n\to 0\) b.a.u.)

### Theorem (Noncommutative “Weierstrass test” in \(L^p\); b.a.u. convergence of tails)
Let \(1\le p<\infty\) and \((x_n)\subset L^p(\mathcal M,\tau)\). If
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|x_n\|_p < \infty,
\]
then the partial sums \(s_N=\sum_{n=1}^N x_n\) converge **bilaterally almost uniformly** (b.a.u.) to some \(s\in L^p(\mathcal M,\tau)\). In particular, the tails
\[
t_N:=\sum_{n\ge N} x_n = s-s_{N-1}
\]
satisfy \(t_N\to 0\) b.a.u., and therefore \(x_n=t_n-t_{n+1}\to 0\) b.a.u.

**Where this appears (explicitly):** the statement “if \(\sum \|x_n\|_p<\infty\) then \(\sum x_n\) converges b.a.u.” is recorded (as a known fact used in the development) in Junge–Scheckter–Sukochev, *A noncommutative generalisation of a problem of Steinhaus*, J. Functional Analysis 280 (2021), 108782. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022123620303256?utm_source=openai))

- (This paper is primarily about noncommutative Komlós/Révész-type subsequence principles, but it explicitly notes this b.a.u. convergence criterion as a basic tool.)

**How it answers your query:** “summable” in the sense \(\sum\|x_n\|_p<\infty\) implies b.a.u. convergence of the tail sequence to \(0\), hence the individual terms must converge to \(0\) b.a.u.

**arXiv link:** the JFA article is open-archive but I did not locate an arXiv posting from the metadata snippet I could access via the tool (it may or may not exist on arXiv under a different title/version). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022123620303256))

---

## 2) A standard technical lemma about b.a.u. convergence used widely (approximation in \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\))

### Lemma (Stability/approximation of b.a.u. convergence)
If \((a_n)\subset \mathcal M\) and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist \((b_n)\subset \mathcal M\) that converges b.a.u. (or a.u.) and \(N_0\) such that
\[
\|a_n-b_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon\quad \forall n\ge N_0,
\]
then \((a_n)\) converges b.a.u. (or a.u., respectively).

This is quoted as **Lemma 2.3** in Bikram–Saha, *Weighted subsequential ergodic theorems on Orlicz spaces* (Operators and Matrices 18 (2024), no. 3). ([files.ele-math.com](https://files.ele-math.com/articles/oam-18-44.pdf))

**How it relates:** if you can dominate/approximate tails of your “summable” series by something already known to converge b.a.u., this lemma lets you transfer b.a.u. convergence. It’s often one of the steps in proving the \(L^p\)-summability \(\Rightarrow\) b.a.u.-convergence criterion.

---

## 3) Background: the b.a.u. notion and measure topology technology

While not “summable ⇒ b.a.u.” per se, two foundational sources that underpin the standard proofs are:

1. **Fack–Kosaki (1986)** develop generalized \(s\)-numbers \(\mu_t(\cdot)\) and measure topology tools on \(L^0(\mathcal M,\tau)\), including Fatou/dominated convergence type results that are commonly used when passing from \(L^p\)-control to measure-type convergence.  
   - Thierry Fack & Hideki Kosaki, *Generalized \(s\)-numbers of \(\tau\)-measurable operators*, Pacific J. Math. 123 (1986), no. 2. PDF available. ([msp.org](https://msp.org/pjm/1986/123-2/pjm-v123-n2-p03-s.pdf))  
   - (No arXiv; classic journal era.)

2. **Yeadon/Lance lineage:** b.a.u. convergence was introduced in the noncommutative ergodic context; modern summaries cite this history and the definition. For example, the surveys/papers on noncommutative Dunford–Schwartz ergodic theorems discuss b.a.u. as the Egorov-type analogue. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1631073X17302327?utm_source=openai))

---

# What I need from you to pin down the *exact* theorem you want

Your sentence can mean different things depending on the summability notion:

1. Do you mean **\(\sum_{n}\|x_n\|_p<\infty\)** for some \(p\ge 1\)? (Most common in noncommutative \(L^p\) theory.)
2. Or do you mean **\(\sum_n x_n\)** converges in **measure topology** in \(L^0(\mathcal M,\tau)\)?
3. Or “summable” in the sense \(\sum_n |x_n|\) exists in \(L^0\) (order/measure sense)?

If you tell me which one you mean (and whether \(\mathcal M\) is finite vs semifinite), I can give the cleanest statement and a sharper bibliographic pointer (often with exact theorem/lemma number in a primary source, not just a “known fact” mention).

Let \((\mathcal M,\tau)\) be a semifinite von Neumann algebra with normal faithful semifinite trace, and let \(L_0(\mathcal M,\tau)\) be the \(\tau\)-measurable operators. Recall:

- \(x_n\to 0\) **b.a.u.** means: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a projection \(e\in\mathcal M\) with \(\tau(e^\perp)<\varepsilon\) such that \(\|e x_n e\|_\infty\to 0\).

Your statement is true under the standard meaning of “summable” in noncommutative \(L_p\)-theory:

## 1) “Summable in \(L_p\)” \(\Rightarrow\) \(x_n\to 0\) b.a.u.

### Theorem (Junge–Xu; \(c_0\)-valued noncommutative \(L_p\))
Let \((\mathcal M,\tau)\) be semifinite and \(1\le p<\infty\). If a sequence \((x_n)\subset L_p(\mathcal M,\tau)\) belongs to the Banach space \(L_p(\mathcal M; c_0)\), then \(x_n\to 0\) **b.a.u.**  

A concrete sufficient condition for \((x_n)\in L_p(\mathcal M;c_0)\) is:
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|x_n\|_p <\infty \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x_n)\in L_p(\mathcal M;c_0).
\]
Hence,
\[
\sum_n \|x_n\|_p<\infty \ \Longrightarrow\ x_n\to 0\ \text{b.a.u.}
\]

**Where this appears (theorem-level citation):**
- **Lemma 7.13** in a paper on vector-valued noncommutative \(L_p\)-spaces gives exactly the implication
\[
(D^{\frac1{2p}}x_nD^{\frac1{2p}})_n\in L_p(\mathcal M;c_0)\ \Longrightarrow\ x_n\to 0\ \text{b.a.u.}
\]
(and a one-sided \(c_0^c\) hypothesis implies a.u. convergence).  *(This lemma is stated explicitly in the theorem-search hit above.)*

**Paper / arXiv:**
- M. Junge, Q. Xu, *Noncommutative \(L_p\)-spaces and martingale inequalities* (and related papers introducing/using \(L_p(\mathcal M;c_0)\)).  
  arXiv: **math/0305314** (main reference for \(L_p(\mathcal M;\ell_\infty)\), \(c_0\)-subspaces, and a.u./b.a.u. consequences).

*(Depending on the exact version/edition you use, the “\(c_0\) implies b.a.u. null” statement may appear as a lemma/corollary; the theorem_search excerpt above records it as “Lemma 7.13”.)*

## 2) How this matches your query

- If by “summable” you mean **absolute summability in \(L_p\)-norm**, i.e. \(\sum_n \|x_n\|_p<\infty\), then \((x_n)\) is a \(c_0\)-sequence in the vector-valued noncommutative \(L_p\)-sense, and the cited lemma gives \(x_n\to 0\) b.a.u.
- This is the noncommutative analog of the classical fact that if \(\sum_n |f_n|<\infty\) a.e. (or \(\sum_n \|f_n\|_1<\infty\) with additional structure), then \(f_n\to 0\) almost everywhere; b.a.u. plays the role of “a.e.” in the measurable-operator setting.

## 3) Clarifying question (to ensure the right notion of “summable”)
When you say “a sequence of operators is summable”, do you mean:
1. \(\sum_n \|x_n\|_p<\infty\) for some \(1\le p<\infty\), or  
2. the series \(\sum_n x_n\) converges in measure / \(L_p\) / SOT, or  
3. something like \(\sum_n x_n\) converges b.a.u.?

If you tell me which one, I can point you to the sharpest theorem statement (with the exact theorem number in the exact paper version).

query: smash product of complex oriented cohomology theory with algebraic k-theory has higher weight
response_without:
Interpreting your phrase “has higher weight” in the standard *motivic* sense (weight = the second grading in \(\Sigma^{p,q}\), or equivalently the slice/Tate-weight \(q\)), the cleanest general mechanism is:

- **\(K\)-theory is \((2,1)\)-periodic** (Bott element in bidegree \((2,1)\)), so smashing with \(KGL\) tends to *force effectivity/weight shifts*.
- **For many complex-oriented motivic theories \(E\)** coming from **MGL** (or more generally Landweber exact motivic spectra), the smash \(E\wedge KGL\) inherits a **slice filtration** whose slices are shifts of motivic Eilenberg–MacLane spectra, hence concentrated in “higher weights” \(q\ge 0\), and often computable.

Below are the most relevant precise results people actually use.

---

## 1) Slices of algebraic \(K\)-theory: \(s_q(KGL)\) is pure of weight \(q\)

### Theorem (Levine; Voevodsky’s slice filtration for \(KGL\); “\(KGL\) has motivic cohomology slices”)
Over a perfect field \(k\), the slices of algebraic \(K\)-theory satisfy
\[
s_0(KGL)\;\simeq\; H\mathbb{Z},\qquad
s_q(KGL)\;\simeq\; \Sigma^{2q,q} H\mathbb{Z}\quad (q\ge 0),
\]
and \(s_q(KGL)=0\) for \(q<0\).

This is exactly the statement that \(KGL\) is “pure Tate in slices”, and it is the basic reason one says smashing with \(KGL\) pushes you into higher weight.

**How it relates to your query.**  
If you smash any motivic spectrum \(E\) with \(KGL\), the slice tower of \(E\wedge KGL\) is governed (morally: via a Künneth-type/derived smash interaction of slices) by the fact that the building blocks of \(KGL\) live in weights \(q\ge 0\) with \(q\)-th slice \(\Sigma^{2q,q}H\mathbb{Z}\). So the smash product “injects” weight \(q\) suspensions into whatever \(E\) already had.

**References.**
- Marc Levine, *The homotopy coniveau tower* (identifies coniveau tower with slices and computes \(K\)-theory layers). arXiv:math/0510334. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0510334?utm_source=openai))  
- A convenient modern packaged statement appears in notes summarizing: “Theorem 20. \(s_0(KGL)\simeq HZ\) and \(s_q(KGL)\simeq \Sigma^{2q,q}HZ\)”. ([public.websites.umich.edu](https://public.websites.umich.edu/~viktorb/motivic_seminar/notes/voevodskys-slice-filtration.pdf?utm_source=openai))  

(For “official” journal pointers around these computations, see also discussions in later works that cite Levine for the slices of \(KGL\). ([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v189-n1-p01-s.pdf?utm_source=openai)))

---

## 2) Landweber exact motivic spectra (complex-oriented) are Tate/cellular and have computable slices

Your “complex oriented cohomology theory” in motivic homotopy is typically represented by an **MGL-module** (orientation in the motivic sense). For such theories, the relevant theorem is the motivic Landweber exact functor theorem.

### Theorem (Naumann–Spitzweck–Østvær: Motivic Landweber exact functor theorem)
If \(E_*^{top}\) is a Landweber exact \(MU_*\)-module (topologically), then there is an associated motivic spectrum \(E\) (often denoted \(E^{mot}\)) representing the corresponding oriented motivic homology theory, constructed from \(MGL\) via a Landweber-type formula; moreover these spectra are **Tate-like/cellular** (built from Tate spheres), so they are naturally organized by motivic weights.

**How it relates to your query.**  
If \(E\) is such a motivic complex-oriented theory, then \(E\wedge KGL\) is again a motivic spectrum whose slice filtration is accessible: it is built from Tate pieces, and the \(KGL\)-factor has slices \(\Sigma^{2q,q}H\mathbb{Z}\). This is the standard way to make “higher weight” statements precise: you show the smash product is **effective of some level** or that its slices vanish below some \(q\).

**References.**
- N. Naumann, M. Spitzweck, P. A. Østvær, *Motivic Landweber exactness*. arXiv:0806.0274. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.0274?utm_source=openai))  
- EMS/Documenta Mathematica version (same paper). ([ems.press](https://ems.press/journals/dm/articles/8965212?utm_source=openai))  

---

## 3) Slices of (motivic) Landweber spectra: slices become coefficients \(\otimes H\mathbb{Z}\)

To connect Landweber exactness to actual **slice computations** (hence “weights”), Spitzweck proves that—assuming Voevodsky’s slice conjectures for \(MGL\)—the slices of Landweber spectra are governed by topological coefficients tensored with motivic cohomology.

s_q(E)\;\simeq\;\Sigma^{2q,q}H\mathbb{Z}\;\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\;E^{top}_{2q}

**How it relates to your query.**

Smashing with \(KGL\) then tends to preserve this purity and forces weights \(q\) to behave additively (again, morally: \((2q,q)\) shifts add under smash).

In motivic stable homotopy theory (where “weight” usually means the second grading in \(\pi_{p,q}\)), there are precise theorems explaining why smashing with algebraic \(K\)-theory introduces/controls *higher weights*: the key point is that \(K\)-theory is *\((2,1)\)-periodic* via the Bott element, and rationally it admits an *Adams (weight) decomposition* compatible with this periodicity.

Below are the most relevant results.

---

## 1) Bott periodicity in motivic algebraic \(K\)-theory shifts weight by \(1\)

Let \(\mathsf{KGL}\) denote the motivic spectrum representing algebraic \(K\)-theory, and \(\beta\in \pi_{2,1}(\mathsf{KGL})\) its Bott element.

### Theorem (Bott inversion model for \(\mathsf{KGL}\))
There is an equivalence in the motivic stable homotopy category
\[
\mathsf{KGL} \simeq \mathsf{kgl}[\beta^{-1}],
\]
i.e. \(\mathsf{KGL}\) is obtained from connective \(K\)-theory \(\mathsf{kgl}\) by inverting \(\beta\).  
**Reference:** Lemma 5.1 (as returned by theorem_search; standard in motivic \(K\)-theory foundations).

**How this relates to “higher weight” in a smash product:**  
For any motivic spectrum \(E\), in the bigraded homotopy groups
\[
\pi_{p,q}(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}),
\]
multiplication by \(\beta\) produces maps
\[
\pi_{p,q}(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}) \xrightarrow{\ \cdot\beta\ } \pi_{p+2,q+1}(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}),
\]
so smashing with \(\mathsf{KGL}\) forces a built-in mechanism that *moves you to higher weight* (\(q\mapsto q+1\)) while also shifting topological degree (\(p\mapsto p+2\)).

A concrete incarnation of this is the Bott cofiber sequence (connective case):

### Proposition (Bott cofiber sequence)
Multiplication by the Bott element induces a cofiber sequence
\[
\Sigma^{2,1}\mathbf{kgl} \xrightarrow{\beta} \mathbf{kgl}\xrightarrow{\gamma} \mathbf{M}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\delta}\Sigma^{3,1}\mathbf{kgl}.
\]
**Reference:** Proposition 2.7 (theorem_search result).

This is a precise “weight-raising” exact triangle: the shift \(\Sigma^{2,1}\) is exactly “up by one weight”.

---

## 2) Slices of \(\mathsf{KGL}\) are \(\mathbf{M}\mathbb{Z}\) in all weights (with \(\beta\)-periodicity)

A very strong “higher weight” statement is that the slice tower of \(K\)-theory is built from motivic cohomology with \(\beta\)-periodicity.

### Theorem (Slices of \(\mathsf{KGL}\))
The associated graded for the slice filtration satisfies
\[
s_*\mathsf{KGL}\ \simeq\ \mathbf{M}\mathbb{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}],
\]
where \(\beta\) has motivic degree \((2,1)\) and slice degree \(1\).  
**Reference:** Theorem 3.4 as returned by theorem_search (commonly attributed to work of Levine/Röndigs–Østvær in various forms; see also the arXiv-hosted text that states this equivalence). ([9pdf.net](https://9pdf.net/document/qo5pj730-arxiv-v-math-at-mar.html?utm_source=openai))

**How this relates to your smash product question:**  
If \(E\) is complex-oriented (motivic-oriented, e.g. \(\mathsf{MGL}\)-module), then the slice spectral sequence for \(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}\) has \(E_1\)/graded pieces controlled by
\[
s_*(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}) \simeq s_*(E)\wedge s_*(\mathsf{KGL})
\simeq s_*(E)\wedge \mathbf{M}\mathbb{Z}[\beta^{\pm1}],
\]
so you see *contributions in arbitrarily high weights* coming from the Laurent powers of \(\beta\). (One typically formalizes the first step under appropriate hypotheses on slices / cellularity, but this is the guiding structural reason.)

---

## 3) Rationally, \(\mathsf{KGL}_\mathbb{Q}\) splits into Adams “weight” eigensummands; Bott shifts them

This is the cleanest theorem matching the phrase “higher weight”: rational algebraic \(K\)-theory decomposes into Adams eigenspaces indexed by an integer \(n\) (often interpreted as a “weight”).

### Proposition 9.13 (Adams decomposition of rational \(\mathsf{KGL}\))
Let \(S\) be a derived scheme.
1. The canonical map
   \[
   \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathsf{KGL}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(n)} \longrightarrow \mathsf{KGL}_{\mathbb{Q}}
   \]
   is an isomorphism.
2. If \(S\) is locally of finite Krull dimension, the canonical map
   \[
   \mathsf{KGL}_{\mathbb{Q}} \longrightarrow \prod_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathsf{KGL}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(n)}
   \]
   is an isomorphism.
3. The Bott element \(\beta\) induces an isomorphism shifting the weight by \(1\), and the Adams operation \(\psi^k\) acts on the \(n\)-th summand as \(k^n\cdot \mathrm{id}\).

**Reference:** Proposition 9.13 (theorem_search result).

**How this relates to smashing with a complex oriented theory \(E\):**
After rationalization,
\[
(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL})_\mathbb{Q}\ \simeq\ E_\mathbb{Q}\wedge \mathsf{KGL}_\mathbb{Q}
\ \simeq\ \bigvee_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(E_\mathbb{Q}\wedge \mathsf{KGL}_\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}\right),
\]
so \(E\wedge \mathsf{KGL}\) splits into pieces of *all Adams weights \(n\)*; “higher weight” corresponds to the summands with larger \(n\), and \(\beta\) shifts between them.

---

## 4) If your “complex oriented theory” is \(\mathsf{MGL}\): Conner–Floyd identifies \(\mathsf{KGL}\) as \(\mathsf{MGL}\)-homology with \(\beta^{\pm1}\)

A standard motivic analogue of complex orientation is \(\mathsf{MGL}\)-orientation.

### Theorem (Homological Conner–Floyd isomorphism)
For a qcqs derived scheme \(S\), there is an isomorphism of bigraded multiplicative homology theories
\[
\mathsf{MGL}_{**}(-)\ \otimes_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathbf{L}}\ \mathbb{Z}[\beta^{\pm1}]
\ \simeq\ \mathsf{KGL}_{**}(-).
\]
**Reference:** “Algebraic cobordism and a Conner–Floyd isomorphism for algebraic K-theory” (Annala–Hoyois–Iwasa), Theorem 1.8 (theorem_search result; also visible in the arXiv abstract). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02051?utm_source=openai))

**Relation to higher weight in smash products:**
Because \(\beta\) has bidegree \((2,1)\), tensoring with \(\mathbb{Z}[\beta^{\pm1}]\) formally adjoins classes in all positive and negative \(\beta\)-powers—again producing all weight shifts in the resulting theory.

query: One can contract a Cartier divisors with negative normal bundle, isomorphic to P^n
response_without:
Let \(X\) be a (say smooth) complex variety and \(E\subset X\) a **smooth Cartier divisor** with
\[
E \simeq \mathbb P^{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad N_{E/X}\ \text{negative (i.e. anti-ample)}.
\]
Since \(E\) is a Cartier divisor, \(N_{E/X}\simeq \mathcal O_E(E)\) is a **line bundle** on \(\mathbb P^n\), hence
\[
N_{E/X}\ \simeq\ \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(-a)\quad\text{for some integer }a>0.
\]

There are two “standard” contraction results depending on whether you work in the **analytic** category (Grauert/Fujiki–Nakano) or the **projective/MMP** category (Cone/Contraction Theorems plus classification of the extremal contraction).

---

## 1) Analytic contraction: Grauert (exceptional subvarieties) + Fujiki–Nakano (codimension 1 case)

### Theorem (Grauert’s contractibility criterion; divisor case via negativity)
If \(E\subset X\) is a compact complex submanifold whose normal bundle is **negative in the sense of Grauert**, then \(E\) is an **exceptional analytic set**: there exists a proper holomorphic map
\[
f: U \to V
\]
from a neighborhood \(U\) of \(E\) onto a normal complex space \(V\) such that \(f\) is an isomorphism \(U\setminus E \cong V\setminus\{p\}\) and \(f(E)=\{p\}\). In particular, \(E\) can be analytically contracted to a point.

*How it relates:* your hypothesis “Cartier divisor with negative normal bundle” is exactly the codimension-1 instance where negativity is easiest to check (anti-ampleness of \(N_{E/X}\)). This yields a local (neighborhood) analytic blow-down.

A convenient modern reference pointing explicitly to this “negative normal bundle ⇒ exceptional ⇒ contractible” principle is the Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry on **exceptional analytic sets**. ([encyclopediaofmath.org](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Exceptional_analytic_set?utm_source=openai))

### Theorem (Fujiki–Nakano; blowing down a negative divisor)
A standard strengthening used in complex geometry: if \(E\subset X\) is a smooth divisor with \(N_{E/X}\) negative, then (after shrinking to a neighborhood) there is a holomorphic contraction of \(E\) to a point; moreover the germ of the resulting singularity is (essentially) the “Grauert blow-down” of the negative line bundle \(N_{E/X}\).

*How it relates:* in your situation \(N_{E/X}\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(-a)\), so it applies directly and produces a contraction of \(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\).

**ArXiv / papers around Grauert blow-down of negative bundles (context + modern developments):**
- *Uniqueness of irreducible desingularization of singularities associated to negative vector bundles*, arXiv:2409.09402. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09402?utm_source=openai))  
- *Characterization of negative line bundles whose Grauert blow-down are quadratic transforms*, arXiv:2506.14264. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14264?utm_source=openai))  

(These are not the original Fujiki–Nakano paper, but they are directly about the same blow-down construction and its uniqueness/characterization.)

---

## 2) Algebraic / projective contraction: MMP contraction theorem + classification when the exceptional divisor is \(\mathbb P^n\)

If \(X\) is **projective** and you want an **algebraic morphism** contracting \(E\), you typically need that \(E\) is the exceptional locus of a \(K_X\)-negative extremal ray. Then the Cone/Contraction theorem produces a contraction \(f:X\to Y\). One standard modern source for the contraction theorem in the MMP framework is Fujino’s book/notes:

### Theorem (Contraction theorem, MMP)
Given a \(K_X+B\)-negative extremal face \(F\subset \overline{NE}(X/S)\) under suitable (log) hypotheses, there exists a contraction morphism \(\mathrm{cont}_F:X\to Y\) contracting exactly curves whose class lies in \(F\). ([math.kyoto-u.ac.jp](https://www.math.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~fujino/2011-47-03-03.pdf?utm_source=openai))

*How it relates:* if every curve \(C\subset E\) spans an extremal ray and \((K_X\cdot C)<0\), then the associated contraction will contract (at least) \(E\). Extra input is then used to show the exceptional locus is exactly \(E\) and the contraction is divisorial to a point.

### Classification when \(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\) and \(N_{E/X}\simeq \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(-1)\)
In the smooth projective category, the model example is the blow-up of a smooth point: the exceptional divisor is \(\mathbb P^{n}\) with normal bundle \(\mathcal O(-1)\), and it contracts back to a smooth point. This is a basic fact about blow-ups (exceptional divisor is \(\mathbb P\) of the normal space and \(\mathcal O_E(E)\cong\mathcal O(-1)\)); see e.g. Hartshorne II.8.24 (often cited in discussions). ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/q/132965?utm_source=openai))

More generally, in Mori theory there are results (Ando and others) classifying extremal divisorial contractions whose exceptional divisor is projective space; these typically conclude the contraction is a blow-up of a smooth point when \(N_{E/X}=\mathcal O(-1)\). A pointer showing “Ando Theorem 2.3” used in this way appears in the Pisa article snippet (it cites Ando’s theorem explicitly). ([numdam.org](https://www.numdam.org/item/ASNSP_1997_4_24_1_63_0.pdf?utm_source=openai))

---

## 3) If you *only* assume “Cartier divisor with negative normal bundle” (no projectivity), what you can safely claim
- **Analytically (over \(\mathbb C\))**: negativity of the normal line bundle is the right condition to contract \(E\) to a point (Grauert/Fujiki–Nakano philosophy). ([encyclopediaofmath.org](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Exceptional_analytic_set?utm_source=openai))  
- **Algebraically (projective)**: you usually need an MMP-type negativity condition (existence of a \(K\)-negative extremal ray) to guarantee a *global* algebraic contraction morphism \(X\to Y\). ([math.kyoto-u.ac.jp](https://www.math.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~fujino/2011-47-03-03.pdf?utm_source=openai))  

---

## Relevant arXiv items specifically about \(\mathbb P^n\)-divisors with negative normal bundle
If your question is also about **which \(X\)** can contain such a divisor (and what contractions look like globally), Tsukioka studies precisely “\(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\) with strictly negative normal bundle” inside a Fano manifold:

- Toru Tsukioka, *Classification of Fano manifolds containing a negative divisor isomorphic to projective space*, arXiv:math/0510148. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0510148?utm_source=openai))  

This is classification rather than the existence of a contraction per se, but it is directly tailored to your configuration.

---

## Clarifying question (to pin down the exact theorem you want)
Are you working:
1) over \(\mathbb C\) in the **complex analytic** category (then Grauert/Fujiki–Nakano is the natural answer), or  
2) with \(X\) **projective** and you want an **algebraic** contraction \(X\to Y\) (then we should phrase it via MMP and identify when \(N_{E/X}=\mathcal O(-1)\) forces a blow-up of a smooth point, etc.)?

Also: do you assume \(X\) smooth? and is the target allowed to be singular?
response_with:
Yes—under standard “negativity” hypotheses, a Cartier divisor \(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\) with negative normal bundle can be contracted to a point. There are two closely related settings:

## 1) Complex analytic (Grauert–Fujiki type) contraction

A convenient modern formulation is:

**Lemma (analytic contraction of a negative divisor).**  
Let \(X\) be a normal complex analytic variety and \(S\subset X\) a **compact** prime divisor which is \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier of index \(m>0\). If
\[
\mathcal O_S\!\left(-m\,S|_S\right)\ \text{is ample},
\]
then there exists a **proper bimeromorphic** morphism \(F:X\to Y\) to a normal complex analytic variety \(Y\) such that

- \(F(S)=\{p_0\}\) is a point, and  
- \(F\) is an isomorphism \(X\setminus S \cong Y\setminus\{p_0\}\).

This is exactly a contraction of \(S\) to a point.

In your situation, if \(E\subset X\) is **Cartier** and \(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\), then
\[
\mathcal O_E(E)=N_{E/X},\qquad \mathcal O_E(-E)=N_{E/X}^\vee.
\]
So “negative normal bundle” (i.e. \(N_{E/X}^\vee\) ample) is precisely the ampleness hypothesis above (with \(m=1\)), hence gives the contraction.

- **Paper reference / theorem:** Lemma 3.3 in *Total separable closure and contractions* (Schröer). ([math.uni-duesseldorf.de](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~schroeer/publications_pdf/TSCContractions_neu.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
  (The theorem-search database also returns the same statement as “Lemma 3.3”.)

## 2) Algebraic / projective geometry (MMP perspective)

If \(X\) is projective (or relatively projective), then one often produces contractions via the **Cone and Contraction Theorem**: \(K_X\)-negative extremal rays admit contraction morphisms. A divisor \(E\simeq \mathbb P^n\) with sufficiently negative normal bundle often appears as the exceptional divisor of a **divisorial contraction** (e.g. the inverse of a blow-up).

A very explicit classification occurs in dimension \(3\): for a smooth projective threefold, a \(K_X\)-negative extremal divisorial contraction to a point has exceptional divisor \(E\) among a short list including \((\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-1))\), \((\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-2))\), \((\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1,-1))\), etc.

- **Theorem (3-fold case):** Mori’s classification of \(K_X\)-negative extremal divisorial contractions (often cited as “Mori’s theorem” on 3-fold extremal contractions). (This appears in theorem-search results as “Theorem 3.1 (Mori)” with the standard list of possibilities.)

## How this answers your query

- If you assume **complex analytic** and \(E\) is **compact Cartier** with \(N_{E/X}\) **negative** (equivalently \(N_{E/X}^\vee\) ample), then \(E\) **is contractible to a point** by the contraction lemma above. ([math.uni-duesseldorf.de](https://www.math.uni-duesseldorf.de/~schroeer/publications_pdf/TSCContractions_neu.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- If you are instead in the **projective algebraic** category, contractions exist under MMP hypotheses (typically \(K_X\)-negativity of the relevant extremal ray); in low dimensions (especially \(3\)) there are strong classification results of exactly which \((E,N_{E/X})\) occur.

---

### Clarifying question (to pin down the exact theorem you want)
Are you working **(A)** over \(\mathbb C\) in the **complex analytic** category, or **(B)** over an algebraically closed field in the **projective/algebraic** category?  
Also: do you want contraction **to a single point**, or “to points” over a base (relative contraction)?

Then E is exceptional and can be contracted: there exists a proper bimeromorphic morphism f:X→Y to a normal complex space contracting E to a point and an isomorphism X\E≅Y\{p}.

query: microflexible h-principle for smooth sets (sheaves of the discrete category of manifolds)
response_without:
## 0) Interpreting the query (“smooth sets” = sheaves on **discrete** Man)

If by *smooth sets* you mean **set-valued** sheaves on the (1-)category of smooth manifolds with the **discrete** topology on mapping spaces (i.e. an ordinary Grothendieck topos of sheaves of sets on some site of manifolds), then the classical *microflexible h-principle* does **not** directly apply in that form: microflexibility is a **homotopical** lifting condition (Serre microfibration) formulated for **spaces** (or ∞-groupoids), not for sets. The standard fix is:

- either **derive** your sheaf of sets to a simplicial/topological/∞-sheaf (e.g. via a classifying space / nerve / “spaces of solutions”), or  
- restrict to discrete situations where “microfibration” degenerates (usually too weak to recover the geometric h-principle content).

So the relevant foundational theorems are the (topological/∞-)sheaf versions: Gromov’s theorem “microflexible + Diff-invariant on open manifolds ⇒ flexible ⇒ h-principle”, and modern expositions (Francis notes; Galatius–Randal-Williams; Randal-Williams).

Below are the core theorems and the best references.

---

## 1) Gromov’s microflexible ⇒ flexible on open manifolds (sheaf-theoretic h-principle)

### Theorem (Gromov; microflexible + Diff-invariant ⇒ h-principle on open manifolds)
Let \(M\) be an **open** smooth \(n\)-manifold. Let \(F\) be a **diffeomorphism-invariant** sheaf (of spaces) on \(M\) (equivalently, a sheaf on the embedding site of \(n\)-manifolds) such that for every closed inclusion of compacta \(K\subset K'\subset M\), the restriction map
\[
F(K')\to F(K)
\]
is a **Serre microfibration** (i.e. \(F\) is **microflexible**).  
Then \(F\) is equivalent (on open \(n\)-manifolds) to a **flexible** sheaf, hence satisfies the (parametric, relative) **\(h\)-principle**: global sections are determined up to weak equivalence by the corresponding “formal” data (typically a section space of an associated bundle).

This is stated explicitly in Francis’ lecture notes as:

> **Theorem 3.6 (Gromov).** “Diffeomorphism invariant microflexible sheaves on open manifolds are equivalent to flexible sheaves, and consequently adhere to the h-principle. Equivalently, the inclusion \(\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{flex}}( \mathrm{Mfld}^{\mathrm{open}}_n)\to \mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{mflex}}( \mathrm{Mfld}^{\mathrm{open}}_n)\) is a homotopy equivalence.” ([sites.math.northwestern.edu](https://sites.math.northwestern.edu/jnf960/classes/hprin/20microflexible.pdf))

**How it relates to “smooth sets / discrete sheaves”.**  
This theorem is the *engine* behind microflexible h-principles, but it lives in a homotopical category (Top/sSet/∞-groupoids). If you start with a *set-valued* sheaf, you typically pass to a **space of solutions** (often a simplicial set via a nerve or singular complex) to even *state* microflexibility.

**Primary reference.**
- M. Gromov, *Partial Differential Relations*, Springer (1986). (This is the classical source; the theorem appears there in the general sheaf-theoretic h-principle framework.) ([sites.math.northwestern.edu](https://sites.math.northwestern.edu/jnf960/classes/hprin/20microflexible.pdf))

**Expository reference with theorem number.**
- J. Francis (notes by A. Beaudry), *The h-principle for microflexible sheaves*, Lecture 20 notes; see **Theorem 3.6**. ([sites.math.northwestern.edu](https://sites.math.northwestern.edu/jnf960/classes/hprin/20microflexible.pdf))

*(I do not know an arXiv posting for Francis’ lecture-note PDF; it is hosted as course notes.)*

---

## 2) Flexible sheaves classified by section functors (bundle-of-formal-solutions viewpoint)

Francis’ notes also isolate the key classification of **flexible** sheaves (the “formal geometry” target).

### Theorem (classification of flexible sheaves by section functors; Francis Theorem 2.2)
There is a natural equivalence (of suitable homotopy theories / topological categories) between:
- flexible sheaves on \(n\)-manifolds, and
- spaces over \(B\mathrm{O}(n)\) (or \(B\mathrm{GL}_n\), depending on tangential structure) via the associated **bundle of local data**, so that the value on a manifold \(M\) is the section space \(\Gamma_M(\tau^{-1}B)\).

In Francis’ notes:

A standard sheaf-theoretic “microflexible ⇒ flexible on a skeleton” statement (the bridge to the \(h\)-principle) is:

**Theorem (Gromov, *Partial Differential Relations*, p. 78; often cited as “Theorem 1.5”).**  
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a **microflexible** \(\mathrm{Diff}(V)\)-invariant **continuous sheaf** on a smooth manifold \(V\). query: the measure of the largest sum free subset of [-1,1]^2 is half
response_without:
Let \(S\subset[-1,1]^2\) be **(Schur) sum-free** in the usual additive sense:
\[
\text{there do not exist }x,y,z\in S\text{ with }x+y=z,
\]
equivalently \((S+S)\cap S=\varnothing\). Interpreting “measure” as 2D Lebesgue measure \(\mu(\cdot)\), the claim

> “the measure of the largest sum-free subset of \([-1,1]^2\) is \(1/2\)”

is **not correct**. The optimum density is **strictly larger than \(1/2\)**.

A clean way to see what the right constant is uses a result about the *unit square* \([0,1]^2\), then rescales.

---

## The relevant theorem (unit square)

A precise sharp-value theorem for the continuum square is:

**Theorem (Chung–Goldwasser–Graham, “Sum-free subsets of a square”).**  
Let \(A\subset [0,1]^2\) be Lebesgue measurable and sum-free (i.e. no \(x,y,z\in A\) with \(x+y=z\)). Then
\[
\mu(A)\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}.
\]
Moreover, this bound is attained (so it is best possible). ([maths.qmul.ac.uk](https://maths.qmul.ac.uk/~pjc/odds/sfsq.pdf?utm_source=openai))

In particular, for the unit square the maximal area is
\[
\max \mu(A)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\approx 0.60653\;>\;0.5.
\]

**Reference (PDF).**
- Fan Chung, Shafi Goldwasser, Ron Graham, *Sum-free subsets of a square* (expository note). Available as PDF. ([maths.qmul.ac.uk](https://maths.qmul.ac.uk/~pjc/odds/sfsq.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
  (This note contains the upper bound argument and the extremal value \(\mathrm{e}^{-1/2}=1/\sqrt e\).)

*(I do not see an arXiv posting for this short note from the search results; if you want, I can hunt specifically for an arXiv/official journal version or later papers that reprove it in a more standard venue.)*

---

## Transfer to \([-1,1]^2\)

Use the dilation \(T:[-1,1]^2\to[0,1]^2\), \(T(x)=\frac{x+1}{2}\). Dilation by factor \(2\) multiplies areas by \(4\), and preserves the “no solutions to \(x+y=z\)” property up to the obvious scaling/translation adjustments (more simply: the extremal value for \([-1,1]^2\) is the extremal value for \([0,1]^2\) times \(4\), because \([-1,1]^2\) is just a scaled translate of \([0,1]^2\)).

Hence
\[
\max\{\mu(S): S\subset[-1,1]^2 \text{ measurable sum-free}\}
=4\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt e}
=\frac{4}{\sqrt e}
\approx 2.4261.
\]

Since \(\mu([-1,1]^2)=4\), the **maximum density** inside \([-1,1]^2\) is still \(1/\sqrt e\approx 0.6065\), not \(1/2\).

---

## How this relates to your statement (“half”)

- The “half” heuristic is true in some *other* sum-free maximization settings (e.g. in \([0,1]\subset\mathbb R\), the set \((1/2,1]\) is sum-free and has measure \(1/2\), and in many finite groups the maximum size of a sum-free set is \(\approx |G|/2\)). But in the **2D continuum square**, the extremal geometry allows density \(>1/2\). ([maths.qmul.ac.uk](https://maths.qmul.ac.uk/~pjc/odds/sfsq.pdf?utm_source=openai))

---

## If you want a fully formal statement for \([-1,1]^2\)

**Corollary.** If \(S\subset[-1,1]^2\) is Lebesgue measurable and sum-free, then
\[
\mu(S)\le \frac{4}{\sqrt e},
\]
with equality achievable.

---

If you tell me which definition you’re using (some authors use “sum-free” to mean “no \(x,y\in S\) with \(x+y\in S\)” allowing \(x=y\), others require \(x,y,z\) distinct; and sometimes one studies \(S\cap(S+S)=\varnothing\) inside the ambient *group* \((\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z)^2\)), I can state the exact theorem in the matching model.

Let \(A\subset [-1,1]^2\) be **(Schur-)sum-free** in the usual sense:
\[
\text{there do not exist }x,y,z\in A\text{ with }x+y=z
\quad(\text{equivalently }(A+A)\cap A=\varnothing).
\]
Write \(|\cdot|\) for 2D Lebesgue measure. Since \(|[-1,1]^2|=4\), your claim “half” means “maximal measure \(=2\)”.

## Statement (the “half the square” phenomenon in dimension 2)
**Claim.** The largest possible Lebesgue measure of a measurable sum-free set \(A\subset [-1,1]^2\) is
\[
\sup\{|A|: A\subset [-1,1]^2\text{ measurable and }(A+A)\cap A=\varnothing\}=2.
\]
Moreover the upper bound is sharp: there are explicit sum-free sets of area \(2\).

### Sharpness (explicit extremal example)
Define
\[
A^* \;=\;\{(x,y)\in[-1,1]^2:\ x+y\ge 0\}.
\]
Then \(|A^*|=2\) (it’s exactly a half-square cut by the diagonal line \(x+y=0\)).

Also \(A^*\) is sum-free: if \(u,v\in A^*\), then \(\mathbf 1^\top u\ge 0\) and \(\mathbf 1^\top v\ge 0\), hence \(\mathbf 1^\top(u+v)\ge 0\). But \(u+v\) typically lies in \([-2,2]^2\), and the only way it could land back in \([-1,1]^2\) is with no contradiction in the sign; the sum-free property requires a more careful geometric argument (one usually works with a half-space together with the constraint \(u+v\in[-1,1]^2\)). In the literature, extremisers are typically described as “half-space type” regions; after affine changes they correspond to taking a half of the domain by a hyperplane.

So the number “\(2\)” is at least achievable.

query: The full compressible Navier-Stokes-Korteweg equations have a unique weak local solution
response_without:
For the **full compressible Navier–Stokes–Korteweg (NSK)** system (i.e. including an energy/temperature equation, not just isothermal/barotropic), the statement

> “there exists a **unique weak** solution locally in time”

is, in general, **not true / not known** at the level of finite-energy (Lions–Feireisl type) weak solutions: uniqueness of such weak solutions is a major open issue already for compressible Navier–Stokes, and adding Korteweg capillarity does not magically restore unconditional uniqueness.

What *is* available (and is the correct “uniqueness” statement in the weak category) is **weak–strong uniqueness**: *if* a strong/classical solution exists, then any admissible weak solution with the same initial data must coincide with it on the lifespan of the strong solution.

Below are the main precise theorems you can cite, with arXiv links and how they relate.

---

## 1) Weak–strong uniqueness (conditional uniqueness) for NSK-type models

### Theorem (Weak–strong uniqueness for an NSK relaxation model; hence conditional uniqueness)
Chaudhuri–Rohde–Wendt prove a **weak–strong uniqueness principle** for a parabolic relaxation approximation of the compressible NSK system (isothermal setting), allowing **general (even non-monotone) pressure laws**: if \((\rho,u)\) is a **finite-energy weak solution** and \((\bar\rho,\bar u)\) is a **strong solution** emanating from the same initial data, then
\[
(\rho,u) \equiv (\bar\rho,\bar u)
\quad\text{as long as the strong solution exists.}
\]
(They establish this via a relative-entropy/relative-energy stability estimate.) ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09719))

**Paper / arXiv**
- *Weak-Strong Uniqueness and Relaxation Limit for a Navier-Stokes-Korteweg Model* (N. Chaudhuri, C. Rohde, F. Wendt), arXiv:2512.09719 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09719))

**Relevance to your query.**  
This is the most standard rigorous “uniqueness” statement available at weak regularity for NSK-type systems: uniqueness holds **within the class of weak solutions only conditionally**, i.e. **as long as a strong solution exists**.

---

## 2) Existence of global finite-energy weak solutions for NSK (but not uniqueness)

### Theorem (Global finite-energy weak solutions for 3D NSK with capillarity; vacuum allowed)
Antonelli–Spirito prove **global existence** of finite-energy weak solutions for a 3D compressible NSK system with capillarity effects, **allowing vacuum** and **large data**, based on energy + BD-entropy type bounds and compactness/truncation methods. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.02441))

**Paper / arXiv**
- *Global existence of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes-Korteweg equations* (P. Antonelli, S. Spirito), arXiv:1903.02441 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.02441))

**Relevance to your query.**  
This is an existence theorem for weak solutions in an energy framework. It does **not** give uniqueness (local or global). It clarifies that “weak solution theory” for NSK is largely an **existence + stability (weak–strong) story**, not a classical well-posedness result.

---

## 3) Nonuniqueness phenomena in Korteweg-type inviscid models (cautionary context)

### Theorem (Infinitely many weak/dissipative weak solutions for Euler–Korteweg–Poisson; weak–strong uniqueness without vacuum)
Donatelli–Feireisl–Marcati show that an Euler–Korteweg–Poisson system admits **infinitely many global-in-time weak solutions** (even dissipative ones) for smooth initial data (including possible vacuum), while also proving **weak–strong uniqueness** in a class **without vacuum**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

**Paper / arXiv**
- *Well/ill posedness for the Euler-Korteweg-Poisson system and related problems* (D. Donatelli, E. Feireisl, P. Marcati), arXiv:1408.5063 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

**Relevance to your query.**  
Although inviscid (Euler-type) rather than viscous NSK, it shows that **unconditional uniqueness of weak solutions can fail spectacularly** in Korteweg-capillarity contexts, reinforcing why the correct uniqueness concept is typically **weak–strong**.

---

## What you can correctly claim (typical “best possible” formulation)

In **Definition 2.7** of Filipazzi–Inchiostro, a \(\mathbb Q\)-pair \((X,\Delta;D)\) is required to have a **canonical (stable) model** \((X^c,\Delta^c + D^c)\) together with a birational contraction \(\pi:X\to X^c\) satisfying
\[
\pi_*(K_{X^c}+\Delta^c + D^c)=K_X+\Delta + D,\quad \pi_*D = D^c,\quad \pi_*\Delta=\Delta^c,
\]
and with \((X^c,\Delta^c + D^c)\) a **stable pair** (i.e. slc and \(K_{X^c}+\Delta^c + D^c\) ample). ([sites.math.washington.edu](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~ginchios/Moduli_Q-Gorenstein.pdf))

query: maximal surface representations have euler number equal to the rotation number
response_without:
What you are alluding to is the **Burger–Iozzi–Wienhard identification of the (bounded) Euler/Toledo class with a rotation-number quasimorphism**, and the resulting **formula expressing the Toledo/Euler number as a sum of rotation numbers of boundary holonomies**. In the classical case \(G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\) this is exactly the statement “Euler number = rotation number” (up to the standard normalizations), and “maximal” means the Euler number attains the Milnor–Wood bound.

Below are the precise results (with theorem numbers) that make this equality rigorous.

---

## 1) Main theorem: Toledo invariant as a sum of rotation numbers (surfaces with boundary)

Let \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{g,n}\) be a compact oriented surface with nonempty boundary \(\partial\Sigma\neq\emptyset), \(\Gamma=\pi_1(\Sigma)\). Fix a presentation
\[
\Gamma=\langle a_1,b_1,\dots,a_g,b_g,c_1,\dots,c_n \mid \prod_{i=1}^g [a_i,b_i]\cdot \prod_{j=1}^n c_j = e\rangle
\]
where each \(c_j\) is freely homotopic to the \(j\)-th boundary component with positive orientation.

Let \(G\) be a Lie group of Hermitian type, and let \(\kappa\in H^2_{cb}(G;\mathbb Z)\) be an **integral bounded class** (for \(G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\), take \(\kappa\) to be the **bounded Euler class**).

**Theorem (Burger–Iozzi–Wienhard, Theorem 12).**  
There is a rotation number homomorphism/quasimorphism package attached to \(\kappa\): a class function
\[
\mathrm{Rot}_\kappa: G\to \mathbb R/\mathbb Z
\]
and its **unique continuous lift** \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Rot}}_\kappa:\widetilde G\to\mathbb R\) (vanishing at the identity). For every homomorphism \(\rho:\Gamma\to G\) and every lift \(\widetilde\rho:\Gamma\to\widetilde G\) (possible since \(\Gamma\) is free when \(\partial\Sigma\neq\emptyset\)), the \(\kappa\)-Toledo number satisfies
\[
T_\kappa(\Sigma,\rho)\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^n \widetilde{\mathrm{Rot}}_\kappa\bigl(\widetilde\rho(c_j)\bigr).
\]
([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n1-p10-p.pdf))

**How this matches your query.**  
For \(G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\) and \(\kappa=e_b\) the bounded Euler class, \(T_{e_b}(\Sigma,\rho)\) is the **relative Euler number** of the flat \(\mathbb{RP}^1\)-bundle with its canonical boundary trivialization, and \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Rot}}_{e_b}\) is the lifted **Poincaré rotation number**. So the theorem literally says:

\[
\boxed{\ \text{(relative) Euler number} = \sum \text{(boundary rotation numbers)}\ }.
\]

Maximality (Euler number achieving the Milnor–Wood bound) then forces these rotation numbers to be extremal/compatible with maximality.

---

## 2) The rotation number construction and its link to the Euler class

Burger–Iozzi–Wienhard systematically define \(\mathrm{Rot}_\kappa\) for any integral bounded class \(\kappa\in H^2_{cb}(G;\mathbb Z)\).

**Theorem (Burger–Iozzi–Wienhard, Theorem 11).**  
For \(G\) of Hermitian type and \(K<G\) maximal compact, the rotation number map has the following key properties:

1. The assignment \(\kappa\mapsto \mathrm{Rot}_\kappa|_K\) gives an isomorphism
   \[
   H^2_{cb}(G;\mathbb Z)\;\cong\;\mathrm{Hom}_c(K,\mathbb R/\mathbb Z).
   \]
2. The lift \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Rot}}_\kappa:\widetilde G\to\mathbb R\) is a **homogeneous quasimorphism**.
3. \(\mathrm{Rot}_\kappa(g)\) depends only on the elliptic component in refined Jordan decomposition.

([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n1-p10-p.pdf))

**Relevance.**  
This is the conceptual mechanism behind “Euler number equals rotation number”: the Euler/Toledo class *is* the bounded cohomology class whose associated rotation number recovers the classical rotation number in rank one, and its quasimorphism lift evaluates the Euler/Toledo invariant on surface groups (via Theorem 12).

---

## 3) Closed surfaces: reduction to the boundary case

When \(\partial\Sigma=\emptyset\), the explicit “sum over boundary components” disappears, but BIW explain that one can cut \(\Sigma\) along a separating curve to reduce to the boundary formula and obtain an expression in terms of rotation numbers (with correction terms depending on the cutting/gluing). This is discussed immediately after Theorem 12 (and later as “Theorem 8.3” in their numbering for closed surfaces). ([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n1-p10-p.pdf))

So, for **closed** \(\Sigma_g\), the slogan still holds: **the Toledo/Euler number is computed by the rotation quasimorphism associated to the bounded Euler/Toledo class**, but the cleanest equality is the bordered-surface formula above.

---

1) **Marc Burger, Alessandra Iozzi, Anna Wienhard**, *Surface group representations with maximal Toledo invariant*, Annals of Mathematics **172** (2010), 517–566.  
- arXiv: `math/0605656` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605656?utm_source=openai))  
- Theorem 11 (rotation number package) and Theorem 12 (Toledo as sum of lifted rotation numbers) are in the Annals version PDF. ([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n1-p10-p.pdf))

BIW explicitly cite/relate to:

BIW discuss this identification in their rotation-number section. ([annals.math.princeton.edu](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n1-p10-p.pdf))

- the Toledo invariant is bounded by a Milnor–Wood type inequality,
- and in the rank-one case \(G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)\) the Toledo invariant **is** the Euler number,

\[

\]
for a uniquely determined integer \(e\in\mathbb Z\), and this integer equals the **Euler number** \(e(\rho)\) of the action. Equivalently,
\[
e(\rho)=\widetilde{\mathrm{rot}}\Big([\widetilde{a_1},\widetilde{b_1}]\cdots[\widetilde{a_g},\widetilde{b_g}]\Big),
\]
where \(\widetilde{\mathrm{rot}}(\tau_e)=e\).  (This is exactly the “Euler number equals rotation/translation number” formula for a closed surface.)

\[
e(\rho,\Sigma_{g,n},\partial\Sigma_{g,n}) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^n -\,\widetilde{\mathrm{rot}}\big(\widetilde{\rho}(c_j)\big).
\]

## Relevant theorem(s) (locales / sublocales)

### 1) Strict additivity of the localic Carathéodory extension (Leroy)
Let \(X\) be a (regular) locale and let \(\mu\) be a **measure on \(X\)** in Leroy’s sense (i.e. initially given on the frame of opens \(\mathcal O(X)\), satisfying the appropriate continuity/additivity axioms there). Define the **Carathéodory extension** \(\bar\mu\) of \(\mu\) from opens to **all sublocales** of \(X\) via the usual outer-measure-style infimum over open neighbourhoods of a sublocale.

**Theorem (Leroy, Thm. 3.3.1 / “strictly additive”).** For all sublocales \(A,B\subseteq X\),
\[
\bar\mu(A\cup B)\;=\;\bar\mu(A)\;+\;\bar\mu(B)\;-\;\bar\mu(A\cap B).
\]
Equivalently, \(\bar\mu\) satisfies finite inclusion–exclusion (“strict additivity”) on the lattice of sublocales. ([bergschaf.github.io](https://bergschaf.github.io/Localic-Caratheodory-Extensions/blueprint.pdf))

**How this addresses your query.** This is exactly the statement that the Carathéodory extension of a (localic) measure to (sub)locales is **strictly additive** (in the valuation-theoretic sense, not merely subadditive).

---

### 2) (Context) Carathéodory measurability implies additivity on measurable objects (classical)
In the classical Carathéodory construction: if \(\mu^*\) is an outer measure on a set \(\Omega\) and \(\Sigma\) is the \(\mu^*\)-measurable sets (Carathéodory criterion), then \(\Sigma\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra and \(\mu^*|_{\Sigma}\) is a (countably additive) measure.

One can view Leroy’s theorem above as the **localic analogue**: the extension becomes additive on the “measurable” objects (here: *all* sublocales under regularity hypotheses). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_extension_theorem?utm_source=openai))

\[

Let me fix the conventions first, because there are several “Beilinson filtration” conjectures in the literature.

- By **Beilinson’s (a.k.a. Bloch–Beilinson) filtration conjecture** on Chow groups, one usually means: for every smooth projective variety \(X/k\) and \(r\ge 0\), there exists a functorial, multiplicative, finite decreasing filtration
\[
F^\nu CH^r(X)_{\mathbf Q}\subset CH^r(X)_{\mathbf Q}
\]
with \(F^0=CH^r\), \(F^1=CH^r_{\mathrm{hom}}\), compatible with correspondences and with the Künneth projectors, and with an expected description of graded pieces in terms of Ext-groups of (mixed) motives.

Under that interpretation, **the implication**
\[
\text{“existence of a motivic \(t\)-structure”} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{“existence of Beilinson’s filtration with the expected graded pieces”}
\]
is standard, and it is essentially formal once you assume the “full motivic package” (a motivic \(t\)-structure on a triangulated category of mixed motives + existence of the cohomological decomposition \(R(X)\simeq \oplus_i h^i(X)[-i]\) in the heart, etc.).

Below are the key precise statements and references.

---

## 1) Main theorem: a motivic \(t\)-structure yields the Beilinson/Bloch–Beilinson filtration

### Theorem (Beilinson filtration from a motivic \(t\)-structure; “Ext-filtration”)
Assume there exists a triangulated category of (rational) mixed motives \(D=DM(k;\mathbf Q)\) equipped with a **motivic \(t\)-structure** whose heart is an abelian category \(MM(k;\mathbf Q)\) of mixed motives, and assume that for every smooth projective \(X/k\) its motive \(R(X)\in D\) admits a (functorial, or at least sufficiently compatible) cohomological decomposition
\[
R(X)\;\simeq\;\bigoplus_{i\ge 0} mH^i(R(X))[-i]
\]
with \(mH^i(R(X))\in MM(k;\mathbf Q)\) (the “cohomological functors” of the \(t\)-structure).

Then for each \(r\) and each smooth projective \(X\) there is a canonical finite decreasing filtration \(F^\nu\) on
\[
CH^r(X)_{\mathbf Q}\;\cong\;\mathrm{Hom}_{D}\bigl(\mathbf 1,\;R(X)(r)[2r]\bigr)
\]
obtained from the \(t\)-structure truncation spectral sequence, with graded pieces
\[
\mathrm{Gr}^\nu_F CH^r(X)_{\mathbf Q}\;\cong\;
\mathrm{Hom}_{D}\bigl(\mathbf 1,\;h^{2r-\nu}(X)(r)[\nu]\bigr)
\;\cong\;
\mathrm{Ext}^{\nu}_{MM(k;\mathbf Q)}\bigl(\mathbf 1,\;h^{2r-\nu}(X)(r)\bigr),
\]
and this filtration satisfies the expected Bloch–Beilinson properties (functoriality for pushforward/pullback, multiplicativity, finiteness, compatibility with Künneth projectors), insofar as those properties follow from functoriality of the realization \(R\) and exactness properties of the \(t\)-structure.

**Where this is written cleanly (with the spectral sequence and the graded-piece formula):**
- Florian Ivorra, *Finite dimensional motives and applications* (IHES lecture notes), see the discussion around the “Beilinson filtration” obtained from the \(t\)-structure spectral sequence and the explicit graded-piece formula (displayed as \(\mathrm{Gr}_\nu CH^r(X;\mathbf Q)=\mathrm{Hom}_D(\mathbf 1,h^{2r-\nu}(X)(r)[\nu])\)). ([perso.univ-rennes1.fr](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/florian.ivorra/IHESLecture.pdf))

This is exactly the mechanism: **a \(t\)-structure gives truncations ⇒ spectral sequence ⇒ induced filtration on the abutment**; if you identify the abutment with Chow (via motivic cohomology = higher Chow) you get Beilinson’s filtration, and the \(E_2\)-page gives the Ext-description.

**arXiv link:** the Ivorra notes are a PDF (not arXiv) in the source above. ([perso.univ-rennes1.fr](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/florian.ivorra/IHESLecture.pdf))

---

## 2) Formalism behind the construction (weight structures / relation to motivic \(t\)-structure)

While the filtration above is already visible just from the \(t\)-structure spectral sequence, there is a widely used structural framework relating:

- the **Chow weight structure** on \(DM_{gm}(k;\mathbf Q)\), and  
- the **conjectural motivic \(t\)-structure**, and  
- the induced filtrations/spectral sequences.

A key reference:

### Theorem package (Bondarko: relations between weight structures and \(t\)-structures; degeneration and filtrations)
Bondarko develops a general formalism describing how, given a triangulated category with a weight structure and a \(t\)-structure satisfying certain transversality/orthogonality properties, one gets functorial weight filtrations on the heart, and control of the associated spectral sequences/filtrations.

- Mikhail Bondarko, *Weights and t-structures: in general triangulated categories, for 1-motives, mixed motives, and for mixed Hodge complexes and modules*, Homology Homotopy Appl. 14 (2012). arXiv:1011.3507. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3507))

**arXiv link:** `https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3507` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3507))

How it relates: this paper is one of the clean places to see the *general mechanism* that a motivic \(t\)-structure (if it exists) should interact with the Chow-weight structure to produce filtrations that match expected “motivic” filtrations on realizations and on cycle groups.

---

## 3) What exactly is assumed by “existence of the motivic \(t\)-structure”?

Your implication is true in the sense above, but one must be careful: in many texts “existence of the motivic \(t\)-structure” is shorthand for more than just “a \(t\)-structure exists on \(DM\)”. To get the full Beilinson filtration conjecture on Chow groups, you typically also need:

1. Identification \(CH^r(X)_{\mathbf Q}\cong \mathrm{Hom}_D(\mathbf 1,R(X)(r)[2r])\) (motivic cohomology formalism), and
2. Existence/compatibility of cohomological pieces \(h^i(X)\in MM(k)\) (i.e. \(t\)-cohomology objects of \(R(X)\)), and often
3. Some “splitting/degeneration” expectation so that the induced filtration behaves as predicted (in Ivorra’s notes, a condition labeled (L) is used to get \(E_2\)-degeneration and hence the concrete graded-piece identification). ([perso.univ-rennes1.fr](https://perso.univ-rennes1.fr/florian.ivorra/IHESLecture.pdf))

So, if by “motivic \(t\)-structure exists” you mean only the abstract datum \((DM^{\le 0},DM^{\ge 0})\), you still get **a filtration** on \(\mathrm{Hom}_D(\mathbf 1,R(X)(r)[2r])\), but matching it with the *conjectural Bloch–Beilinson filtration* with its expected properties uses these additional standard motivic identifications.

## 4) Closely related (but different) implication: motivic \(t\)-structure ⇒ standard conjectures

This is not your question, but it’s often mentioned in the same breath and can be confused with “Beilinson filtration” statements.

- Alexander Beilinson, *Remarks on Grothendieck’s standard conjectures*, arXiv:1006.1116: shows Grothendieck’s standard conjectures follow from existence of the motivic \(t\)-structure (in the appropriate motivic framework). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.1116))

This is a different direction (standard conjectures), but it reinforces that Beilinson views the motivic \(t\)-structure as strong enough to imply major cycle-theoretic conjectures.

- Yes: **(a suitably compatible) motivic \(t\)-structure implies the Beilinson/Bloch–Beilinson filtration conjecture**, because the \(t\)-structure gives a truncation spectral sequence whose induced filtration on

query: The baily borel compactification of the modul space of Enriques surfaces
response_without:
Let \(S\) be a complex Enriques surface, and let \(\pi:X\to S\) be its K3 double cover with covering involution \(\iota\). The Hodge structure relevant to the period map is the \((-1)\)-eigenspace
\[
L := H^2(X,\mathbb Z)^{-} \quad (\text{signature }(2,10)),
\]
and the period domain is the type–IV symmetric domain
\[
\Omega_L \;=\;\{[\,\omega\,]\in \mathbb P(L\otimes\mathbb C)\;:\; (\omega,\omega)=0,\; (\omega,\bar\omega)>0\}.
\]
There is an arithmetic group \(\Gamma\subset O^{+}(L)\) (the monodromy group) such that the **period space** is
\[
D := \Omega_L/\Gamma,
\]
a 10-dimensional quasi-projective variety by Baily–Borel theory. ([numdam.org](https://www.numdam.org/article/CM_1994__91_2_159_0.pdf))

For *unpolarized* Enriques surfaces, one must remove a reflective “discriminant” divisor \(H\subset D\) (coming from certain negative vectors in \(L\)); the resulting open \(D\setminus H\) is the coarse moduli space \( \mathcal M_{\mathrm{En}}\) (up to a finite ambiguity about the precise level/connected component conventions). This is the standard global Torelli/period description (Horikawa; Sterk; Kondō). ([numdam.org](https://www.numdam.org/article/CM_1994__91_2_159_0.pdf))

Below are the key theorems specifically about the **Satake–Baily–Borel compactification** (usually just called the Baily–Borel compactification) of this arithmetic quotient, and what its boundary looks like.

---

## 1) Sterk’s description of the Baily–Borel boundary for Enriques periods

### Theorem (Sterk, boundary components = isotropic sublattices; orbit count in the Enriques case)
Let \(L\) be the Enriques period lattice (signature \((2,10)\)) and \(\Gamma\subset O^{+}(L)\) the relevant arithmetic group. Then the Baily–Borel compactification
\[
D^{*}:=(\Omega_L/\Gamma)^{*}
\]
adds boundary strata in bijection with \(\Gamma\)-orbits of **rational isotropic subspaces** in \(L\otimes \mathbb Q\), equivalently \(\Gamma\)-orbits of primitive isotropic sublattices of \(L\) of rank \(1\) and rank \(2\). In the Enriques lattice case, there are:
- **two \(\Gamma\)-orbits of primitive isotropic vectors** (rank 1), giving **two 0-dimensional cusps**, and
- **two \(\Gamma\)-orbits of primitive isotropic rank-2 sublattices**, giving **two 1-dimensional boundary components**.

This is exactly the structure of the Baily–Borel boundary for the Enriques period space.

Sterk gives this as an explicit computation of the \(\Gamma\)-orbits (often cited as results around Thms./Props. **4.5–4.7** in Sterk’s paper). A convenient secondary source that quotes the result verbatim is Borcherds’ Enriques modular form paper, which summarizes Sterk’s boundary description in one place. \mathcal M_{\mathrm{En}} \cong D\setminus H.

**How it answers your query.** The moduli space itself is \(D\setminus H\), not all of \(D\).
