query: Solutions of singular linear systems  in term of adjugate matrix gate
response_without:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\) be **singular** and consider the linear system
\[
Ax=b.
\]
You asked for solutions “in terms of the adjugate matrix” \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\). The key point is that the adjugate still satisfies \(A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)\,A=(\det A)I\), hence **equals 0** when \(\det A=0\); nevertheless, when \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n-1\) the adjugate is rank-one and gives a very explicit description of solvability and solutions.

---

## 1) Core identities (hold even when \(A\) is singular)

### Theorem (Adjugate identity)
For every \(A\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\),
\[
A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)\,A=(\det A)I_n.
\]
In particular, if \(\det A=0\) then
\[
A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=0,\qquad \operatorname{adj}(A)\,A=0.
\]
This implies:
- every column of \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) lies in \(\ker(A)\);
- every row of \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) lies in \(\ker(A^\top)\).

(These are standard determinant/cofactor facts; see any linear algebra text; also summarized in the “Adjugate matrix” entry ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjugate_matrix?utm_source=openai)).)

---

## 2) The rank-\(n-1\) (corank 1) case: adjugate gives solvability and a solution

From here on assume
\[
\rank(A)=n-1.
\]

### Theorem (Structure of \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) when \(\rank(A)=n-1\))
If \(\rank(A)=n-1\), then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\neq 0\) and
\[
\rank(\operatorname{adj}(A))=1,
\]
so \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=u v^\top\) for some nonzero vectors \(u,v\), with
\[
Au=0,\qquad A^\top v=0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{adj}(A))=\ker(A),\qquad \ker(\operatorname{adj}(A))=\operatorname{im}(A).
\]
A clean statement of \(\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{adj}(A))=\ker(A)\) for \(\rank(A)=n-1\) appears in the MathOverflow/StackExchange literature (with proofs using multilinear determinants). ([math.stackexchange.com](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4857171/adjugate-of-rank-n-1-matrix?utm_source=openai))  
(Also, the rank-one fact is summarized in standard references and expository notes. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjugate_matrix?utm_source=openai)))

### Theorem (Adjugate solvability test for \(\rank(A)=n-1\))
Assume \(\rank(A)=n-1\). Then the system \(Ax=b\) is solvable **iff**
\[
\operatorname{adj}(A)\,b=0.
\]

**Reason:** \(\ker(\operatorname{adj}(A))=\operatorname{im}(A)\). So \(b\in\operatorname{im}(A)\) (i.e. solvable) iff \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b=0\).

This is just the rank-\(n-1\) specialization of the general rank criterion for solvability (Rouché–Capelli), but now written using \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouch%C3%A9%E2%80%93Capelli_theorem?utm_source=openai))

### Theorem (Adjugate produces a particular solution after a rank-1 normalization)
Assume \(\rank(A)=n-1\) and \(Ax=b\) is solvable. Pick any \(y\in\mathbb{F}^n\) such that
\[
y^\top \operatorname{adj}(A)\, b \neq 0
\]
for the *modified* right-hand side below (see next line). Define a rank-1 “fix”
\[
\widetilde A := A + b y^\top.
\]
Then \(\widetilde A\) is invertible for a generic choice of \(y\), and one can recover a particular solution by solving \(\widetilde A x = b\). Moreover, \(\widetilde A^{-1}\) can be expressed using adjugates:
\[
\widetilde A^{-1}=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(\widetilde A)}{\det(\widetilde A)}.
\]
This is a common way adjugates enter singular systems: you perturb to invertible (rank-1 update) and then use adjugate/inverse formulas (cf. rank-1 update literature such as Sherman–Morrison-type ideas; adjugate itself is classical). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman%E2%80%93Morrison_formula?utm_source=openai))

(If you want, I can give a more direct “closed form” solution using left/right nullvectors \(v,u\) with \(A^\top v=0\), \(Au=0\), which is often the cleanest in corank 1; it is equivalent to the rank-one factorization \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=c\,u v^\top\).)

---

## 3) What if \(\rank(A)\le n-2\)? (Adjugate becomes zero)

### Theorem (Adjugate vanishes for rank \(\le n-2\))
If \(\rank(A)\le n-2\), then every \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) minor is zero, hence
\[
\operatorname{adj}(A)=0.
\]
So the adjugate contains **no information** about solvability/solutions in that case (you must use ranks, generalized inverses, etc.). ([nhigham.com](https://nhigham.com/2020/06/16/what-is-the-adjugate-of-a-matrix/?utm_source=openai))

---

## 4) “Generalized Cramer rules” (when you really want determinantal formulas)

For singular (or rectangular) systems people replace \(A^{-1}\) by a generalized inverse (Moore–Penrose, Drazin, etc.) and then derive determinantal/adjugate-like expressions.

### Relevant paper (determinantal/adjugate analogues for generalized inverses)
- **“Analogues of the adjoint matrix for generalized inverses and corresponding Cramer rules”** (arXiv:1004.4761). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.4761?utm_source=openai))

### Relevant paper (Cramer rules for generalized inverse solutions)
- **“Cramer’s Rule for Generalized Inverse Solutions of Some Matrices Equations”** (arXiv:1503.06997). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.06997?utm_source=openai))

These develop formulas that *look like* \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b/\det(A)\) but remain meaningful when \(\det(A)=0\), by using minors/determinants associated with the chosen generalized inverse.

---

## Clarifying question (so I can give the exact formula you need)
Do you mean the **special corank-1 case** \(\rank(A)=n-1\), or the **general singular case** \(\rank(A)\le n-2\)?  

- If \(\rank(A)=n-1\): I can give a fully explicit solution parametrization using \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) (via its rank-one factorization) and state it as “all solutions = particular + \(\ker(A)\)”.  
- If \(\rank(A)\le n-2\): then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=0\), and you likely want a generalized-inverse Cramer rule (arXiv papers above).

Let \(A\in \Bbb F^{n\times n}\) be **singular** and consider the linear system
\[
A x=b .
\]
The adjugate (classical adjoint) \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) still satisfies the fundamental identity
\[
A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)\,A=\det(A)\,I=0 .
\]
So \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b\in \ker(A)\) for every \(b\). The key point is that for a *generic* singular matrix (rank \(n-1\)) the adjugate has rank \(1\) and encodes the unique left/right null vectors; this gives a clean solvability test and a “Cramer-like” description.

## 1) Rank \(n-1\) (nullity \(1\)): solvability and adjugate structure

### Theorem (Adjugate is rank one and equals an outer product)
If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n-1\), let \(v\neq 0\) span \(\ker(A)\) and let \(u\neq 0\) span \(\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\) (the left nullspace). Then
\[
\operatorname{adj}(A)=c\, v u^{\mathsf T}
\]
for some nonzero scalar \(c\). In particular, \(\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{adj}(A))=1\). (If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\le n-2\) then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=0\).)

This is stated, for example, as:

- **Lemma 4.3**: \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=c\, v u^{\mathsf T}\) when \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n-1\), and \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=0\) when \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<n-1\).  
  Paper: *[look up from arXiv via the lemma below]* (see theorem_search result “Lemma 4.3” above).
- **Lemma A.2** (same content).  
- Also appears as **Lemma 6.12** with an added solvability criterion below.

(These are standard linear algebra facts; the theorem_search results above pinpoint them as numbered lemmas inside specific arXiv papers.)

### Theorem (Fredholm alternative in finite dimensions; solvability test)
Assume \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n-1\) and let \(u\) span \(\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\). Then
\[
Ax=b \text{ is solvable } \Longleftrightarrow u^{\mathsf T}b=0.
\]
This appears explicitly as **Lemma 6.12(i)** in the theorem_search results.

### Consequence: what \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b\) tells you
Using \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=cvu^{\mathsf T}\),
\[
\operatorname{adj}(A)b = c\, v\, (u^{\mathsf T}b).
\]
So:

- If \(u^{\mathsf T}b\ne 0\) (inconsistent case), then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b\) is a **nonzero** multiple of the right nullvector \(v\).
- If \(u^{\mathsf T}b=0\) (consistent case), then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b=0\).

Equivalently, for rank \(n-1\),
\[
Ax=b \text{ solvable } \Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{adj}(A)b=0.
\]
(because \(c\neq 0\) and \(v\neq 0\).)

## 2) Can you write a solution \(x\) “in terms of \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\)”?

For \(\det(A)\neq 0\), Cramer gives \(x=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)b\).  
For \(\det(A)=0\), there is **no** formula of that form in general, because \(\operatorname{adj}(A)b\in\ker(A)\) and therefore cannot equal a typical particular solution.

What you *can* do (still rank \(n-1\)):

### (a) Parametrize all solutions once one particular solution is known
If \(Ax=b\) is solvable and \(x_0\) is one solution, then all solutions are
\[
x = x_0 + t\,v,\qquad t\in\Bbb F,
\]
where \(v\) spans \(\ker(A)\). Since \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=c v u^{\mathsf T}\), **any nonzero column of \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\)** is a multiple of \(v\), so you can extract \(v\) directly from \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\).

### (b) Determinantal (Cramer-type) formulas for *components* exist under extra normalization
One common approach: replace one equation by a normalization (e.g. enforce \(u^{\mathsf T}x=0\) or fix one coordinate), forming an \((n\times n)\) nonsingular augmented system; then Cramer’s rule applies. Then \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=0\) (see Lemma 4.3 / Proposition 8.4 in the theorem_search results). In that case \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) contains **no information** about solvability of \(Ax=b\); you must use other rank/compatibility conditions.

query: the solutions to the system of quantum hydrodynamics are unique
response_without:
Uniqueness for “the quantum hydrodynamics (QHD) system” is **not true in general**: there are **published non-uniqueness** results for natural notions of weak solution, but there are also **conditional uniqueness** results (typically *weak–strong uniqueness* in regimes excluding vacuum, or uniqueness in special 1D stationary/subsonic settings, etc.). What is true depends strongly on:

- which QHD model (inviscid Euler–Korteweg/QHD vs viscous quantum Navier–Stokes/QNS, with/without Poisson, etc.),
- the solution concept (distributional weak, dissipative weak, measure-valued, strong/classical),
- and whether vacuum (ρ=0) is allowed.

Below are the most relevant theorems and references.

---

## 1) Non-uniqueness of weak solutions for (inviscid) QHD

### Theorem (Markowich–Sierra: non-uniqueness of weak QHD solutions)
They show that **weak solutions of the QHD system are not unique** in general, with non-uniqueness tied to changes in the topology (number of connected components) of the support of the density (“nodal domains”) over time. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04161))

- **Paper:** *Non-Uniqueness of Weak Solutions of the Quantum-Hydrodynamic System*  
  **Authors:** Peter A. Markowich, Jesus Sierra  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:1805.04161` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04161))  
  (Journal version: *Kinetic & Related Models* 12 (2019), no. 2, 347–356. ([aimsciences.org](https://www.aimsciences.org/article/doi/10.3934/krm.2019015?utm_source=openai)))

**How this relates to your query.** If your claim is “solutions to the QHD system are unique,” it is **false** at least for the standard weak-solution framework addressed in this work.

---

## 2) Infinitely many global weak solutions (ill-posedness) for Euler–Korteweg–Poisson (includes QHD as a special case)

### Theorem (Donatelli–Feireisl–Marcati: infinitely many global weak solutions)
For a broad Euler–Korteweg–Poisson class (containing QHD), they prove **existence of infinitely many global-in-time weak solutions** for smooth initial data, including cases with vacuum, via convex integration–type ideas. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

- **Paper:** *Well/ill posedness for the Euler-Korteweg-Poisson system and related problems*  
  **Authors:** Donatella Donatelli, Eduard Feireisl, Pierangelo Marcati  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:1408.5063` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))  
  (Also appears in *Communications in Partial Differential Equations*; see journal listing. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03605302.2014.972517?utm_source=openai)))

**How this relates.** This gives a very strong negative answer to “are solutions unique?” for the inviscid capillarity/QHD-type models at the weak level: **non-uniqueness can be massive (infinitely many solutions)**.

---

## 3) Weak–strong uniqueness (conditional uniqueness) for QHD/Euler–Korteweg-type systems

A standard “best-possible” uniqueness statement in compressible fluid PDE is:

> If a strong (smooth) solution exists, then any admissible weak solution with the same initial data must coincide with it (on the lifespan of the strong solution).

This does **not** give uniqueness among all weak solutions, but it gives uniqueness in the presence of a strong solution.

### Theorem (Donatelli–Feireisl–Marcati: weak–strong uniqueness without vacuum)
In `arXiv:1408.5063`, after establishing ill-posedness for weak solutions, they also prove a **weak–strong uniqueness principle in a class excluding vacuum**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

- **Paper:** *Well/ill posedness for the Euler-Korteweg-Poisson system and related problems*  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:1408.5063` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

### Theorem (Giesselmann–Lattanzio–Tzavaras: relative energy identity ⇒ weak–strong uniqueness)
They develop a **relative energy/relative entropy** framework for Korteweg-type Hamiltonian flows, and explain that it yields **stability and weak–strong uniqueness** for Euler–Korteweg and also provides identities relevant to QHD. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00801?utm_source=openai))

- **Paper:** *Relative energy for the Korteweg theory and related Hamiltonian flows in gas dynamics*  
  **Authors:** Jan Giesselmann, Corrado Lattanzio, Athanasios E. Tzavaras  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:1510.00801` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00801?utm_source=openai))

### Theorem (Giesselmann–Tzavaras: weak–strong uniqueness for Euler–Korteweg with nonconvex energies)
They extend the relative energy method to **non-monotone/nonconvex pressures** and still obtain **weak–strong uniqueness**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01663?utm_source=openai))

- **Paper:** *Stability properties of the Euler-Korteweg system with nonmonotone pressures*  
  **Authors:** Jan Giesselmann, Athanasios E. Tzavaras  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:1611.01663` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01663?utm_source=openai))

**How these relate.** These are the main “positive” uniqueness results one can safely cite for QHD-type PDE: **uniqueness holds conditionally** (weak–strong) under regularity and typically **no vacuum**.

### Result (Antonelli–Marcati: global finite-energy weak solutions; no uniqueness claimed)
They construct global finite-energy weak solutions to a QHD system, and explicitly do not provide uniqueness. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.0846))

- **Paper:** *On the Finite Energy Weak Solutions to a System in Quantum Fluid Dynamics*  
  **Authors:** Paolo Antonelli, Pierangelo Marcati  
  **arXiv:** `arXiv:0802.0846` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.0846))

**How this relates.** It shows that the natural energy framework is compatible with global weak existence, but **does not support a blanket uniqueness statement**.

## 5) A (special) uniqueness result in a 1D stationary/subsonic boundary value setting

### Theorem (Gamba–Jüngel: uniqueness in a subsonic class for certain pressures)
In a one-dimensional quantum-hydrodynamic *trajectory* / boundary-value setting, they prove **uniqueness in the class of “subsonic” solutions** for certain isentropic pressure laws (they refer to this as *Theorem 5.1* in the PDF). ([web.ma.utexas.edu](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/gamba/papers/quantum-hydro.pdf))

  **Statement excerpt location:** mentions “Finally, we prove uniqueness … in the class of ‘subsonic’ solutions (Theorem 5.1).” ([web.ma.utexas.edu](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/gamba/papers/quantum-hydro.pdf))

**How this relates.** This is an example where **uniqueness is true**, but it is **not** the general Cauchy problem for multidimensional QHD; it’s a **restricted 1D regime**.

---

# Bottom line (mathematically correct summary)

- **General uniqueness of (finite-energy) weak solutions for QHD is false**: there are **explicit non-uniqueness** results, and even **infinitely many** weak solutions for related QHD/Euler–Korteweg–Poisson systems. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04161))  
- The best robust “uniqueness” statement available for these models is typically **weak–strong uniqueness** (relative entropy/energy method), usually **assuming no vacuum** and enough smoothness of the strong solution. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5063))

If you tell me **which QHD system** you mean (inviscid vs viscous, with/without Poisson, domain/boundary conditions) and **what solution class** (classical, strong in \(H^s\), weak finite-energy, dissipative weak, etc.), I can point you to the sharp uniqueness theorem for that exact setting (with the precise hypotheses).

“Solutions to the system of quantum hydrodynamics are unique” is **not true in full generality** unless you specify (i) *which QHD model* (quantum Euler vs quantum Navier–Stokes / Euler–Korteweg / etc.), (ii) the *class of solutions* (strong/classical vs weak/finite-energy/dissipative), and (iii) the *regularity/non-vacuum assumptions*. What **is** widely available are **conditional uniqueness** results (typically *weak–strong uniqueness*): a weak/finite-energy solution is unique **as long as** a strong solution exists with the same initial data.

Below are theorem statements that directly support this “conditional uniqueness” form for quantum-hydrodynamic-type systems.

---

## 1) Weak–strong uniqueness for **pressureless quantum Navier–Stokes** (periodic domain)

**Theorem (weak–strong uniqueness; pressureless QNS).**  
Let \(\Omega=\mathbb T^d\) with \(d=2\) or \(3\). Let \((\varrho,u)\) be a **weak solution** to the *pressureless quantum Navier–Stokes* system on \((0,T)\times \Omega\), and let \((r,U)\) be the corresponding **strong solution** with the **same initial data**. Then
\[
(\varrho,u)=(r,U)\quad\text{on }(0,T)\times\Omega,
\]
i.e. weak and strong solutions coincide (weak–strong uniqueness).  

This is exactly a uniqueness statement in the natural “weak vs strong” framework for QHD with viscosity and Bohm-type quantum term.

**Precise reference (theorem number).** Theorem 17 (as returned by theorem search): “Weak solutions and strong solutions starting from identical initial data must coincide for the pressureless quantum Navier-Stokes system on a periodic domain in two or three dimensions.”  

**How it answers your query.** It proves **uniqueness within the class of weak solutions, provided a strong solution exists** (conditional uniqueness).

**Paper info.** The theorem-search output does not include the paper title/arXiv ID; if you want, tell me whether you mean *pressureless* QNS specifically and I can pin down the exact arXiv record/title for this Theorem 17.

---

## 2) Weak–strong uniqueness for **Euler–Korteweg / quantum Euler-type** dissipative solutions

Many QHD formulations are equivalent (after changes of variables) to **Euler–Korteweg** systems (capillarity/quantum pressure). A standard modern uniqueness concept is:

- **dissipative solution** (or “finite energy weak solution”),
- **strong solution** (smooth, positive density),
- **relative entropy** method ⇒ weak–strong uniqueness.

**Theorem (weak–strong uniqueness for Euler–Korteweg).**  
Assume a specific Korteweg/quantum-capillarity structure (often encoded by a choice of \(\mu(\rho)\) and \(K(\rho)\), and a pressure law \(p(\rho)\) satisfying parameter constraints). Let \((\rho,u)\) be a **dissipative solution** of the Euler–Korteweg system with given initial data, and let \((r,U)\) be a **strong solution** with the same initial data. Then the dissipative solution coincides with the strong one on their common interval of existence:
\[
(\rho,u)=(r,U).
\]

**Precise reference (theorem number).** Theorem 23 (theorem-search output): it states that dissipative and strong solutions coincide for Euler–Korteweg under structural assumptions such as \(\mu(\rho)=\rho^{(s+3)/2}\) (equivalently \(K(\rho)=\frac{(s+3)^2}{4}\rho^s\)) with constraints like \(\gamma\ge s+2\), \(s\ge -1\).

**How it answers your query.** Again, this gives **uniqueness** in the sense relevant for QHD: **no two dissipative/finite-energy solutions can differ if one of them is strong** (or, equivalently, if a strong solution exists then it is the unique finite-energy/dissipative one).

**Paper info.** Same note: I can provide the exact paper title + arXiv link for this Theorem 23 once you confirm which Euler–Korteweg/QHD formulation you’re using (there are multiple closely-related arXiv works with theorem numbering like this).

---

## 3) Important caveat: global uniqueness of weak solutions is generally *not* expected

Without a strong solution hypothesis (or additional monotonicity/1D structure/small data assumptions), **global uniqueness of weak solutions** for compressible Euler/Korteweg/QHD-type systems is typically **open or false** in many settings. So the correct mathematical statement is usually one of:

- **local-in-time classical (strong) uniqueness** for smooth data (standard PDE theory), and/or
- **weak–strong uniqueness** (relative entropy / modulated energy).

query: Stochastic localization approximately conserves entropy when started from Ising measure
response_without:
Below are the main “approximate entropy conservation” results for **stochastic localization started from an Ising (Gibbs) measure** that are used in the modern mixing/functional-inequality literature.

---

## 1) Entropy conservation along Ising stochastic localization (Chen–Eldan): differential inequality ⇒ multiplicative conservation

### Theorem (entropy conservation under covariance control; as stated e.g. in *Fast Mixing in Sparse Random Ising Models*)
Let \((\mu_t)_{t\ge 0}\) be a stochastic localization process (with possibly time-varying control matrices \(C_t\)) started from an Ising measure \(\mu_0=\mu_{J,h}\) on \(\{\pm1\}^n\). Assume that for every \(h'\in\mathbb R^n\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
\bigl\|\, C_t \,\mathrm{Cov}(\mu_{J_t,h'})\, C_t \,\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le \alpha_t .
\]
Then for any \(\varphi>0\),
\[
\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_1}(\varphi)\big]\;\ge\;
\exp\!\left(-\int_0^1 \alpha_t\,dt\right)\,\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_{J,h}}(\varphi).
\]
This is explicitly presented as Lemma 3.18 in a recent exposition and is described there as a mild generalization of Chen–Eldan’s **Proposition 39 + Lemma 40** (with the stronger version “implicitly proved” already in their Lemma 40). ([amitrajaraman.github.io](https://amitrajaraman.github.io/publications/sparse-ising.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**How it matches your query.**  
This is precisely an **approximate conservation of entropy**: the localization martingale does not destroy entropy by more than a multiplicative factor, controlled by an integral of (controlled) covariance growth along the path.

**Paper pointer.**
- Yuansi Chen, Ronen Eldan, *Localization Schemes: A Framework for Proving Mixing Bounds for Markov Chains* (arXiv:2203.04163). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04163?utm_source=openai))  
  (In this paper, the relevant ingredients are labeled **Proposition 39** and **Lemma 40**; multiple later works cite these as the “conservation of entropy” step.) ([ieee-focs.org](https://ieee-focs.org/FOCS-2024-Papers/pdfs/FOCS2024-1oojWxXs5YAKfs3z3lBRMF/167400a120/167400a120.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**arXiv link:** `https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04163` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04163?utm_source=openai))

---

## 2) “Entropy conservation inequality” as a hypothesis to transfer MLSI/mixing (Chen–Eldan Theorem 47)

### Theorem (Chen–Eldan, “Theorem 47” as used in Ising applications)
Let \(\mu=\mu_{J,h}\) be an Ising model and \((\mu_t)_{0\le t\le 1}\) be a stochastic localization scheme initialized at \(\mu\). Suppose:

1. (**Entropy conservation**) there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for all \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R_+\),
\[
\frac{\mathbb E[\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_1}(f)]}{\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu}(f)}\ge \varepsilon.
\]
2. (**Component MLSI**) almost surely \(\mathrm{CMLSI}(P_{\mu_1})\ge \delta\).

Then one can deduce a modified log-Sobolev inequality / mixing consequence for the original Glauber dynamics (the theorem is used as a “localize + prove MLSI on the localized end + transfer back” mechanism).

A clean statement of the above appears (as **Theorem 3.19**) in the same recent exposition, explicitly attributing it to **[CE22, Theorem 47]**. ([amitrajaraman.github.io](https://amitrajaraman.github.io/publications/sparse-ising.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**How it matches your query.**  
This isolates “entropy conservation” as an abstract functional inequality that must be verified for stochastic localization started at an Ising measure, and then used as a bridge to global functional inequalities/mixing.

**Paper pointer.**
- Yuansi Chen, Ronen Eldan, *Localization Schemes…* (arXiv:2203.04163), Theorem 47 (numbering in that manuscript). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04163?utm_source=openai))

---

## 3) Entropy factorization viewpoint (Caputo–Chen–Parisi 2025): stochastic localization yields approximate Shearer/entropy tensorization

While not always phrased as “entropy conservation along \(t\mapsto\mu_t\)”, a closely related (and downstream) structural consequence is that stochastic localization can be used to prove **entropy factorization / approximate Shearer inequalities** for Gibbs measures.

### Theorem family (entropy factorization from stochastic localization; high-temperature/uniqueness-type regimes)
Caputo–Chen–Parisi develop stochastic-localization-based bounds implying approximate Shearer-type inequalities (entropy tensorization/factorization) for spin systems, including Ising, in regimes up to tree-uniqueness thresholds.

**How it matches your query.**  
Entropy factorization can be seen as an integrated/functional form of “entropy doesn’t collapse under decomposition/localization”: the decomposition induced by localization approximately preserves relative entropy structure across blocks/subsets.

**Paper pointer.**
- Pietro Caputo, Zongchen Chen, Daniel Parisi, *Factorizations of relative entropy using stochastic localization* (arXiv:2503.19419). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19419?utm_source=openai))

**arXiv link:** `https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19419` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19419?utm_source=openai))

---

## What to cite (quick “most relevant” list)

1. **Chen–Eldan (2022)**: *Localization Schemes: A Framework for Proving Mixing Bounds for Markov Chains* — this is the core reference where the Ising stochastic localization scheme is analyzed and where **Proposition 39 / Lemma 40** are the standard cited source for “conservation of entropy”.  
   arXiv:2203.04163 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04163?utm_source=openai))

2. **A convenient explicit inequality** (often quoted in later work): the multiplicative bound
\(\mathbb E[\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_1}(\varphi)] \ge e^{-\int \alpha_t}\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_0}(\varphi)\)
under an operator-norm covariance control. ([amitrajaraman.github.io](https://amitrajaraman.github.io/publications/sparse-ising.pdf?utm_source=openai))

3. **Caputo–Chen–Parisi (2025)** for entropy factorization consequences via the same stochastic localization technology.  
   arXiv:2503.19419 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19419?utm_source=openai))

A clean “approximately conserves entropy” statement (in the sense of *entropy at the end of localization is not much smaller than initial entropy, in expectation*) appears as the following lemma for **Ising-model stochastic localization**.

**Lemma (Entropy comparison / approximate conservation for Ising stochastic localization).**  
Let \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) be a stochastic localization process with (possibly time-varying) control matrices \((C_t)\), started at an Ising Gibbs measure \(\mu_0=\mu_{J,h}\). Assume that for every external field \(h'\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\),

\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_1}(\varphi)\bigr]\ \ge\ \exp\!\left(-\int_0^1 \alpha_t\,dt\right)\,\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu_{J,h}}(\varphi).
\]
This is exactly an **approximate entropy conservation** bound: the expected entropy loss along localization is controlled by \(\int_0^1\alpha_t dt\).

The lemma is described there as a mild generalization of results in Chen–Eldan (2022) (their Proposition 39 and Lemma 40), and “implicitly proved” in their Lemma 40.

In the same source, the “entropy conservation inequality” is used as an input to bootstrap modified log-Sobolev inequalities (MLSI) for the original Ising measure:

**Theorem (Entropy conservation + MLSI at the end ⇒ MLSI at start).**  
If a stochastic localization scheme \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) initialized at \(\mu_{J,h}\) satisfies (i) an entropy conservation inequality
\[

\]
and (ii) almost surely \(C_{\mathrm{MLSI}}(P_{\mu_1})\ge \delta\), then \(\mu_{J,h}\) has MLSI constant at least \(\varepsilon\delta\).

query: Homtopy groups of the set of projections in a C*-algebra
response_without:
Let \(A\) be a (complex) \(C^*\)-algebra and let \(\mathrm{Proj}(A)\) denote the set of self-adjoint idempotents in \(A\) (or in a matrix stabilization \(M_\infty(A)\)), topologized in the norm topology. The homotopy groups of “the space of projections” are not usually computed directly; rather, the key structural results identify (a group-completion / classifying-space construction built from) projections with **\(K\)-theory**, and then \(\pi_\ast\) becomes \(K_\ast\) (up to the standard 2-periodicity).

Below are the most relevant precise theorems and how they answer your query.

---

## 1) \(\pi_0\) of projections = \(K_0\) (after stabilization + group completion)

### Theorem (classical definition/identification of \(K_0\) via projections)
For a unital \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\), let
\[
V(A)=\{[p] : p\in M_\infty(A)\ \text{a projection}\}/\sim
\]
where \(\sim\) is Murray–von Neumann equivalence (equivalently, stable unitary equivalence), and define addition by block sum \([p]+[q]=[p\oplus q]\). Then \(V(A)\) is an abelian monoid, and its Grothendieck group completion satisfies
\[
K_0(A)\ \cong\ G(V(A)).
\]
Moreover, homotopy of projections in \(M_\infty(A)\) refines these equivalence relations in the sense used in operator \(K\)-theory, and \(K_0(A)\) is a homotopy invariant of \(A\). ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/F93692DAB8A19EC94BEE58E158AC0C91/9780511623806c2_p15-34_CBO.pdf/projections_and_unitary_elements.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**How this relates to homotopy groups:** this gives the “\(\pi_0\)-level” answer: connected components (stable/homotopy classes) of projections encode \(K_0\). If you literally take \(\mathrm{Proj}(M_\infty(A))\) as a topological space, \(\pi_0\) is closely tied to the positive cone \(V(A)\), and its group completion is \(K_0(A)\).

**Reference (book-level standard):**
- Bruce Blackadar, *K-Theory for Operator Algebras* (standard reference; see its projection-based construction). ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7336561/k-theory-for-operator-algebras-bruce-blackadar?utm_source=openai))  
- Rørdam–Larsen–Laustsen, *An Introduction to K-Theory for C\(^*\)-Algebras*, Ch. 2 “Projections and Unitary Elements”. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/F93692DAB8A19EC94BEE58E158AC0C91/9780511623806c2_p15-34_CBO.pdf/projections_and_unitary_elements.pdf?utm_source=openai))

(These are books/notes rather than arXiv papers; for operator \(K\)-theory this is the canonical place the theorem is stated carefully.)

---

## 2) Higher \(\pi_n\): projections lead to a representing space for \(K\)-theory (via Fredholm models)

A clean way to package “all homotopy groups of a space built from projections” is to use representing spaces for \(K\)-theory (Fredholm operators). This is the standard theorem that turns \(\pi_n\) into \(K^{-n}\).

### Theorem (Atiyah–Jänich: Fredholm operators represent complex \(K\)-theory)
Let \(\mathrm{Fred}(\mathcal H)\) be the space of Fredholm operators on an infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), with the norm topology. Then for every compact Hausdorff space \(X\),
\[
[X,\mathrm{Fred}(\mathcal H)]\ \cong\ K^0(X),
\]
naturally in \(X\). Equivalently, \(\mathrm{Fred}(\mathcal H)\) is a classifying space for (complex) \(K\)-theory. ([ncatlab.org](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Atiyah-J%C3%A4nich%2Btheorem?utm_source=openai))

**How this relates to projections:** projections model vector bundles (Serre–Swan), and Fredholm operators provide a convenient infinite-dimensional classifying space whose homotopy type matches the group-completion of the “monoid of projections”. In particular, once you identify a \(K\)-theory representing space \(K(A)\) built from projections (or equivalently from Fredholm operators with coefficients), its homotopy groups are \(K\)-groups.

**Paper (arXiv) reference:**
- N.C. Phillips & B. Thom? (actually the arXiv item is): *Atiyah-Jänich theorem for \(\sigma\)-C\(^*\)-algebras* (gives a coefficient/generalized version and is a good modern citable source for the representing-space statement). arXiv:1612.03287 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03287?utm_source=openai))

---

## 3) Coefficients in a \(C^*\)-algebra: homotopy groups of the “\(K\)-theory space” of \(A\) are \(K_\ast(A)\)

What you likely want is: build a topological space \(K(A)\) from projections (or Fredholm operators with coefficients in \(A\)) such that \(\pi_n(K(A))\) *is* \(K_n(A)\).

### Theorem (Representability of \(K\)-theory for \(C^*\)-algebras by a space/spectrum; \(\pi_n = K_n\))
There is a canonical topological \(K\)-theory space (indeed an infinite loop space / spectrum) \(K(A)\) functorially associated to a \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\) such that
\[
\pi_n(K(A))\ \cong\ K_n(A)\qquad (n\in\mathbb Z),
\]

Let me phrase this in the standard “collisional kinetic theory” way:

- For the **Landau collision operator** \(Q_L\), the set of equilibria (i.e. distributions \(f\ge 0\) with \(Q_L(f,f)=0\)) consists exactly of **Maxwellians**.
- For the **Vlasov–Maxwell–Landau (VML)** system, the full equilibrium condition also includes the **Vlasov transport with self-consistent fields**. Under the usual whole-space/periodic setting with finite mass/energy and no external forcing, the physically relevant equilibria are **global Maxwellians with vanishing fields** (or constant fields depending on gauge/topology). Near-equilibrium theories linearize around such global Maxwellians.

Below are the key theorems/results one typically cites.

---

## 1) Equilibria of the Landau collision operator are Maxwellians (Landau H-theorem / characterization by entropy dissipation)

### Theorem (Characterization of equilibria for the Landau equation)
Consider the (spatially homogeneous) Landau equation
\[
\partial_t f = Q_L(f,f), \qquad f=f(t,v)\ge 0,\ v\in \mathbb R^3,
\]
with finite mass, momentum, and energy. Define the entropy
\[
H(f)=\int_{\mathbb R^3} f\log f\,dv
\]
and the entropy dissipation \(D(f)\ge 0\) (explicit quadratic form in \(\nabla_v \log f\)). Then:

1. \( \dfrac{d}{dt}H(f(t)) = -D(f(t)) \le 0\).
2. \(D(f)=0\) **if and only if** \(f\) is a (global) Maxwellian
\[
\mu_{\rho,u,T}(v)=\frac{\rho}{(2\pi T)^{3/2}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{|v-u|^2}{2T}\Big),
\quad \rho>0,\ u\in\mathbb R^3,\ T>0.
\]

This is the precise statement behind the slogan “equilibria are Maxwellians”.

**Where this is stated (explicitly):**
- In Carrapatoso’s notes, after writing the entropy dissipation, it states: “It follows that any equilibrium is a Maxwellian distribution \(\mu_{\rho,u,T}\).” ([carrapatoso.perso.math.cnrs.fr](https://carrapatoso.perso.math.cnrs.fr/articles/compumat2013.pdf))

**Primary references (classical/standard):**
- C. Villani, *A review of mathematical topics in collisional kinetic theory* (a standard survey source for the H-theorem/entropy dissipation framework). In VML, the collision term is exactly the Landau operator (acting in \(v\) at each \((t,x)\)), so any equilibrium must at least satisfy \(Q_L(f,f)=0\), hence must be Maxwellian in \(v\) (possibly with parameters depending on \(x\), before using the Vlasov–Maxwell part to rule out \(x\)-dependence).

- **Collision equilibrium:** the right-hand side collision operator vanishes, forcing Maxwellian structure in \(v\).

If one allows **nontrivial stationary electromagnetic fields**, boundary effects, or special geometries, the collision operator still enforces **Maxwellian-in-\(v\)** structure, but the Vlasov–Maxwell constraints can admit more complicated stationary states (e.g. depending on invariants of motion). query: sign of the cup-i product associated to alexander-whitney diagonal approximation
response_without:
What ultimately controls the **signs** in the cup-\(i\) products coming from the **Alexander–Whitney (AW) diagonal approximation** is the graded Koszul rule: every time (on the chain level) you *transpose tensor factors* of degrees \(p\) and \(q\), you pick up \((-1)^{pq}\). The cup-\(i\) products are then built from a coherent system of chain homotopies \(D_i\) witnessing the failure of AW to be (graded) cocommutative; these homotopies encode exactly the higher “commutativity defects”, and their coboundary formulas force specific sign patterns (over \(\mathbb Z\); over \(\mathbb F_2\) the signs disappear).

Below are the most relevant precise results and references.

---

## 1) AW diagonal and the basic \((-1)^{pq}\) sign (cup product)

Let \(C_*(X)\) be a (normalized) chain complex of a simplicial set and let
\[
AW \colon C_*(X\times X)\to C_*(X)\otimes C_*(X)
\]
be the Alexander–Whitney map. Composing with the geometric diagonal \(\Delta\colon X\to X\times X\) gives a chain approximation to the diagonal
\[
D_0 \coloneqq AW\circ \Delta_* \;:\; C_*(X)\to C_*(X)\otimes C_*(X).
\]

For cochains \(u\in C^p(X;R)\), \(v\in C^q(X;R)\), the (AW) cup product is
\[
u\smile v \;=\; (u\otimes v)\circ D_0 \in C^{p+q}(X;R),
\]
and the **graded-commutativity on cohomology**
\[
[u]\smile [v] \;=\; (-1)^{pq}[v]\smile [u]
\]
comes from the fact that \(D_0\) is not cocommutative on the chain level but is cocommutative up to a chain homotopy, together with the Koszul sign \((-1)^{pq}\) from swapping tensor factors.

A modern formulation emphasizing “broken symmetry of Alexander–Whitney” as the origin of these coherent homotopies appears in Kaufmann–Medina-Mardones. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02571))

**Paper / link.**
- Ralph M. Kaufmann, Aníbal M. Medina-Mardones, *Cochain level May–Steenrod operations*, arXiv:2010.02571. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02571))

(They build cup-\(i\) and higher operations from the AW defect-of-symmetry viewpoint.)

---

## 2) Cup-\(i\) products as higher homotopies \(D_i\) of the AW diagonal defect

A standard way to package cup-\(i\) is: choose maps
\[
D_i \;:\; C_n(X)\to (C_*(X)\otimes C_*(X))_{n+i}\quad (i\ge 0)
\]
with \(D_0\) the AW diagonal approximation, and define for \(u\in C^p\), \(v\in C^q\):
\[
u\smile_i v \;\in\; C^{p+q-i}(X), \qquad
(u\smile_i v)(\sigma) \;=\; (u\otimes v)\bigl(D_i(\sigma)\bigr),
\]
for \(\sigma\in C_{p+q-i}(X)\).
This definition is stated explicitly (over \(\mathbb F_2\)) in Liang’s notes. ([tongtongliang.github.io](https://tongtongliang.github.io/data/SteenrodOperations.pdf))

### Coboundary (Hirsch/Steenrod) identity and signs
Over \(\mathbb F_2\) (so no signs), Liang records the coboundary formula:
\[
\delta(u\smile_i v)
= u\smile_{i-1} v \;+\; v\smile_{i-1} u \;+\; (\delta u)\smile_i v \;+\; u\smile_i (\delta v),
\]
(which is the mod 2 version of the general integral-sign formula). ([tongtongliang.github.io](https://tongtongliang.github.io/data/SteenrodOperations.pdf))

Over \(\mathbb Z\) or a general commutative ring, the **same identity holds with Koszul signs**; the term where you interchange \(u\) and \(v\) picks up \((-1)^{(p-i)(q-i)}\) (and further sign contributions depending on the precise grading conventions for \(\delta\) and for the symmetry isomorphism \(T\colon a\otimes b\mapsto (-1)^{|a||b|}b\otimes a\)). Different authors bake these signs either into the definition of \(D_i\) or into the definition of \(\smile_i\), but the governing principle is always: *the “swap” is the graded symmetry, hence Koszul signs*.

**Paper / link (axiomatic uniqueness, which implicitly fixes the sign conventions up to unique isomorphism once axioms are chosen).**
- Aníbal M. Medina-Mardones, *An axiomatic characterization of Steenrod’s cup-\(i\) products*, arXiv:1810.06505. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.06505))  
  This proves that “reasonable” (natural, minimal, etc.) constructions of cup-\(i\) on normalized chains are **isomorphic (not merely homotopic)** to Steenrod’s original one, so once you specify the graded symmetry/sign convention, the cup-\(i\) signs are essentially forced. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.06505))

**Expository reference / link (explicit \(D_i\)-definition).**
- Tongtong Liang, *An Introduction to Steenrod Operations* (notes, PDF). ([tongtongliang.github.io](https://tongtongliang.github.io/data/SteenrodOperations.pdf))

---

## 3) Practical “answer” to “what is the sign?”

Because there are multiple incompatible sign conventions in the literature, the most robust way to state “the sign” is:

1. **Fix the graded symmetry**
   \[
   T(a\otimes b)=(-1)^{|a||b|}b\otimes a

   on \(C_*(X)\otimes C_*(X)\).

2. Define \(D_0 = AW\circ \Delta_*\).

3. Choose \(D_1\) a chain homotopy between \(D_0\) and \(T D_0\), i.e.
   \[
   \partial D_1 + D_1\partial = TD_0 - D_0.
   \]
   Higher \(D_i\) then iteratively encode higher coherences.

4. Define \(u\smile_i v = (u\otimes v)\circ D_i\). Then **every occurrence of “swap \(u\) and \(v\)” contributes Koszul signs** dictated by degrees, and the coboundary identity (the integral version of Liang’s) pins down the remaining signs.

query: Smooth DM stack is uniquely determined by codimension one locus
response_without:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a smooth Deligne–Mumford (DM) stack (separated, finite type) and write \(\pi:\mathcal X\to X\) for its coarse moduli space. Your slogan “uniquely determined by the codimension one locus” is literally true under standard hypotheses (tame + generically trivial stabilizer), and the precise mechanism is: **\(\mathcal X\) is obtained from the “canonical stack” \(X^{\mathrm{can}}\) by taking root stacks along the ramification divisor**, i.e. along codimension-1 data.

## 1) Main theorem (“bottom-up characterization”)

### Theorem (Bergh–Rydh, *A “bottom up” characterization of smooth Deligne–Mumford stacks*, IMRN 2017, Theorem 1)
Let \(\pi:\mathcal X\to \mathcal Y\) be a **relative coarse space** morphism, where:

- \(\mathcal X\) is a **smooth, separated, tame** DM stack of finite type over a field \(k\),
- \(\mathcal X\) has **trivial generic stabilizer**,
- \(\mathcal Y\) is the coarse space (an algebraic space/stack with tame quotient singularities).

Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq \mathcal Y\) be the **ramification divisor** of \(\pi\), with irreducible components \(\mathcal D_i\) and ramification indices \(e_i\) along \(\mathcal D_i\).

Then \(\pi\) factors (canonically, up to unique isomorphism) through the **root stack** of the **canonical stack** \(\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{can}}\) along \(\mathcal D\) with orders \(e_i\):
\[
\mathcal X \longrightarrow \sqrt[\vec e]{\ \mathcal D\ /\ \mathcal Y^{\mathrm{can}}\ } \longrightarrow \mathcal Y^{\mathrm{can}} \longrightarrow \mathcal Y,
\]
and this factorization *recovers* \(\mathcal X\) from \(\mathcal Y\) together with the codimension-1 ramification data \((\mathcal D_i,e_i)\). In particular (as the authors emphasize), **\(\mathcal X\) is determined by its coarse space and the stabilizer orders in codimension 1**. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/imrn/article/2017/21/6469/3061093))

**How it answers your query.**  
Codimension-1 inertia/ramification (the divisor \(\mathcal D\) and integers \(e_i\)) plus the coarse space determines the entire smooth tame DM stack with generically trivial stabilizer; higher-codimension stabilizers and the full group structures are forced by this data. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.05478))

**arXiv / paper**
- “A ‘bottom up’ characterization of smooth Deligne–Mumford stacks” (Bergh–Rydh), arXiv:1503.05478 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.05478))

## 2) Canonical stack: “isomorphism away from codimension \(\ge 2\)” + uniqueness

A key input is the **canonical stack** \(X^{\mathrm{can}}\to X\) of a variety/algebraic space \(X\) with tame quotient singularities: it is smooth DM, has coarse space \(X\), and is an isomorphism over the codimension \(\ge 2\) complement.

### Theorem (Universal property of canonical stacks; Bergh–Rydh, Theorem 4.6 as quoted in Remark 1)
If \(\mathcal X\) is a smooth DM stack with coarse space \(X\) such that \(\mathcal X\to X\) is an isomorphism away from a locus of codimension \(\ge 2\), then \(\mathcal X\) is **terminal** among smooth DM stacks with trivial generic stabilizer admitting a dominant codimension-preserving morphism to \(X\). ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/imrn/article/2017/21/6469/3061093))

**How it relates.**  
This is the “codimension \(\ge 2\) doesn’t matter” part: once you’ve fixed the coarse space, there is a unique way to make it smooth stacky **without changing anything in codimension 1** (i.e. stack structure only in codimension \(\ge 2\)), namely the canonical stack. Then Bergh–Rydh’s Theorem 1 says that any additional stack structure in codimension 1 is exactly root constructions along divisors with specified indices.

## 3) Important caveats / failure modes

Bergh–Rydh explicitly note the characterization **fails if you drop smoothness or separateness**: there can be non-isomorphic stacks with the same coarse space and the same codimension-1 stabilizer orders. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/imrn/article/2017/21/6469/3061093))  
So the clean “determined by codimension one locus” principle is fundamentally a **smooth separated tame** phenomenon.

## 4) Minimal “takeaway formulation” (what to cite in your own work)

Under: smooth + separated + tame + generically trivial stabilizer,

- \(\mathcal X\) is determined by its coarse space \(X\),
- and the **ramification divisor** (equivalently: the list of codimension-1 components where inertia is nontrivial, together with the ramification indices / stabilizer orders \(e_i\)),

because
\[
\mathcal X \cong \big(\sqrt[\vec e]{D/X^{\mathrm{can}}}\big)^{\mathrm{can}}
\]
(up to the precise formulation in Theorem 1).

If you tell me your exact intended meaning of “codimension one locus” (e.g. “agreement on an open substack whose complement has codimension \(\ge 2\)” vs “same coarse space + same inertia orders at height-1 points”), I can restate the theorem in the exact form you need and isolate the clean corollary you should quote.
response_with:
A statement of the form “a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack is uniquely determined by its codimension‑one locus” is **false in that generality**: you can modify a DM stack in codimension ≥2 (e.g. by inserting a gerbe along a codimension‑2 substack) without changing what you see in codimension 1. What *is* true (and widely used) is that **for smooth separated tame DM stacks with trivial generic stabilizer**, the stack is determined by its **coarse space plus codimension‑one stabilizer/ramification data** (equivalently: by the stack structure along divisors).

Below are precise theorems that capture the correct “codimension‑one determination” principle.

---

## 1) “Bottom-up” reconstruction from coarse space + codimension‑1 stabilizers

### Theorem (Geraschenko–Satriano, “Bottom Up characterization”)
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a **smooth separated tame Deligne–Mumford stack** of finite type over a field \(k\) with **trivial generic stabilizer**, and let \(\pi:\mathcal X\to X\) be its coarse moduli space. Then \(\mathcal X\) is **determined (up to unique isomorphism)** by:
- the coarse space \(X\), and
- the **ramification divisor** of \(\pi\) on \(X\), i.e. equivalently the **orders of stabilizers at codimension‑1 points** of \(X\).

This is exactly the slogan: *“to specify such a stack it is enough to specify a variety and the orders of stabilizers of codimension‑1 points.”* ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.05478?utm_source=openai))

**Paper:** *A “bottom up” characterization of smooth Deligne–Mumford stacks*  
**arXiv:** 1503.05478 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.05478?utm_source=openai))  
(Also published in IMRN; see Oxford page.) ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/imrn/article/2017/21/6469/3061093?utm_source=openai))

**How it answers your query:** it gives a precise hypothesis under which “codimension‑1 data” (together with the coarse space) uniquely determines the smooth DM stack.

---

## 2) Uniqueness via “isomorphism of coarse spaces + unramified in codim 1”

### Corollary / Lemma (as surfaced by theorem_search)
Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) be a morphism of **smooth separated tame DM stacks** with **trivial generic stabilizers**. If
1) \(f\) induces an **isomorphism of coarse moduli spaces**, and  
2) \(f\) is **unramified in codimension 1**,  
then \(f\) is an **isomorphism of stacks**.

This appears as:

- **Corollary 10.** “If \(f\) is unramified in codimension 1 and induces an isomorphism of coarse spaces, then \(f\) is an isomorphism.”  
- **Lemma 6.49.** A variant with “finite diagonal” in place of “tame/separated” hypotheses.

(These are theorem-search hits; the precise paper metadata should be checked in the arXiv PDF once you identify which source they come from in your context.)

**How it answers your query:** if two smooth DM stacks agree on the coarse space and have the same codimension‑1 stackiness (expressed by “unramified in codim 1”), then they must be globally equal.

---

## 3) Special case: inertia trivial in codimension ≤ 1 ⇒ coarse space determines the stack

### Proposition (Vistoli; also cited in Geraschenko–Satriano context)
A **smooth separated** Deligne–Mumford stack whose **inertia is trivial in codimension at most 1** is determined by its **coarse moduli space**.

This is essentially the “no codimension‑1 stackiness” case: if the stabilizers vanish generically and along divisors, there is no divisor-level data to record, and the coarse space alone recovers the stack.

This proposition is referenced in the literature as Vistoli’s Proposition 2.8 (uniqueness follows from the proof, as noted by others). ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/21109/stacks-determined-by-their-coarse-moduli-spaces?utm_source=openai))

**How it answers your query:** it is a clean codimension‑one determination statement, but only when *there is no codimension‑1 inertia at all*.

---

## Important caveat (why “codimension‑1 locus” alone is not enough)

query: Generically trivial gerbe over a smooth curve has trivial fibers
response_without:
Let \(C\) be a smooth integral curve over a field \(k\), with function field \(K=k(C)\), generic point \(\eta=\mathrm{Spec}(K)\), and closed points \(x\in C\). Let \(\mathcal G\to C\) be a gerbe (say fppf/étale) banded by a smooth commutative group scheme \(A\) (typical cases: \(A=\mathbf G_m\), \(A=\mu_n\), a torus, etc.). “Generically trivial” means \(\mathcal G|_\eta\) is neutral (has a section over \(\eta\)).

Below are the main results one typically uses to pass from generic triviality to triviality on fibers; what is true depends strongly on the band \(A\) and on whether you mean “trivial over the residue field \(k(x)\)” or “trivial over the henselization/completion at \(x\)”.

---

## 1) \(\mathbf G_m\)-gerbes: **generic triviality does *not* force all fibers to be trivial**

A \(\mathbf G_m\)-gerbe on \(C\) corresponds to a class
\[
[\mathcal G]\in H^2(C,\mathbf G_m)=\mathrm{Br}(C).
\]
Generic triviality means its image in \(\mathrm{Br}(K)\) is \(0\).

### Theorem (Purity / unramified Brauer for curves; injectivity \(\mathrm{Br}(C)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{Br}(K)\))
For \(C\) regular integral of dimension \(1\), the restriction map
\[
\mathrm{Br}(C)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Br}(K)
\]
is injective. Equivalently, a \(\mathbf G_m\)-gerbe on \(C\) which is neutral over \(\eta\) is already neutral over \(C\) (globally).

**Consequence.** If a \(\mathbf G_m\)-gerbe is generically trivial, then it is *globally* trivial; hence every geometric fiber is trivial.  
But note: this uses *generic triviality in \(\mathrm{Br}(K)\)* for the class coming from \(\mathrm{Br}(C)\). If your gerbe is only defined on a dense open \(U\subset C\), “generically trivial” does **not** imply it extends/trivializes on all of \(C\) without extra hypotheses.

A standard modern reference for Brauer groups and gerbes in AG contexts is:
- Max Lieblich, *Moduli of twisted sheaves*, arXiv:math/0411337. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411337?utm_source=openai))  
  (Gerbes ↔ \(H^2(-,\mathbf G_m)\), Brauer-theoretic viewpoint; used extensively for curves/surfaces.)

However, if instead you mean the following stronger-sounding statement:

> “A \(\mathbf G_m\)-gerbe on \(C\) that is trivial over \(K\) has *trivial fiber gerbes* over every closed point \(x\) (i.e. over \(k(x)\)).”

That statement is **not generally correct as a standalone local assertion**: even if the global class is \(0\), the induced gerbe on the residue field may be nontrivial because “pullback to the fiber” is not the same as “specialization of a Brauer class,” and residue fields can have nontrivial Brauer groups. So one must be careful about what “fiber” means (base-change gerbe \(\mathcal G\times_C \mathrm{Spec}(k(x))\) vs. the class in the stalk / henselization, etc.).

---

## 2) Finite / multiplicative type bands (\(\mu_n\), tori): generic triviality often implies “trivial at all but finitely many points”, not necessarily at every point

If your gerbe is banded by \(\mu_n\) (or more generally by a finite flat group scheme), its class lies in \(H^2(C,\mu_n)\). Generic triviality means it dies in \(H^2(K,\mu_n)\). One usually gets **unramifiedness** outside finitely many points, but triviality at *every* closed point can fail without additional conditions.

A relevant modern reference in the “extend/trivialize torsors/gerbes over curves” direction is:
- (Cambridge/Nagoya paper) *Extending torsors under quasi-finite flat group schemes*, which develops criteria for extending generically defined torsors over a regular curve model; see in particular results around Theorem 4.4. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/54919E7D45F790B08A67F03A446FF5CA/core-reader?utm_source=openai))  
  (This is torsors rather than gerbes, but many gerbes are obtained by “delooping” torsors, and the same obstruction-theory/local extension issues appear.)

---

## 3) Non-abelian gerbes / \(G\)-gerbes and Grothendieck’s “\(H^2\)” theorem over \(cd\le 1\) fields

If your base field \(k\) has cohomological dimension \(\le 1\) (e.g. \(k\) algebraically closed; also finite fields have \(cd=1\) for \(\ell\ne \mathrm{char}(k)\) in the appropriate sense), then there are very strong vanishing/local-global statements for non-abelian \(H^2\) of algebraic groups.

### Theorem (Grothendieck; non-abelian \(H^2\) over \(cd(k)\le 1\))
Over a perfect field \(k\) of cohomological dimension \(1\), all non-abelian \(H^2\)-cohomology sets of (reasonable) algebraic groups are trivial (equivalently: every banded gerbe is neutral).

A convenient reference focusing on this statement and related local-global principles:
- *Grothendieck’s theorem on non-abelian \(H^2\) and local-global principles*, arXiv:math/9803113. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9803113?utm_source=openai))

**Relevance to your query.** If your “generically trivial gerbe” is actually a gerbe over the *function field* \(K=k(C)\) (not over \(C\)!) and \(K\) has \(cd\le 1\) (e.g. \(k\) algebraically closed and \(C\) a curve, so \(cd(K)=1\) by Tsen/Lang), then every such gerbe is already trivial over \(K\). But this is a statement at the generic point level, not a specialization-to-fibers statement.

---

## 4) If your gerbe is actually the gerbe of liftings of a generically trivial \(G\)-torsor (Grothendieck–Serre-type input)

Many geometric “gerbes over a curve” arise as obstruction gerbes attached to torsors/principal bundles. Then what you need is often:

> generically trivial torsor on a regular 1-dimensional base \(\Rightarrow\) torsor trivial (or trivial on specified opens / stalks).

This is in the orbit of the Grothendieck–Serre conjecture and its relatives. In mixed characteristic / relative settings, recent work proves strong “unramified” versions (trivial off codimension \(\ge 2\), etc.), but for a curve codimension \(\ge 2\) is empty, so these often imply global triviality under hypotheses (isotropy, simply-connectedness, etc.).

Recent references in this direction include:
- *Unramified Grothendieck–Serre for isotropic groups*, arXiv:2311.08660. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08660?utm_source=openai))  
- *Unramified case of Grothendieck–Serre for totally isotropic simply-connected group schemes*, arXiv:2204.05442. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05442?utm_source=openai))  
- *Grothendieck–Serre in the quasi-split unramified case*, arXiv:2009.05299. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.05299?utm_source=openai))  

**Relevance to your query.** If your gerbe is the *classifying gerbe of reductions / liftings* attached to a \(G\)-torsor that is generically trivial, then these results (under their group-theoretic hypotheses) can imply the torsor is trivial on the whole curve, hence all associated gerbes become neutral, hence fibers are trivial.

---

## What I need from you to give a clean “Theorem X ⇒ trivial fibers” statement

Your sentence can be true, false, or true with extra hypotheses depending on the setup. Please specify:

1) Band \(A\): \(\mathbf G_m\)? \(\mu_n\)? a torus? a finite group? a connected reductive group \(G\) (non-abelian gerbe)?  
2) Base field \(k\): algebraically closed? finite? number field? arbitrary?  
3) What “fiber trivial” means: neutral over \(k(x)\)? over \(\mathcal O_{C,x}^h\)? over \(\widehat{\mathcal O}_{C,x}\)?  
4) Is the gerbe defined on all of \(C\) or only on a dense open \(U\subset C\)?

With those choices fixed, I can point to the exact purity/localization sequence (abelian case) or the exact Grothendieck–Serre theorem needed (non-abelian case), with theorem numbers and a proof sketch tailored to your situation.
response_with:
Interpreting your query as:

> Let \(X\) be a smooth connected curve over a field \(k\) with function field \(K=k(X)\). Let \(\mathcal G\to X\) be a gerbe (often banded by a smooth group scheme \(G\), or by \(\mu_n\), or \(\mathbf G_m\)). If \(\mathcal G\) is **generically trivial** (neutral over \(\Spec K\)), does it follow that the **fibers** \(\mathcal G_x\) over (closed) points \(x\in X\) are trivial/neutral?

As stated, this is **false in general**: a gerbe can be neutral over the generic point but have **nontrivial special fibers** (ramification). The right replacement statement is: “generically trivial + *unramified* (extends across codimension 1) \(\Rightarrow\) trivial fibers,” and in dimension 1 “unramified” is exactly what controls all fibers.

Below are precise arXiv-level results that capture the correct picture, and (when they apply) give fiberwise triviality.

---

## 1) \(\mu_n\)-gerbes on a regular scheme: “generically trivial” \(\Leftrightarrow\) “trivial on some nonempty open”, but **not** fiberwise trivial

**Theorem (equivalences for \(\mu_n\)-gerbes; regular base).**  
Let \(X\) be a **regular scheme**, \(n\ge 1\), and \(\beta\in H^2(X,\mu_n)\) with associated \(\mu_n\)-gerbe \(\mathcal G\to X\). Then the following are equivalent:

1. \(\mathcal G\to X\) is Zariski locally trivial.
2. \(\mathcal G\) is trivial over some nonempty open \(U\subseteq X\).
3. The image of \(\beta\) in \(\mathrm{Br}(k(X))\) is zero.  
(and further equivalent conditions)

This is exactly the “generically trivial iff trivial on a dense open” principle for \(\mu_n\)-gerbes on regular schemes.

- Where it answers your query: it shows *generic triviality forces triviality on a big open*, but it does **not** imply anything about the fibers at points in \(X\setminus U\); those fibers can be nontrivial.

**Reference (arXiv):** the theorem appears in arXiv literature in the form returned by the semantic theorem search as “Proposition 2” (equivalences (i)–(iv)).

---

## 2) Local (DVR / henselian) structure: generically trivial gerbes may become trivial only after modifying the base (root stacks)

A clean formulation in the 1-dimensional local setting (henselian DVR) is:

**Proposition (torus-banded gerbe over a root stack of a henselian DVR).**  
Let \(\mathcal R\) be the root stack of a henselian DVR \(R\). Let \(T\to \mathcal R\) be a torus and \(\mathcal T\to \mathcal R\) a \(T\)-banded gerbe which is generically trivial. Then, after replacing \(\mathcal R\) by a *further root stack*, \(\mathcal T\) becomes trivial.

- Meaning for your query: even in a 1-dimensional local setting, “generically trivial” does **not** automatically force the special fiber to be trivial on the original base; you may need a *tame stacky modification* to kill the residual twisting. This is a precise mechanism for why “generic trivial” does not imply “trivial fibers” in general.

**Reference (arXiv):** the semantic search returned this as **Proposition 4.9** (about root stacks of a henselian DVR and torus-banded gerbes).

---

## 3) For torsors (degree-1 cohomology), there *is* a strong “generically trivial ⇒ trivial” theorem (Grothendieck–Serre type)

If your “gerbe” is actually coming from a **\(G\)-torsor** (i.e. class in \(H^1\), not \(H^2\)), then there is a powerful affirmative statement over semilocal regular rings, hence over local rings of points on a smooth curve:

**Theorem (Grothendieck–Serre conjecture for many smooth group schemes).**  
Let \(k\) be a field, \(R\) a geometrically regular semilocal \(k\)-algebra with fraction field \(K\), and \(G\) a smooth \(k\)-group scheme satisfying mild hypotheses. Then every **generically trivial** \(G\)-torsor over \(R\) is trivial; equivalently
\[
\ker\!\big(H^1(R,G)\to H^1(K,G)\big)=0.
\]

- Relation to your query: if you are trying to prove “generic triviality forces triviality at all local rings \( \mathcal O_{X,x}\)” for a \(G\)-torsor on a smooth curve \(X\), this theorem is exactly the needed input: apply it to (a semilocalization of) \( \mathcal O_{X,x}\). Then the **fiber** over \(x\) is trivial because the torsor is already trivial over \(\Spec \mathcal O_{X,x}\).

**Reference (arXiv):** semantic result labeled **Theorem (thm:GS-main)**.

(Important: this addresses torsors/\(H^1\), not general gerbes/\(H^2\).)

---

## What is the correct “fiberwise triviality” statement for gerbes on curves?

For a smooth curve \(X\), a gerbe banded by \(\mathbf G_m\) (or \(\mu_n\)) corresponds to a Brauer class \(\alpha\in \mathrm{Br}(X)\) (or \(H^2(X,\mu_n)\)). There is a **ramification (residue) theory** at each closed point \(x\). The right criterion is:

- If \(\alpha|_{K}=0\) (generically trivial), then \(\alpha\) is supported on finitely many points, but **can have nonzero residues there**, so the fibers at those points can be nontrivial.
- If in addition all residues at closed points are zero (i.e. \(\alpha\) is *unramified*, equivalently \(\alpha\in \mathrm{Br}(X)\) comes from \(\mathrm{Br}(k)\) in many situations), then you do get triviality constraints on fibers (often after restricting to suitable topology / imposing existence of sections).

So: **generic triviality alone is not enough** for fiberwise triviality of a gerbe; you need an unramifiedness condition (or an extension/trivialization over all DVRs).

---

## Clarifying question (to give the exact theorem you want)
When you say “gerbe,” which case are you in?

1) a \(\mathbf G_m\)- or \(\mu_n\)-gerbe (Brauer class / twisted sheaves), or  
2) a \(G\)-gerbe for some smooth group \(G\) (nonabelian \(H^2\)), or  
3) actually a \(G\)-**torsor** (principal bundle, \(H^1\))?

And what does “trivial fibers” mean precisely: trivial as a gerbe over \(\Spec k(x)\), or existence of a section over \(\Spec \mathcal O_{X,x}\), or Zariski/étale local triviality near \(x\)?

If you answer those, I can point to the exact arXiv theorem (with number and link) matching your intended statement, or produce a counterexample in the inappropriate cases.
tool_calls: Let X be a smooth connected curve over a field k with function field K. If a G-gerbe over X is trivial over Spec(K), then it is trivial over Spec(O_{X,x}) for every point x of X, hence has trivial residual fibers.

judgment.reason: A is more useful overall: it correctly says the statement is false in general for gerbes and distinguishes H^2-gerbes from H^1-torsors, giving more precise theorem-style formulations and a clearer explanation of the role of ramification/unramifiedness. B contains a serious correctness problem: for a smooth integral curve, injectivity Br(C)->Br(K) implies a generically trivial G_m-gerbe on C is globally trivial, so its fiber pullbacks are trivial; B first states this, then incorrectly says the fiber statement is not generally correct, creating internal inconsistency. A’s citations are still somewhat weak/underspecified, but B’s are more tangential and less directly matched to the query.

query: You can recover a field from its Milnor K theory
response_without:
Below are (as far as I know) the cleanest *reconstruction* results of the form “the Milnor \(K\)-theory of a field determines the field (up to the usual inseparable ambiguity)”, together with precise hypotheses and where to find them.

---

## 1) Cadoret–Pirutka: the graded Milnor \(K\)-ring determines the function field (in many cases)

### Theorem (field reconstruction from \(K_*^M\), special case)
Let \(F/k\) be a finitely generated **regular** field extension of **transcendence degree \(\ge 2\)** over a **perfect** field \(k\). Then \(F^\times/k^\times\), endowed with the equivalence relation “algebraic dependence over \(k\)”, determines \(F\) up to \(k\)-isomorphism, functorially.

In particular, when \(k\) is **algebraically closed** or **finite**, the **isomorphism class of the graded Milnor \(K\)-ring** \(K_*^M(F)\) determines the **isomorphism class of \(F\)**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))

**Paper:** *Reconstructing function fields from Milnor K-theory* — Anna Cadoret, Alena Pirutka.  
**arXiv:** `arXiv:1808.04944` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))

**How it addresses your query.** This is a direct positive answer (for finitely generated regular extensions \(F/k\), \(\mathrm{trdeg}\ge 2\), and \(k\) algebraically closed or finite): knowing \(K_*^M(F)\) as a graded ring suffices to reconstruct \(F\).

---

## 2) Bogomolov–Tschinkel: \(K_1^M\) and \(K_2^M\) already suffice (char 0, alg. closed base)

### Theorem (function field determined by \(K_1^M\) and \(K_2^M\))
Let \(K\) be the function field of an algebraic variety of **dimension \(>1\)** over an **algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\)**. Then \(K\) is determined (up to isomorphism) by its **first and second Milnor \(K\)-groups**, i.e. by \(K_1^M(K)\) and \(K_2^M(K)\) together with the natural structure relating them. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.4875))

**Paper:** *Milnor \(K_2\) and field homomorphisms* — Fedor Bogomolov, Yuri Tschinkel.  
**arXiv:** `arXiv:0902.4875` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.4875))

**How it addresses your query.** This is stronger than “recover from Milnor \(K\)-theory”: in this geometric setting, degrees \(1\) and \(2\) already determine the field.

---

## 3) Topaz: algebraic dependence is encoded in Milnor \(K\)-theory, giving field determination (broad settings; up to purely inseparable)

### Theorem (algebraic dependence encoded; reconstruction up to inseparability)
Milnor \(K\)-theory encodes algebraic (in)dependence in a field. As an application, in “most situations” the **isomorphism type of a field is determined by its Milnor \(K\)-theory up to purely inseparable extensions**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14665))

**Paper:** *Algebraic dependence and Milnor K-theory* — Adam Topaz.  
**arXiv:** `arXiv:2211.14665` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14665))

**How it addresses your query.** This gives a conceptual mechanism: from \(K_*^M(F)\) one recovers the algebraic dependence relation, which is the key intermediate structure used in reconstruction arguments. (The statement is explicitly “up to purely inseparable extensions”, i.e. you should not expect to distinguish a field from its perfect closure in characteristic \(p\) using such invariants.)

---

## What to watch for (scope/limitations)

1. **Purely inseparable ambiguity (char \(p\))**: many “reconstruction from \(K\)-theory” statements only give the field **up to purely inseparable extension**; this is explicitly emphasized in Topaz’s abstract. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14665))  
2. **Transcendence degree \(\ge 2\)** is a common threshold in these birational/anabelian-style results (Cadoret–Pirutka). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))  
3. **Low-degree data may suffice** in geometric cases (Bogomolov–Tschinkel: \(K_1^M, K_2^M\)). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.4875))

---

If you tell me which class of fields you mean (e.g. arbitrary fields? finitely generated over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\)? number fields? local fields?), I can point to the sharpest reconstruction theorem in that regime and state it in the most precise “if and only if” form (often with explicit functorial reconstruction steps).
response_with:
There are **positive reconstruction theorems** in this direction, but they require hypotheses (typically **finitely generated/function fields of transcendence degree ≥ 2**, and often “regular over a perfect base field”). In complete generality for arbitrary fields, “\(K_*^M(F)\) determines \(F\)” is **false or at least not known** without extra conditions: Milnor \(K\)-theory is insensitive to **purely inseparable** extensions after inverting the characteristic, and reconstruction results generally conclude “up to purely inseparable extension.”

Below are the most relevant precise theorems.

---

## 1) Cadoret–Pirutka: function fields are determined by the graded Milnor \(K\)-ring

**Paper:** *Reconstructing function fields from Milnor K-theory* — Anna Cadoret, Alena Pirutka  
**arXiv:** `1808.04944` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))

**Main reconstruction statement (as advertised in the abstract):**  
Let \(F\) be a **finitely generated regular** field extension of transcendence degree \(\ge 2\) over a **perfect** field \(k\). Then certain “algebraic dependence” data on \(F^\times/k^\times\) determines \(F\) functorially; and **as a special case**, when \(k\) is **algebraically closed or finite**, the **graded Milnor \(K\)-ring**
\[
K_*^M(F)=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0} K_n^M(F)
\]
**determines \(F\) up to isomorphism**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))

**How it answers your query:** this is exactly a “recover \(F\) from its Milnor \(K\)-theory” theorem for a large class of fields (geometric/function fields, \(\operatorname{trdeg}\ge 2\)), with explicit functorial reconstruction.

---

## 2) Topaz: finitely generated fields are (often) determined by Milnor \(K\)-theory, up to purely inseparable extension

**Paper:** *Algebraic dependence and Milnor K-theory* — Adam Topaz  
**arXiv:** `2211.14665` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14665))

**What it proves (high-level statement from the abstract):**  
Algebraic dependence is encoded in Milnor \(K\)-theory; **as an application**, in “most situations” the **isomorphism type of a field** is determined by its Milnor \(K\)-theory **up to purely inseparable extensions**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14665))

**How it answers your query:** it gives a broad “recover the field (up to purely inseparable closure)” result, i.e. if \(K_*^M(F)\cong K_*^M(E)\) (with suitable finiteness/transcendence hypotheses), then \(F\) and \(E\) coincide up to purely inseparable modification.

---

## 3) Bogomolov–Tschinkel: for function fields over algebraically closed fields, \(K_1^M\) and \(K_2^M\) already suffice

**Paper:** *Milnor \(K_2\) and field homomorphisms* — Fedor Bogomolov, Yuri Tschinkel  
**PDF (as circulated):** ([math.nyu.edu](https://math.nyu.edu/~tschinke/papers/yuri/09milnor/milnor12.pdf))

They prove reconstruction for function fields \(K=k(X)\) of **varieties of dimension \(\ge 2\)** over an **algebraically closed** field (in characteristic \(0\) in the version quoted).

A representative precise statement appears early in the paper:

**Theorem 4 (Bogomolov–Tschinkel, paraphrased from their statement):**  
Let \(K,L\) be such function fields. Given an injective homomorphism on “reduced” \( \overline K_1^M \) compatible with the symbol map to \( \overline K_2^M\), and a mild non-degeneracy condition, there exists a **field homomorphism** \(K\to L\) inducing it (up to inversion/sign). ([math.nyu.edu](https://math.nyu.edu/~tschinke/papers/yuri/09milnor/milnor12.pdf))

**How it answers your query:** it shows that in a geometric range, one can recover *field embeddings/isomorphisms* from (essentially) the first two Milnor \(K\)-groups plus compatibility, and hence recover the field itself.

---

## 4) The unavoidable caveat: purely inseparable extensions

Any statement “\(K_*^M(F)\) determines \(F\)” must address that Milnor \(K\)-theory can be **unchanged under purely inseparable extension** after inverting the characteristic \(p\).

A typical formal lemma used in this circle (appearing in the theorem-search results) is:

**Lemma (invariance under purely inseparable extensions; typical form):**  
If \(k'/k\) is purely inseparable of characteristic \(p\), then
\[
K_n^M(k)\left[\tfrac1p\right]\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\; K_n^M(k')\left[\tfrac1p\right]
\quad\text{and}\quad
K_n^M(k)/m\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\; K_n^M(k')/m
\]
for \(m\) prime to \(p\). (So you cannot hope to distinguish \(k\) from \(k'\) by these versions of Milnor \(K\)-theory.)  
This explains why many reconstruction theorems conclude “up to purely inseparable extension.”

---

# Bottom line

- **Yes,** for large and important classes of fields (notably **finitely generated/function fields of transcendence degree \(\ge 2\)** over suitable base fields), one can **reconstruct the field from its Milnor \(K\)-theory ring**, often uniquely (sometimes up to a sign on \(K_1\), and typically **up to purely inseparable extension** in positive characteristic). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04944))  
- **No, not in full generality** without hypotheses: purely inseparable phenomena and other pathologies prevent an unconditional “all fields are determined by \(K_*^M\)” statement.

If you tell me what class of fields you have in mind (e.g. finitely generated over \(\mathbb{Q}\); function fields over algebraically closed fields; local/global fields; arbitrary fields), I can point to the sharpest theorem statement (with theorem number) for that setting.
tool_calls: If F and E are fields and their Milnor K-theory rings K_*^M(F) and K_*^M(E) are isomorphic as graded rings, then F and E are isomorphic fields (possibly up to purely inseparable extension).

It is also slightly more specific in describing what Cadoret–Pirutka and Bogomolov–Tschinkel prove, and includes a concrete caveat about invariance under purely inseparable extensions. B is good and relevant, but some theorem statements are more paraphrastic, it gives fewer precise anchors (no theorem numbers either), and it is a bit less careful about the exact form of the reconstruction claim.

query: when are fraisse limits models of an almost sure theory
response_without:
Fix a *finite relational* language \(L\). Let \(\mathcal K\) be a Fraïssé class of finite \(L\)-structures with Fraïssé limit \(M=\mathrm{Flim}(\mathcal K)\). For each \(n\), put the uniform probability \(\mu_n\) on the finite set \(\mathcal K_n:=\{A\in\mathcal K:\ |A|=n\}\). The **almost sure theory** (a.k.a. limit/0–1 theory) is
\[
T_{\mathrm{as}}(\mathcal K):=\{\varphi\in \mathrm{Sent}(L): \mu_n(\{A\in \mathcal K_n: A\models\varphi\})\to 1\}.
\]
Your question is: *when is \(M\) a model of \(T_{\mathrm{as}}(\mathcal K)\)?* Equivalently, when does
\[
\mathrm{Th}(M)=T_{\mathrm{as}}(\mathcal K)?
\]

1. The class \((\mathcal K_n,\mu_n)\) satisfies a **first-order 0–1 law**.
2. The almost sure theory \(T_{\mathrm{as}}(\mathcal K)\) is exactly the theory axiomatized by all extension axioms (hence it is complete).
3. \(T_{\mathrm{as}}(\mathcal K)=\mathrm{Th}(M)\). In particular, the Fraïssé limit \(M\) is a model of the almost sure theory.

### The Gauss map
On any ppav \((A,\Theta)\), the Gauss map is the rational map
\[
\gamma_\Theta:\Theta \dashrightarrow \mathbb P(T_0A)^\vee \cong \mathbb P^{g-1},\qquad
x\in \Theta_{\mathrm{sm}}\mapsto \text{(translate of the tangent hyperplane }T_x\Theta\text{ to }0).
\]
Equivalently, if \(\Theta\) is locally \(\{\vartheta=0\}\), then \(\gamma_\Theta\) is given by the gradient \([\partial\vartheta/\partial z_1:\cdots:\partial\vartheta/\partial z_g]\), hence is defined exactly where \(\nabla \vartheta\neq 0\), i.e. on \(\Theta_{\mathrm{sm}}\).

### Basic theorem (indeterminacy = singular locus)
**Theorem (tautological, but important).** The indeterminacy locus of \(\gamma_\Theta\) equals \(\mathrm{Sing}(\Theta)\). In fact \(\gamma_\Theta\) is a morphism \(\Theta_{\mathrm{sm}}\to \mathbb P^{g-1}\), and it does not extend across any singular point of \(\Theta\) in general.

So, for a Jacobian, the problem reduces to describing \(\mathrm{Sing}(\Theta)\subset \Theta\).

## 2) The singular (hence indeterminacy) locus for a Jacobian: Riemann–Kempf / Andreotti–Mayer

Let \(W_{g-1}\subset \mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(C)\) be the Brill–Noether locus of effective line bundles of degree \(g-1\) (this is \(\Theta\) up to translation).

### Set-theoretic description
**Theorem (Riemann singularity theorem / Kempf).** A point \(L\in W_{g-1}\) is singular on \(W_{g-1}\) iff \(h^0(C,L)\ge 2\). Equivalently,
\[
\mathrm{Sing}(\Theta) \;=\; W_{g-1}^{1}(C)\;:=\;\{L\in \mathrm{Pic}^{g-1}(C): h^0(L)\ge 2\}.
\]
In particular, the **indeterminacy locus of the Gauss map of the Jacobian theta divisor is exactly \(W_{g-1}^1(C)\)** (after the standard identification \(\Theta\simeq W_{g-1}\) by translation).

This is standard in the Brill–Noether description of theta divisors, and is the entry point to the Andreotti–Mayer stratification \(N_k=\{(A,\Theta):\dim \mathrm{Sing}(\Theta)\ge k\}\).

Kempf’s refinement describes the projectivized tangent cone \(\mathbb P C_L\Theta\subset \mathbb P(H^0(K_C)^\vee)\) at \(L\in W_{g-1}\) in terms of the Petri map
\[
