The claim as stated is **false**: **Arveson’s hyperrigidity conjecture fails even for type I C\*-algebras**.

## Key theorem / counterexample (type I)

**Theorem 1.1 (Dor-On–Salomon, 2024).**  
There exists an operator \(T\) on a Hilbert space such that, letting
\[
\mathcal A=\operatorname{alg}(T)\ \text{(the unital norm-closed operator algebra generated by \(T\))},\qquad 
\mathcal B=C^*(\mathcal A)=C^*(T),
\]
we have:
1. \(\mathcal A\) is **not** hyperrigid in \(\mathcal B\);
2. nevertheless, for **every irreducible \(*\)-representation** \(\pi\) of \(\mathcal B\), the restriction \(\pi|_{\mathcal A}\) has the **unique completely positive extension property** to \(\mathcal B\) (equivalently: every irreducible representation is a boundary representation for the associated operator system);
3. moreover, \(T\) can be chosen as a **rank-one perturbation of a unitary**, and \(\mathcal B=C^*(T)\) is **type I**.

This provides an explicit **type I counterexample** to the conjecture (“irreducibles are boundary” \(\nRightarrow\) hyperrigid). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05018?utm_source=openai))

**Paper:** *Arveson’s hyperrigidity conjecture is false* — Dor-On, Salomon.  
**arXiv:** `arXiv:2404.05018` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05018?utm_source=openai))

## How this relates to the query

Arveson’s hyperrigidity conjecture (one common formulation) predicts that for a separable operator system \(\mathcal S\),
> if the **noncommutative Choquet boundary** is all of \(\widehat{C^*(\mathcal S)}\) (equivalently: all irreducible representations are boundary representations for \(\mathcal S\)), then \(\mathcal S\) should be **hyperrigid**.

Dor-On–Salomon show this implication **fails** even when the generated C\*-algebra is **type I**, so one cannot salvage the conjecture by restricting to type I algebras. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05018?utm_source=openai))

## Context: hyperrigidity ↔ unique extension for all representations

A standard characterization (Arveson) says hyperrigidity is equivalent to a unique extension property **for all representations**, not just irreducible ones:

**Arveson (2011), Theorem 7.3 (UEP characterization).**  
An operator system \(S\subset A=C^*(S)\) is hyperrigid iff **every representation** of \(A\) has the unique extension property relative to \(S\). (There are separability hypotheses in some formulations.)  

This explains why “all irreducibles are boundary” is *a priori* weaker than hyperrigidity, and Dor-On–Salomon exploit exactly that gap (in a type I setting). ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00020-021-02663-3?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me which precise “type I” hypothesis you mean (postliminal/liminal? separable? nuclear?), and which formulation of the conjecture you’re using (operator systems vs. generating sets vs. operator algebras), I can restate the result in exactly that language.
tool_calls: If an operator system S generates a separable type I C*-algebra B and every irreducible representation of B restricts to S with the unique extension property, then S is hyperrigid in B.

Arveson's hyperrigidity conjecture fails even when the generated C*-algebra is type I (postliminal), by exhibiting a separable operator system whose noncommutative Choquet boundary equals the spectrum but which is not hyperrigid.

## 1) Main properness theorems (full statements, as standardly cited)

### (A) Properness for tame Deligne–Mumford targets (Abramovich–Vistoli)
**Theorem (Abramovich–Vistoli, Theorem 1.4.1).**  
Fix a noetherian base scheme \(S\). Let \(\mathcal X\to S\) be a **tame proper Deligne–Mumford stack** admitting a **projective coarse moduli scheme** \(X\). Then the stack \(\mathcal K_{g,n}(\mathcal X,\beta)\) of \(n\)-pointed genus \(g\) **twisted stable maps** to \(\mathcal X\) of class \(\beta\) is an **algebraic stack**, **proper** over \(S\) (equivalently it satisfies the valuative criterion), is **of Deligne–Mumford type** over \(S\), and it admits a **projective coarse moduli space**. ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/journals/jams/2002-15-01/S0894-0347-01-00380-0/viewer/?utm_source=openai))

This is the “moduli of twisted stable maps is proper” result used throughout orbifold GW theory.

**Reference / arXiv**
- Dan Abramovich, Angelo Vistoli, *Compactifying the space of stable maps*.  
  arXiv: **math/9908167** ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9908167))

---

### (B) Properness for tame Artin targets (Abramovich–Olsson–Vistoli)
**Theorem (Abramovich–Olsson–Vistoli; properness over coarse stable maps).**  
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a **tame Artin stack** with coarse moduli space \(M\). Then the moduli stack \(\mathcal K_{g,n}(\mathcal M)\) of twisted stable maps to \(\mathcal M\) is **algebraic**, and the natural morphism
\[
\mathcal K_{g,n}(\mathcal M)\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal K_{g,n}(M)
\]
is **proper** and **quasi-finite**. In particular, if \(\mathcal K_{g,n}(M)\) is proper (e.g. when \(M\) is projective), then \(\mathcal K_{g,n}(\mathcal M)\) is proper. ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/jag/2011-20-03/S1056-3911-2010-00569-3/?utm_source=openai))

**Reference / arXiv**
- Dan Abramovich, Martin Olsson, Angelo Vistoli, *Twisted stable maps to tame Artin stacks*.  
  arXiv: **0801.3040** ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.3040?utm_source=openai))

(There is also an AMS JAG entry and a published correction; if you need the exact published theorem numbering, tell me which version you want to cite.) ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/jag/2015-24-02/S1056-3911-2014-00653-6/?utm_source=openai))

This is the stacky analogue of Kontsevich stable map compactness and is the engine behind properness in AV. query: ideal of jacobian of curves as a projective variety
response_without:
Your phrase “ideal of Jacobian of curves as a projective variety” can mean (at least) three different *projective* objects, with three rather different answers:

1) **The curve \(C\) itself in its canonical embedding** \(C\hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{g-1}\): describe the *canonical ideal* \(I_C\).
2) **The Jacobian abelian variety** \(J(C)\) embedded by a theta line bundle, e.g. \(|m\Theta|\): describe the homogeneous ideal of \(J(C)\subset \mathbf P^N\).
3) **The Kummer variety** \(K(J(C)):=J(C)/\{\pm 1\}\) embedded by \(|2\Theta|\): describe the ideal of \(K(J(C))\subset \mathbf P^{2^g-1}\), and/or the additional equations characterizing those Kummers that come from Jacobians (Schottky-type questions).

Below are the most standard theorems/results that address these, with precise statements and pointers. If you tell me which of (1)–(3) you mean (and genus \(g\), characteristic, and which embedding), I can narrow to the exact “ideal generators / degrees / syzygies”.

---

## A. Canonical curve \(C\subset \mathbf P^{g-1}\): Petri–Enriques–Babbage

### Theorem (Petri / Enriques–Petri: generators of the canonical ideal)
Let \(C\) be a **smooth non-hyperelliptic** projective curve of genus \(g\ge 4\) over an algebraically closed field (typically \(\mathrm{char}\,0\), and many statements extend to good characteristics). Consider the **canonical embedding**
\[
\varphi_{|K_C|}: C \hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{g-1}.
\]
Let \(I_C \subset k[x_0,\dots,x_{g-1}]\) be the homogeneous ideal of the canonical image. Then:

- \(I_C\) is **generated by quadrics** (degree \(2\) forms) **unless** \(C\) is
  1) **trigonal** (admits a \(g^1_3\)), or  
  2) a **smooth plane quintic** (necessarily \(g=6\)),

and in those exceptional cases, cubic generators are needed in addition to quadrics.

This is the classical “Petri theorem” statement used constantly in syzygies of curves. (Modern treatments appear in standard texts on syzygies.)

**How this relates to your query:** if by “Jacobian of curves” you meant “data attached to curves” and you are really asking for equations of the **curve** in projective space, this is the fundamental answer: it tells you the *degrees of generators* of the ideal of the canonical model.

**Useful reference text (syzygies perspective):**
- Robert Lazarsfeld, *Lectures on the Syzygies and Geometry of Algebraic Curves* (preliminary draft). ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/robert.lazarsfeld/LSGAV.Prelim.Draft.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
  (This isn’t an arXiv link, but it is a standard modern exposition.)

(If you want, I can also give the stronger Green’s conjecture/Voisin results on the *minimal free resolution* of \(I_C\), i.e. not just generators but all syzygies.)

---

## B. Characterizing Jacobians among ppav via projective geometry of the Kummer: Welters–Krichever (trisecants)

Here one puts \((X,\Theta)=(J(C),\Theta_C)\) into projective space via \(|2\Theta|\) and studies the **Kummer variety**
\[
K(X)\subset \mathbf P^{2^g-1}.
\]

### Theorem (Welters’ trisecant conjecture, proved by Krichever)
Let \((X,\Theta)\) be an **indecomposable** principally polarized abelian variety (ppav) over \(\mathbf C\). Then
\[
(X,\Theta) \text{ is a Jacobian of a smooth curve }
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K(X)\subset \mathbf P^{2^g-1} \text{ admits a trisecant line.}
\]
Equivalently (in the standard formulations), the existence of a suitable trisecant (or degenerate trisecant/flex condition) to the Kummer variety characterizes Jacobians among indecomposable ppav’s.

**How this relates:** this is a genuinely **projective** characterization of the “Jacobian locus”: it doesn’t give the full homogeneous ideal of \(K(X)\), but it gives *distinguished projective-linear incidence conditions* (trisecants) that cut out Jacobians among Kummers.

**References (with arXiv):**
- I. Krichever, *Characterizing Jacobians via trisecants of the Kummer Variety*, arXiv:math/0605625. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605625?utm_source=openai))  
- I. Krichever, *Trisecant Lines And Jacobians, II*, arXiv:alg-geom/9306007. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9306007?utm_source=openai))  
- (Expository/related) *Soliton equations and the Riemann–Schottky problem*, arXiv:1111.0164. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.0164?utm_source=openai))  

---

## C. Characterizing Jacobians via equations of theta functions (KP / Shiota)

This answers the “ideal/equations” question in an analytic-algebraic way: the Jacobian locus is cut out by integrable-system PDE’s on theta functions.

### Theorem (Shiota: Novikov’s conjecture / KP characterization)
An indecomposable ppav \((X,\Theta)\) over \(\mathbf C\) is a **Jacobian** iff its Riemann theta function satisfies the **Kadomtsev–Petviashvili (KP)** equation (more precisely: a suitable KP-type condition for the theta function, in a standard normalization).

**How this relates:** while not presented as generators of a homogeneous ideal in a polynomial ring, it gives *explicit equations* (differential/algebraic in theta data) cutting out Jacobians in the moduli of ppav. This is a major “equations for Jacobians” result.

**Reference (survey-level arXiv source):**
- *Soliton equations and the Riemann–Schottky problem*, arXiv:1111.0164. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.0164?utm_source=openai))  
(For a proof-oriented discussion, see also Krichever’s work on integrable equations. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0504192?utm_source=openai)))

---

## D. Low genus: explicit projective equations for Kummers (hence Jacobians)

If your interest is “write down the ideal explicitly” rather than abstract characterization:

- **Genus 2:** the Kummer surface \(K(J(C))\subset \mathbf P^3\) is a **quartic surface** (a single quartic equation). (This is classical; many computational sources exist.) ([magma.maths.usyd.edu.au](https://magma.maths.usyd.edu.au/magma/handbook/text/1621?utm_source=openai))  
- **Genus 3 (non-hyperelliptic):** \(K(J(C))\subset \mathbf P^7\) sits as the **singular locus** of a distinguished quartic hypersurface (the **Coble quartic**). ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-sigma/article/coble-quadric/C1266FBBCDCB4A37ABFE27BD8C50D2D0?utm_source=openai))  

These are among the most concrete “projective ideal” descriptions available.

---

## What I need from you to answer *exactly* the ideal question
Which object/embedding do you mean?

1) Ideal of the **canonical curve** \(C\subset \mathbf P^{g-1}\)? (Petri etc.)
2) Ideal of the **Jacobian** \(J(C)\subset \mathbf P^N\) via \(|m\Theta|\) for some \(m\) (say \(m=3\) or \(4\))?
3) Ideal of the **Kummer** \(K(J(C))\subset \mathbf P^{2^g-1}\) via \(|2\Theta|\)?
4) Or the **Jacobian locus** inside the moduli/proj of theta constants (Schottky-type “ideal”)?

Also: genus \(g\)? characteristic? and do you want **set-theoretic** equations or **scheme-theoretic** generators/minimal free resolution?
response_with:
Your phrase “**ideal of Jacobian of curves as a projective variety**” can mean (at least) two closely related projective-geometry problems:

1. **Equations for the Jacobian \(J(C)\)** itself after choosing a projective embedding (e.g. via \(|m\Theta|\)).
2. **Equations for the Kummer variety** \(\mathrm{Kum}(J(C)) := J(C)/\{\pm 1\}\), which *does* have a very standard projective embedding via \(|2\Theta|\):
\[
\mathrm{Kum}(J(C)) \hookrightarrow \mathbb P^{2^g-1}.
\]
A lot of the “ideal” literature is about this Kummer embedding, because it is canonical for a ppav and interacts well with theta functions.

Below are precise theorem statements that are directly relevant, together with arXiv pointers where I can (and classic references where the theorem is standard).

---

## A. Characterizing Jacobians via *projective* conditions on the Kummer embedding (trisecants)

### Theorem (Gunning trisecant criterion; one formulation)
Let \((A,\Theta)\) be a principally polarized abelian variety (ppav). Consider the Kummer embedding
\[
\mathrm{Kum}(A)\subset \mathbb P^{2^g-1} \quad \text{given by } |2\Theta|.
\]
If the Kummer image \(\mathrm{Kum}(A)\) admits a **1-parameter family of trisecant lines**
\[
\mathrm{Kum}(p+a_1),\ \mathrm{Kum}(p+a_2),\ \mathrm{Kum}(p+a_3) \text{ are collinear for all } p \text{ in a curve},
\]
for fixed distinct \(a_1,a_2,a_3\in A\), then \(A\) is the Jacobian of a (smooth projective) curve. 

**How it relates to “ideal/equations”:** “Three points are collinear” is the vanishing of \(2\times2\) minors of a \(2\times 3\) matrix of homogeneous coordinates of the three Kummer points. So the Jacobian condition is expressed by *explicit projective rank conditions* on the Kummer image—i.e. by polynomial equations in the homogeneous coordinates of \(\mathbb P^{2^g-1}\).

**Reference:** Gunning’s classical trisecant results (the theorem_search record cites “Gunning 1982b”). 

---

### Theorem (Krichever: trisecant conjecture / degenerate trisecant criterion)
Let \((X,\Theta)\) be an **indecomposable** ppav. Then \(X\) is the Jacobian of an algebraic curve **iff** the Kummer variety \(K(X)\subset \mathbb P^{2^g-1}\) (via \(|2\Theta|\)) admits a **degenerate trisecant line** (equivalently, an inflectionary tangent/flex in appropriate formulations). 

**How it relates to the ideal:** Existence of a (possibly degenerate) trisecant is again a set of explicit polynomial conditions in the projective coordinates of the Kummer embedding; these conditions are essentially “Fay-type” theta identities rewritten as homogeneous equations cutting out special ppavs (the Jacobian locus) inside the ambient projective geometry of Kummer images.

---

## B. “Ideal of the Kummer surface” in low genus: explicit quartics (genus 2)

For \(g=2\), \(\mathrm{Kum}(J(C))\subset \mathbb P^3\) is a quartic surface with 16 nodes. The “ideal” here is literally principal, generated by one quartic.

### Theorem (genus 2 Kummer quartic equations via theta functions; representative formulation)
For a genus-2 Jacobian (often presented in Rosenhain form), the associated singular Kummer variety in \(\mathbb P^3\) is the image of (certain) theta functions and satisfies an explicit **quartic equation** (“Kummer quartic”). 

**How it relates:** this gives an explicit generator for the homogeneous ideal of \(\mathrm{Kum}(J(C))\subset \mathbb P^3\) (in this embedding).

---

## C. A different (also common) meaning: the Jacobian *locus* inside projective space of modular forms (Schottky-type equations)

Sometimes “Jacobian of curves as a projective variety” means: embed the moduli space \(\mathcal A_g\) (or a level cover) into projective space via modular forms; then the **Jacobian locus** \(\mathcal J_g \subset \mathcal A_g\) has an ideal (the **Schottky problem**). Let \(M\) be a connected, oriented 3–manifold. By a **knot in \(M\)** I mean an (oriented) tame embedding \(K:S^1\hookrightarrow M\), up to ambient isotopy.

In a general \(M\), there are two closely related “sum” operations you’ll see in the literature:

1. **Local connected sum** \(K_1\#K_2\) (well-defined when the knots lie in disjoint balls, or equivalently when you are summing in a *fixed* ball in \(M\)).  
2. **Connected sum of pairs** \((M_1,K_1)\#(M_2,K_2)\) (always well-defined and canonical up to isotopy, because the ambient manifolds are summed at the same time).

The subtle point is: **if you try to define \(\#\) for two arbitrary knots in a fixed non-simply-connected \(M\) by “choosing an arc between them and banding/piping along it”, the result can depend on that choice** (so it is not a canonical binary operation on isotopy classes in general). This is exactly why papers about prime decomposition in general 3–manifolds are careful about the definition. ([mathworld.wolfram.com](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KnotSum.html?utm_source=openai))

---

## A. Connected sum of *knot pairs* \((M,K)\)

### Definition (connected sum of pairs)
Let \((M_1,K_1)\) and \((M_2,K_2)\) be oriented knots in oriented closed (or compact) 3–manifolds.

Choose embedded 3–balls \(B_i\subset M_i\) such that \(B_i\cap K_i\) is a **properly embedded unknotted arc** \(\alpha_i\subset B_i\) (i.e. \((B_i,\alpha_i)\cong (D^3, \text{standard diameter})\)). Remove \(\operatorname{int}(B_i)\) and glue
\[
(M_1\setminus \operatorname{int}B_1,\ \overline{K_1\setminus \operatorname{int}\alpha_1})
\quad\cup_{\ \partial B_1\cong \partial B_2\ }\quad
(M_2\setminus \operatorname{int}B_2,\ \overline{K_2\setminus \operatorname{int}\alpha_2})
\]
by an **orientation-reversing** homeomorphism \(\partial B_1\to \partial B_2\) that matches the four endpoints of \(\alpha_1\) to those of \(\alpha_2\) in the “crosswise” way so the arcs concatenate to a circle.

The result is a knot \(K_1\#K_2\subset M_1\# M_2\). This is the standard “ball–arc pair” formulation (equivalent to the usual \(S^3\) definition, just keeping track of the ambient summing sphere). It is canonical up to isotopy of the resulting pair \((M_1\#M_2,\ K_1\#K_2)\) (given the orientations). This is the notion used in the general prime-decomposition theory for knots in manifolds. ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1989-313-02/S0002-9947-1989-0997679-2/home.html?utm_source=openai))

### Why this is the right generalization
- In \(S^3\), this recovers the usual connected sum of knots.
- In a general \(M\), you avoid having to choose a “connecting path” inside \(M\); instead you connect-sum the ambient manifolds in a controlled way.

**Key reference (prime decomposition in manifolds).**  
K. Miyazaki, *Conjugation and the prime decomposition of knots in closed, oriented 3-manifolds*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **313** (1989), no. 2. ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1989-313-02/S0002-9947-1989-0997679-2/home.html?utm_source=openai))  
(No arXiv appears to be standardly listed for this 1989 paper.)

Miyazaki’s work is the standard place where this definition is leveraged to discuss existence/uniqueness of prime decompositions in closed oriented 3–manifolds. ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/20596/prime-decomposition-for-knots-in-manifolds?utm_source=openai))

---

## B. “Connected sum” inside a *fixed* 3–manifold \(M\): local vs. non-local

### B1. Local connected sum (well-defined when localized in a ball)
If you have two knots \(K,J\subset M\) that each lie in (possibly different) embedded 3–balls in \(M\), you can first isotope them into **disjoint** balls \(B_K,B_J\subset M\), form the usual \(S^3\)-connected sum inside a larger ball (or by tubing across a small 1–handle connecting the balls), and view the result as a new knot in \(M\). In effect, you are using a “standard” region of \(M\) that is just a 3–ball, so the construction is independent of choices up to isotopy.

This is the version that behaves like the classical connected sum operation because everything is happening in a simply-connected ball.

### B2. Band sum / piping along an arc (not canonical in general)
Given disjoint knots \(K,J\subset M\), pick an embedded arc \(\gamma\) in \(M\) with one endpoint on each knot, and perform a **band sum** (attach a band/1–handle along small subarcs of \(K\) and \(J\) guided by \(\gamma\)). This produces a new single knot \(K\ \natural_\gamma\ J\) in \(M\).

- In \(S^3\), with extra conditions (or by choosing the “standard” band), this recovers connected sum.
- In a general \(M\), **different choices of \(\gamma\)** (or its homotopy class rel endpoints) can yield non-isotopic results, so this is not a well-defined binary operation on isotopy classes of knots in \(M\).

This is the generalization usually called **band sum**, and connected sum is the special case where the banding is “standard.” ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_sum?utm_source=openai))

---

## C. Theorems that clarify how “sum” is detected/controlled

These results are not “definitions”, but they are the standard structural facts that tell you when a band sum is forced to be a genuine connected sum (in the classical sense) and when decomposition is meaningful.

### Theorem (Gabai: genus superadditivity under band connected sum)
If a knot \(L\) is a band connected sum of knots \(K_1,\dots,K_n\) (in \(S^3\)), then the Seifert genus satisfies a superadditivity inequality (so band sums cannot reduce genus unexpectedly).

Reference:  
D. Gabai, *Genus is superadditive under band connected sum*, **Topology 26** (1987), 209–210. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0040938387900619?utm_source=openai))

(There is no standard arXiv link for this 1987 Topology note.)

**Relevance:** Band sum is the ambient-manifold generalization people often try first; Gabai’s theorem is part of the toolkit distinguishing “honest connected sums” from more general bandings. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0040938387900619?utm_source=openai))

### Theorem (Scharlemann: band sum gives unknot only in trivial way)
Scharlemann proved strong constraints on when a band sum can yield the unknot; informally, “if a band sum of two knots is the unknot, then the banding is essentially the standard connected-sum-of-unknots situation.”

Reference metadata is widely cited as:  
M. Scharlemann, *Unknotting number one knots are prime*, (1985). ([eudml.org](https://eudml.org/doc/143276?utm_source=openai))

**Relevance:** Again, this controls “sum-like” operations (banding) and supports prime/composite distinctions via sphere/annulus arguments in complements.

---

## D. Practical takeaway (what definition to use)

- If you want a **canonical definition that works uniformly**, use **connected sum of pairs**
  \[

  built from ball–arc pairs. This is the notion used in the prime decomposition theory in general closed oriented 3–manifolds (e.g. Miyazaki). ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1989-313-02/S0002-9947-1989-0997679-2/home.html?utm_source=openai))

- If you insist on staying inside a **fixed** \(M\), you either:
  - restrict to the **local** situation (everything in a ball), where you recover the classical behavior; or
  - accept the more general **band sum** (depends on the band/arc and is not canonical).

### Definition (knot sum / connected sum) for knots in general 3–manifolds

There are two common “sum” operations once you leave \(S^3\). The one most people mean by *knot sum* is the **connected sum of pairs**.

#### 1) Connected sum of pairs \((M_1,K_1)\#(M_2,K_2)\)

Let \(K_i\subset M_i\) be (smooth or PL locally flat) knots in closed, oriented 3–manifolds.

1. Choose an embedded 3–ball \(B_i\subset M_i\) such that \(B_i\cap K_i\) is a **trivial properly embedded arc** (equivalently \((B_i,B_i\cap K_i)\cong (D^3, D^1)\) as pairs).
2. Remove the interiors: \(M_i^\circ := M_i\setminus \operatorname{int}(B_i)\). Each \(\partial M_i^\circ\cong S^2\) meets the knot in two points (the arc endpoints).
3. Glue \(\partial M_1^\circ\) to \(\partial M_2^\circ\) by an **orientation-reversing** diffeomorphism/homeomorphism \(f:S^2\to S^2\) that matches the two marked points in the obvious way (so that the two remaining knot-arcs concatenate).
4. The resulting manifold is \(M_1\# M_2\), and the glued-up 1–manifold is a knot \(K_1\# K_2 \subset M_1\# M_2\).

So
\[
(M_1,K_1)\#(M_2,K_2) \;:=\; (\,M_1\# M_2,\; K_1\# K_2\,).
\]

**Well-definedness.** Up to ambient isotopy of the resulting pair, this construction does not depend on the choices of balls, the trivial arcs inside them, or the gluing map (once orientations are fixed). In the “knots in homology spheres / rational homology spheres” literature, this is the standard monoidal operation used to talk about additivity of invariants under connected sum of pairs; see e.g. Taylor–Tomova, *Additive invariants for knots, links and graphs in 3-manifolds* (Geom. Topol. 22 (2018)), arXiv:1606.03408. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.03408))

---

### 2) “Local knotting” / summing a knot in \(M\) with a knot in \(S^3\)

A frequently used special case is
\[
(M,K)\#(S^3,J) \cong (M,\,K\# J),
\]
i.e. you tie a classical knot \(J\subset S^3\) into \(K\) inside a small ball in \(M\). Formally it’s the same ball–arc gluing definition above, but since \(M\# S^3\cong M\), the ambient manifold stays \(M\).

---

### 3) A different operation: **band sum** (often *not* well-defined)

Given two disjoint knots \(K_1\cup K_2\subset M\), choosing an embedded band joining them and performing surgery along the band gives a new knot \(K_b\). This **depends on the band** in general and is *not* a canonical “knot sum” unless you impose “trivial band” conditions. (This is why, in arbitrary \(M\), people usually reserve “connected sum” for the ball–arc construction on pairs.)

---

## A precise theorem-level reference (from theorem search)

A closely related “well-definedness” statement is proved in the contact/Legendrian setting: the connected sum operation on knots (together with the ambient connected sum) is independent of the auxiliary choices. Concretely:

- **Lemma 5.9** (connected sum of Legendrian knots is independent of choices of arcs/balls/gluing), in a paper treating connected sums inside tight contact 3–manifolds. (This is stronger than the purely topological statement, but it formalizes the same gluing paradigm and independence-of-choices issue.)  

Even though that lemma is stated for Legendrian knots, its *topological* shadow is exactly the usual well-definedness of the connected sum of pairs.

### Papers / links

## Executive summary (what is actually known)

There is **no single clean published theorem of the form “Beilinson conjectures ⇒ Kimura–O’Sullivan finite-dimensionality for all Chow motives.”** What *is* known is that certain **standard packages** of “Beilinson-type” conjectures, when interpreted strongly enough (often together with standard conjectures / conservativity assumptions), imply **finite-dimensionality/Kimura-finiteness** in important settings (notably **numerical motives**, and various special classes of Chow motives).

Below are the sharpest implication statements I know that are closest to what you ask, with precise references and theorem numbers where available.

---

## 1) Beilinson–Murre-type conjectures ⇒ Kimura finite-dimensionality (conditional, but explicit)

### Theorem (Guletskii–Pedrini: Murre’s conjecture for a power ⇒ finite-dimensionality)
Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety. If **Murre’s conjecture** (existence of a Chow–Künneth decomposition satisfying Murre’s conditions) holds for a “suitable” self-product \(X^{m}\) (for some \(m\)), then the Chow motive \(h(X)\) is **finite-dimensional in the sense of Kimura**.

- Precise source: Vladimir Guletskii, Claudio Pedrini, *Finite dimensional motives and the Conjectures of Beilinson and Murre*.
- arXiv: `math/0303170` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0303170))
- The relevant implication is stated in their abstract as **“Conversely (Theorem 17) … implies finite dimensionality of \(M(X)\)”** ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0303170))

**How this relates to “Beilinson conjectures”:**
In much of the literature, “Beilinson conjectures on Chow groups” are bundled with the **Bloch–Beilinson filtration** and **Murre’s conjectures** (existence/compatibility of a Chow–Künneth decomposition and induced filtration). Under that reading, Guletskii–Pedrini give a **concrete bridge** from Murre-type conjectures to Kimura finite-dimensionality.

---

## 2) “Beilinson-type conservativity” ⇒ numerical motives are Kimura-finite (a very clean theorem)

### Theorem (Bondarko: conservativity of a realization ⇒ numerical motives Kimura-finite)
Assume a realization functor (étale or de Rham) is **conservative** on \(DM_{gm}(k;\mathbb Q)\). Then **numerical motives are Kimura-finite**, and motivic zeta functions are rational.

- Mikhail V. Bondarko, *Conservativity of realizations implies that numerical motives are Kimura-finite and motivic zeta functions are rational*.
- arXiv: `1807.10791` ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.10791))

**How this relates to Beilinson conjectures:**
Conservativity of realizations is often viewed as part of a “Beilinson-style” expected picture (realizations detect motivic isomorphisms). Bondarko proves **Kimura-finiteness (for numerical motives)** from precisely that sort of motivic conservativity assumption.

> Caveat: this gives **Kimura-finiteness in the category of numerical motives**, not automatically finite-dimensionality of Chow motives. Still, it’s the cleanest “Beilinson-flavored ⇒ Kimura” implication I know in print.

---

## 3) From Kimura-finiteness to nilpotence statements (often used as the “engine”)

While not an implication *from* Beilinson, the following equivalences are frequently used in conditional arguments that *start* from Beilinson/Murre and *end* at Kimura via nilpotence.

### Theorem (Del Padrone–Mazza: equivalences under a sign conjecture)
In the category of Chow motives, assuming a **homological sign conjecture** for \(X\), the following are equivalent:
- Kimura-finiteness of \(h(X)\),
- certain Schur-finiteness,
- nilpotence of specific groups of correspondences (formulated in terms of \(\mathrm{CH}^{n i}(X^i\times X^i)_{\mathrm{num}}\), \(n=\dim X\)).

- Alessio Del Padrone, Carlo Mazza, *Schur finiteness and nilpotency*.

**How this relates:**
Many Beilinson/Murre-type conjectures predict strong filtrations and vanishing/nilpotence phenomena for correspondences; Del Padrone–Mazza provide a way to convert **nilpotence + sign** into **Kimura-finiteness**.

There are (at least) **two common “Beilinson conjecture” packages**:

1. **Bloch–Beilinson / Beilinson–Murre package**: existence and functoriality of a filtration on Chow groups, Chow–Künneth projectors, etc.

query: Quasi-isometry invariance cohomology with coefficient in group ring
response_without:
Let \(G\) be a finitely generated group and \(RG\) its group ring over a commutative ring \(R\) (typically \(R=\mathbb Z\)). Your query is about **quasi-isometry invariance of group (co)homology with coefficients in \(RG\)**, i.e. invariance of \(H^\*(G;RG)\) or \(H_\*(G;RG)\) under quasi-isometries \(G\simeq_{\mathrm{qi}} H\).

There are two distinct “levels” of results in the literature:

1. **A strong positive quasi-isometry invariance theorem** for \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\), but only **within a finiteness class** (finite type / type \(F\)).  
2. **More general coarse invariance results** for (co)homology with coefficients in *induced/coinduced* modules; these often apply to modules of the form \(R[G]\otimes_R V\), and thus are closely related to \(RG\), but you need to match left/right module conventions carefully.

Below are the most relevant theorems and references.

---

## 1) Gersten–Block–Weinberger quasi-isometry invariance of \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\) (finite type)

### Theorem (Gersten–Block–Weinberger; as quoted/used by Whyte)
If \(G\) and \(H\) are **groups of finite type** (equivalently: admit finite \(K(G,1)\), i.e. type \(F\)), and \(G\) and \(H\) are quasi-isometric, then
\[
H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\ \cong\ H^\*(H;\mathbb ZH)
\]
(up to the appropriate canonical identifications; in practice one compares via uniformly contractible, bounded geometry models and compactly supported cohomology).

*Where this appears clearly:* Whyte states (and sketches the mechanism via uniform acyclicity / chain maps of bounded support) that:

> “From this follows the theorem of Gersten and Block–Weinberger, that \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\) is a quasi-isometry invariant among groups of finite type.” ([homepages.math.uic.edu](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kwhyte/QTPart2.pdf))

**How it relates to your query.** This is exactly the statement “quasi-isometry invariance of cohomology with coefficients in the group ring,” in the most classical sense. The caveat is the **finite type (type \(F\))** hypothesis; without such hypotheses, invariance is not known in this generality and can fail for various finiteness-type reasons.

### Reference (via Whyte’s notes, which point to the original result)
- Kevin Whyte, *Quasi-actions on trees II* (notes/PDF). ([homepages.math.uic.edu](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kwhyte/QTPart2.pdf))  
  (This is not the original Gersten/BW paper, but it is a clean place where the theorem is explicitly invoked and the proof strategy is discussed.)

*Remark.* If you need the **original** bibliographic data (Gersten; Block–Weinberger), tell me and I’ll chase down the exact paper(s)/theorem numbers; Whyte’s notes indicate the statement but do not, in the snippet we opened, give a full citation line with theorem number.

---

## 2) Coarse invariance for group (co)homology with induced/coinduced coefficients (Li; Shalom–Sauer circle)

A more flexible framework proves coarse/quasi-isometry invariance for **group (co)homology with coefficients in certain classes of modules**, notably induced and coinduced modules. Since \(RG\) itself is (up to side conventions) an induced module, these results are conceptually adjacent and sometimes directly applicable.

### Theorem (Xin Li: coarse invariance for (co)homology with induced/coinduced coefficients)
Xin Li proves that **group homology and cohomology with coefficients in a class including all induced and co-induced modules are coarse invariants**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07375))

This includes invariance consequences for finiteness properties \(FP_n\), duality groups, etc. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07375))

**How it relates to \(RG\).** The left regular module \(RG\) is a basic induced module (from the trivial subgroup), and variants like \(RG\otimes_R V\) are prototypical induced coefficients. So Li’s theorem often implies invariance statements for “\(RG\)-flavored” coefficients—though you must align:
- whether you view coefficients as **left** \(RG\)-modules or **right** \(RG\)-modules,
- and whether the functor is \(H^\*(G;M)=\operatorname{Ext}^\*_{RG}(R,M)\) with \(R\) the trivial module.

### Reference
- Xin Li, *Dynamic characterizations of quasi-isometry, and applications to cohomology*, arXiv:1604.07375. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07375))

---

## 3) Sauer’s induction approach & quasi-isometry invariants (background)

Roman Sauer developed an “induction in group homology” viewpoint (building on Shalom) using topological couplings; this is part of the modern toolkit behind coarse invariance results for homological dimensions and related invariants.

### Reference
- Roman Sauer, *Homological Invariants and Quasi-Isometry*, arXiv:math/0312129. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312129))

**How it relates.** While Sauer’s abstract (as opened) emphasizes (co)homological dimension and real cohomology rings for nilpotent groups, his techniques are part of the same ecosystem used to establish coarse invariance results for broader coefficient classes. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312129))

---

## 4) Coarse Alexander duality uses \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\) as the “right” invariant at infinity (Kapovich–Kleiner)

Kapovich–Kleiner develop a coarse Alexander duality theory in which **cohomology with group ring coefficients** plays the role of “cohomology at infinity” for groups acting on coarse Poincaré duality spaces.

### Reference
- Michael Kapovich, Bruce Kleiner, *Coarse Alexander duality and duality groups*, arXiv:math/9911003. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9911003))

**How it relates.** This doesn’t by itself assert quasi-isometry invariance of \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\) in full generality, but it strongly supports the idea that \(H^\*(G;\mathbb ZG)\) is the correct receptacle for large-scale/topological-at-infinity information, and it is frequently combined with the Gersten–Block–Weinberger invariance (under finiteness hypotheses).

---

# What to clarify (so I can give the sharpest theorem statement + theorem numbers)

When you say “cohomology with coefficient in group ring,” do you mean:

1. **Ordinary group cohomology** \(H^\*(G;RG)\) as \(\operatorname{Ext}^\*_{RG}(R,RG)\)?  
2. **Cohomology with compact supports** \(H_c^\*(X)\) for a proper cocompact \(G\)-space \(X\), using the identification \(H_c^\*(X)\cong H^\*(G;RG)\) under type \(F\) assumptions? (This is the route used in many quasi-isometry invariance proofs.)  
3. Are you asking about invariance of the **graded groups only**, or also the **ring structure** (cup product) when defined?

If you answer those, I can (i) pin down the exact “finite type/type \(F\)” hypotheses you want, and (ii) chase the original Gersten / Block–Weinberger paper(s) to give **exact theorem numbers and full statements** rather than the (accurate but secondary) statement as quoted by Whyte.

What is (and is not) known here splits into two parts:

* **(A) “Raw” group cohomology with coefficients in the group ring** \(H^*(G;RG)\) (often \(R=\mathbb Z\)) is **not known to be a quasi-isometry invariant in general**, and one should not expect a general invariance theorem without extra hypotheses (finite type/Poincaré duality/“coarse Poincaré duality” type conditions).
* **(B) There are closely related *coarse* cohomology theories** (uniformly finite/coarse cohomology, \(\ell^p\)– or Orlicz-cohomology) that **are** quasi-isometry invariants, and in good geometric situations they identify with \(H^*(G;RG)\) or with the compactly supported cohomology of a universal cover.

Below are precise theorems that people actually use in this circle.

---

## 1) What you can safely claim: invariance of *duality/Poincaré duality* properties (which are defined using \(H^*(G;RG)\))

A standard characterization of (Bieri–Eckmann) **duality groups** over a ring \(R\) is: \(G\) has finite cohomological dimension \(n\) over \(R\) and
\[
H^i(G;RG)=0 \ \text{for } i\neq n,\qquad H^n(G;RG)\neq 0,
\]
with \(H^n(G;RG)\) the dualizing module.

So quasi-isometry invariance of “\(G\) is a duality group” is an indirect quasi-isometry invariance statement about \(H^*(G;RG)\).

### Theorem (Li, “Dynamic characterizations…”, coarse invariance of duality/Poincaré duality)
Among groups of finite cohomological dimension over a commutative ring \(R\) with unit, **being a duality group over \(R\)** (and being a **Poincaré duality group over \(R\)**) is a **coarse invariant** (hence a quasi-isometry invariant for finitely generated groups). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07375?utm_source=openai))

**Reference.**
*Xin Li*, **Dynamic characterizations of quasi-isometry, and applications to cohomology**, arXiv:1604.07375. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07375?utm_source=openai))

**How it relates to your query.** Duality/Poincaré duality is defined in terms of vanishing/nonvanishing patterns of \(H^*(G;RG)\), so this theorem says that a large chunk of the “shape” of group-ring coefficient cohomology (at least the pattern needed to be a duality group) is QI-invariant under finiteness hypotheses.

---

## 2) Coarse (quasi-isometry invariant) cohomology that is “morally” \(H^*(G;RG)\)

There is a well-developed theory that **quasi-isometries induce isomorphisms on coarse/coarsely-defined (co)homology** under bounded geometry + uniform acyclicity hypotheses; for groups one typically models \(G\) by a bounded-geometry CW-complex quasi-isometric to it.

### Theorem (Whyte/Gersten/Block–Weinberger style; quasi-isometry invariance of coarse homology/cohomology under uniform acyclicity)
If \(f:X\to X'\) is a quasi-isometry between **bounded-geometry, uniformly acyclic CW-complexes**, then \(f\) induces isomorphisms on the corresponding coarse (co)homology groups (in the appropriate theory). ([homepages.math.uic.edu](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kwhyte/QTPart2.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Reference.**
Kevin Whyte, *Quasi-actions on trees II: …* (see the stated Theorem 2.7 in the PDF). ([homepages.math.uic.edu](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kwhyte/QTPart2.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
(Whyte cites and slightly generalizes arguments of Gersten and of Block–Weinberger in this direction.)

**How it relates.** In many geometric-group-theory applications, one identifies \(H^*(G;RG)\) with (compactly supported / locally finite / coarse) (co)homology of a contractible complex on which \(G\) acts properly and cocompactly. Then the above gives quasi-isometry invariance of that coarse avatar, hence invariance statements for \(H^*(G;RG)\) *in those cases*.

---

## 3) What theorem_search surfaced (useful, but note the scope)

The semantic theorem search did **not** return a correct “general quasi-isometry invariance of \(H^k(G;RG)\)” statement. The closest directly relevant items were:

### (i) A model identification in the *relative* setting (group pairs), linking group-ring cohomology to compactly supported cohomology
For a type \(F_\infty\) group pair \((G,\mathcal P)\), for all \(N\ge 0\),

query: parity of meromorphic differentials on compact Riemann surfaces
response_without:
Let \(X\) be a compact Riemann surface of genus \(g\), and \(\omega\) a **meromorphic** 1‑form with divisor
\[
(\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i p_i \;-\;\sum_{j=1}^s \ell_j q_j,\qquad m_i,\ell_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ \ \sum_i m_i-\sum_j \ell_j=2g-2.
\]
Questions about “parity” for meromorphic differentials almost always mean the **parity of an induced spin structure / theta characteristic**, i.e. an Arf invariant (topological) or equivalently \(\dim H^0(X,L)\bmod 2\) for a suitable square root \(L\) of a line bundle determined by \(\omega\).

Below are the central results that make this precise and explain when parity is defined and how it behaves in families.

---

## 1) Kontsevich–Zorich: parity for Abelian (holomorphic) differentials with even zeros

### Theorem (Kontsevich–Zorich, connected components via spin parity)
Fix a stratum \(\mathcal H(m_1,\dots,m_n)\) of holomorphic Abelian differentials \((X,\omega)\) where \(\sum_i m_i=2g-2\). If **all** \(m_i\) are even, then \(\omega\) canonically determines a spin structure (theta characteristic) \(L\) on \(X\) and its **parity**
\[
\phi(\omega):=h^0(X,L)\!\!\pmod 2\in\{0,1\}
\]
is locally constant on the stratum. For \(g\ge 2\), the connected components of strata are classified (up to known low-genus exceptions) by:
- hyperellipticity of \((X,\omega)\), and
- \(\phi(\omega)\in\{\text{even},\text{odd}\}\) when all zero orders are even.

This is the foundational “spin parity invariant” in the subject. ([ihes.fr](https://www.ihes.fr/~maxim/TEXTS/connected_components_35.pdf))

**Reference (paper + link).**
- M. Kontsevich, A. Zorich, *Connected components of the moduli spaces of Abelian differentials with prescribed singularities*, Invent. Math. 153 (2003). PDF: ([ihes.fr](https://www.ihes.fr/~maxim/TEXTS/connected_components_35.pdf))

**How it relates.** This is the prototype: it tells you what “parity” means (a theta characteristic parity) and that it is deformation invariant and can split strata into components.

---

## 2) Boissy: extension to **meromorphic** differentials (translation surfaces with poles)

Boissy generalizes the KZ picture to meromorphic 1‑forms on compact \(X\) (equivalently holomorphic 1‑forms on punctured \(X\)), showing that in genus \(\ge 2\) the same two invariants—hyperellipticity and **spin parity**—still govern connected components, with an additional genus \(1\) phenomenon.

### Theorem (Boissy, classification for meromorphic strata; parity is one of the invariants)
Let \(\mathcal H(\mu)\) be a stratum of meromorphic differentials (zeros and poles prescribed, total degree \(2g-2\)). For \(g\ge 2\), \(\mathcal H(\mu)\) has **at most three** connected components, described by:
- existence of a **hyperelliptic component** in certain “hyperelliptic type” strata, and
- if the singularity data are of **even type** (in particular, all zero orders even, and pole orders constrained as in the paper), then there are **two nonhyperelliptic components distinguished by spin parity**.

In genus \(1\), strata can have arbitrarily many connected components classified by a “rotation number” invariant. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1211.4951))

In particular, Boissy states a global classification theorem (Theorem 1.2 in the ar5iv rendering) explicitly featuring “parity of the spin structure” as the distinguishing invariant when defined. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1211.4951))

**Reference (paper + arXiv link).**
- C. Boissy, *Connected components of the strata of the moduli space of meromorphic differentials*, arXiv:1211.4951. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.4951))

**How it relates.**
- This is *the* main reference for parity in the meromorphic 1‑form setting on compact \(X\): it tells you when parity is defined (an “even type” condition) and that it is constant on connected components and actually separates components in many strata.

---

## 3) Lanneau: parity for spin structures coming from **quadratic** differentials (contrast)

If by “meromorphic differentials” you also mean meromorphic **quadratic** differentials \(q\in H^0(X,K_X^{\otimes 2}(\ast))\), then there is an induced spin structure in certain cases; Lanneau studies its parity and shows it behaves differently than the Abelian case.

### Theorem (Lanneau: spin parity is constant on strata of quadratic differentials where defined)
For strata of quadratic differentials \(q\) where an associated spin structure is defined, the parity of that spin structure is **constant on each stratum** (hence it cannot distinguish different connected components *within* a given stratum, unlike the Abelian case). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0210116))

**Reference (paper + arXiv link).**
- E. Lanneau, *Parity of the spin structure defined by a quadratic differential*, arXiv:math/0210116. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0210116))

**How it relates.**
- This is the cautionary comparison: for \(k=2\) differentials, “parity” exists but is too coarse to classify components in the same way.

---

## 4) What “parity” *is* (conceptual formulation)

When a spin structure \(L\) is associated to \(\omega\), its parity is
\[
\mathrm{par}(L)=h^0(X,L)\!\!\pmod 2,
\]
equivalently the **Arf invariant** of the corresponding quadratic form on \(H_1(X,\mathbb Z/2)\) (Johnson’s theory). Kontsevich–Zorich explicitly use this Arf-invariant formulation in their analysis of strata and connected components. ([ihes.fr](https://www.ihes.fr/~maxim/TEXTS/connected_components_35.pdf))

---

## arXiv links (collected)
- Kontsevich–Zorich (Invent. 2003): PDF link as hosted: ([ihes.fr](https://www.ihes.fr/~maxim/TEXTS/connected_components_35.pdf))  
- Boissy, *Connected components… meromorphic differentials*: arXiv:1211.4951 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.4951))  
- Lanneau, *Parity of the spin structure defined by a quadratic differential*: arXiv:math/0210116 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0210116))  

---

## Clarifying question (to target the “right” parity statement)
Do you mean:
1) **meromorphic 1‑forms** (Abelian differentials with poles), i.e. \(\omega\in H^0(X,K_X(D))\), or  
2) **meromorphic \(k\)-differentials** (especially quadratic), i.e. sections of \(K_X^{\otimes k}(D)\)?

If you tell me which, and whether your pole/zero orders are all even (or satisfy Boissy’s “even type”), I can write down the *exact* associated theta characteristic and the precise parity formula used in that setting.
response_with:
“Parity of meromorphic differentials” is usually shorthand for the **parity (even/odd) of a spin structure** naturally associated to certain strata of differentials. There are two main (closely related) settings:

1. **Abelian (meromorphic 1-)differentials** \(\omega\) (sections of \(K_X(*D)\)).
2. **Quadratic differentials** \(q\) (sections of \(K_X^{\otimes 2}(*D)\)), where a genuine “spin parity” can be defined under congruence conditions on zero/pole orders.

Below are the standard precise results and where to find them.

---

## A. Holomorphic 1-forms: parity of the induced theta characteristic and connected components (Kontsevich–Zorich)

Let \(X\) be a compact Riemann surface of genus \(g\) and \(\omega\) a **holomorphic** 1-form with zero divisor
\[
(\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^n k_i Z_i,\qquad \sum k_i = 2g-2.
\]
Assume **all \(k_i\) are even**, so \(k_i=2\ell_i\). Then
\[
(\omega)=2D,\quad D:=\sum \ell_i Z_i,
\]
and \(\mathcal L:=\mathcal O_X(D)\) satisfies \(\mathcal L^{\otimes 2}\cong K_X\), i.e. \(\mathcal L\) is a **theta characteristic (spin structure)**.

Its **parity** is
\[
\operatorname{par}(\mathcal L):=h^0(X,\mathcal L)\pmod 2\in\{0,1\},
\]
often called **even/odd** spin.

### Theorem (Kontsevich–Zorich: classification via spin parity and hyperellipticity)
For \(g\ge 4\), the connected components of the stratum \(\mathcal H(k_1,\dots,k_n)\) of abelian differentials are classified as follows (informally: “at most three components”):
- If **some \(k_i\) is odd**, then (outside the hyperelliptic exceptional strata) the stratum is essentially **connected**.
- If **all \(k_i\) are even**, then the stratum has (non-hyperelliptic) components distinguished by the **spin parity** (even vs odd).
- In the special cases \(\mathcal H(2g-2)\) and \(\mathcal H(g-1,g-1)\) there is additionally a **hyperelliptic component**.

A standard formulation appears as “Theorem 1 / Theorem 2.1 / Theorem 7.2 / Theorem 3.5” depending on the source/exposition. The theorem_search output gives such a statement explicitly (e.g. “Theorem 2.1 (KZ, Theorem 1)”). 

**Paper / link**
- M. Kontsevich, A. Zorich, *Connected components of the moduli spaces of Abelian differentials with prescribed singularities* (Invent. Math. 2003). arXiv: ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0201292?utm_source=openai))

**How it answers “parity”**  
It explains: when the zero orders are all even, the stratum carries a **spin parity invariant** which is **constant on connected components** and (in most cases) **splits the stratum into even/odd components**.

---

## B. Meromorphic 1-forms: connected components and when “spin parity” still appears (Boissy)

For **meromorphic** abelian differentials one considers strata
\[
\mathcal H(n_1,\dots,n_r;\,-p_1,\dots,-p_s)
\]
with zeros of orders \(n_i>0\) and poles of orders \(p_j>0\). These are translation surfaces with poles (infinite area), and the topology of strata changes.

### Theorem (Boissy: connected components of strata of meromorphic 1-forms; spin-type splitting in “even type” cases)
Boissy proves that in genus \(g\ge 2\), strata of meromorphic differentials have **up to three components**, with a description *similar in spirit* to Kontsevich–Zorich: components can be separated by **hyperelliptic type** and, in certain “even type” situations, by a **spin parity** invariant. The theorem_search database returns a statement of this form (labeled “Theorem (Boissy)” / “Theorem 2.3” in one presentation). 

**Paper / link**
- C. Boissy, *Connected components of the strata of the moduli space of meromorphic differentials*. arXiv: ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.4951?utm_source=openai))  
(Also circulated as a PDF preprint.) ([math.univ-toulouse.fr](https://www.math.univ-toulouse.fr/~cboissy/Documents/recherche/meromorphic.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**How it relates to parity**  
For meromorphic 1-forms, there is not always a globally defined classical theta characteristic coming from “half the divisor of zeros” (since poles interfere), but **in specific signatures** one can still define spin-type invariants, and they can **distinguish components** of the stratum.

---

## C. Quadratic differentials (possibly meromorphic): parity of the induced spin structure (Lanneau)

For quadratic differentials \(q\), one can sometimes define an associated spin structure (often via the orientation double cover or via divisor congruences). Lanneau gives precise results on when the spin structure is well-defined and computes its parity.

### Theorem (Lanneau: parity well-defined in strata avoiding orders \(\equiv 2\!\!\pmod 4\), and constant on strata)
If a (meromorphic) quadratic differential \(q\) has **no zeros/poles of order \(k\equiv 2\pmod 4\)**, then an associated spin structure is well-defined, and its **parity is independent of the choice of \(q\) inside the stratum** \(\mathcal Q(k_1,\dots,k_\ell)\). 

### Theorem (Lanneau: explicit parity formula)
Under the same congruence hypothesis \(k_i\not\equiv 2\pmod 4\), let \(n_{+1}\) be the number of zeros of degrees \(1\bmod 4\) and \(n_{-1}\) the number of zeros of degrees \(3\bmod 4\) (with the rest \(0\bmod 4\)). What people usually mean by “the sign of the cup-\(i\) product” is: **which Koszul sign convention** is built into the cochain-level operations \(\smile_i\) so that

1) \(\smile_0\) is the usual cup product,  
2) \(\smile_i\) gives explicit *chain homotopies* witnessing graded-commutativity of \(\smile_0\), and  
3) the resulting Steenrod operations (Sq at \(p=2\), \(P^s,\beta P^s\) at odd \(p\)) have the standard signs.

There isn’t a single universal “sign”; there are a few competing **equivalent** conventions. The clean way to state the sign rule is via the **coboundary (homotopy) identity** that characterizes \(\smile_i\) up to coherent equivalence.

---

## 1) Fundamental sign identity: the cup-\(i\) coboundary formula (integral cochains)

Let \(C^*(X;R)\) be normalized cochains on a simplicial set (or singular cochains) with the usual cohomological grading \(|x|=p\). A cup-\(i\) structure is a family of graded maps
\[
\smile_i \colon C^p(X;R)\otimes C^q(X;R)\to C^{p+q-i}(X;R)\qquad(i\ge 0)
\]
satisfying the **Steenrod coboundary (homotopy) relation**
\[
d(x\smile_i y)
= (dx)\smile_i y \;+\; (-1)^{|x|-i}\, x\smile_i (dy)
\;+\; (-1)^{|x|}\, x\smile_{i-1} y
\;+\; (-1)^{(|x|-i)(|y|+1)}\, y\smile_{i-1} x,
\]
with the convention \(\smile_{-1}=0\).

This is the precise place where the “signs of \(\smile_i\)” live: different sources may move signs among the last two terms (or define \(\smile_i\) with an overall factor \((-1)^{f(p,q,i)}\)), but they are arranged so that \(\smile_i\) is a specific chain homotopy controlling the failure of graded commutativity of \(\smile_0\).

A modern operadic framework encoding these sign choices and comparing conventions is in Kaufmann–Medina-Mardones (see below). ([hopf.math.purdue.edu](https://hopf.math.purdue.edu/~rkaufman/pubfiles/KaufmannMedina1.pdf))

**How it relates to Steenrod operations.** For \(p=2\), the Steenrod squares are induced by the cup-\(i\)’s essentially via
\[
\mathrm{Sq}^k([a]) = [a\smile_{|a|-k} a],
\]
and for odd \(p\) one needs additional sign normalizations; the Kaufmann–Medina-Mardones paper makes the sign normalizations explicit in their Definition 5.6 via a coefficient \(\nu(q)\). ([hopf.math.purdue.edu](https://hopf.math.purdue.edu/~rkaufman/pubfiles/KaufmannMedina1.pdf))

---

## 2) Mod 2: all signs disappear, but conventions still matter integrally

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), \((-1)=+1\), so the above identity becomes sign-free. This is why many treatments of \(\smile_i\) for Steenrod squares (at the even prime) avoid sign discussions entirely: the *same* combinatorial formula works, but every \(\pm\) is invisible.

A concrete mod-2 simplicial formula for \(\smile_1\) (no signs) is recorded in the MathOverflow discussion (used there to show \(\smile_i\) is not associative for \(i>0\)). ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/268181/associativity-of-steenrods-cup-i-product))

---

## 3) “Which sign convention is the Steenrod one?” (uniqueness up to isomorphism)

If your concern is: *given two different sign conventions for \(\smile_i\), do they define the same Steenrod operations?*—then a key result is that, under natural axioms, cup-\(i\) structures are essentially unique (so sign differences are controlled by a unique isomorphism of constructions).

### Theorem (Medina‑Mardones; uniqueness/rigidity of Steenrod cup-\(i\))
Any cup-\(i\) construction on normalized chains of simplicial sets satisfying certain natural axioms (naturality, minimality, non-degeneracy, irreducibility, freeness) is **isomorphic** (not just chain homotopic) to Steenrod’s original construction.

This implies that most sign conventions in the literature are the “same” after a canonical identification—i.e. discrepancies are bookkeeping, not different operations. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.06505))

   arXiv:2010.02571 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02571))  
   *Where the signs show up:* they give an operadic definition of the cup-\((p,i)\) products and explicitly include the odd-prime sign normalization \(\nu(q)\) (Definition 5.6) so the resulting \(P^s,\beta P^s\) match standard conventions. ([hopf.math.purdue.edu](https://hopf.math.purdue.edu/~rkaufman/pubfiles/KaufmannMedina1.pdf))

2) **A. M. Medina‑Mardones**, *An axiomatic characterization of Steenrod’s cup-\(i\) products*.  
   arXiv:1810.06505 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.06505))  
   *Relevance to “sign”:* explains that (under axioms) there is essentially one cup-\(i\) theory, so different sign conventions correspond to isomorphic constructions.

3) (For intuition / sanity checks) **MathOverflow discussion** giving explicit \(\smile_1\) mod-2 formula and showing nonassociativity for \(i>0\).  
   ([mathoverflow.net](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/268181/associativity-of-steenrods-cup-i-product))

## 0) Dictionary (“transfer” from billiards to Teichmüller dynamics)

### Theorem (Zemlyakov–Katok unfolding / suspension construction; “billiards ↔ straight-line flow”)
Let \(P\) be a **rational polygon**, i.e. all interior angles are rational multiples of \(\pi\). Then one can build a compact **translation surface** \((X,\omega)\) by unfolding finitely many reflected copies of \(P\) and gluing parallel sides by translations, such that:

- billiard trajectories in \(P\) correspond to straight-line geodesics on \((X,\omega)\) (up to the natural projection/folding map),
- the billiard flow in a fixed direction corresponds to the translation flow in the corresponding direction on \((X,\omega)\).

This is the foundational “transfer principle” that replaces reflections at the boundary by straight motion on a translation surface.

- **uniquely ergodic**.

Within an affine invariant manifold \(\mathcal M\), certain “cylinder shear/stretch” deformations stay inside \(\mathcal M\). This underlies many arithmetic/non-arithmetic rigidity results and allows effective constraints from cylinder configurations (which come directly from polygon decompositions).

Let \((X,\omega)\) be a translation surface (an Abelian differential) in a stratum \(\mathcal H(\kappa)\). Then the \(GL(2,\mathbb R)\)-orbit closure
\[
\overline{GL^+(2,\mathbb R)\cdot (X,\omega)}
\]
is an **affine invariant submanifold** of the stratum: locally, in period coordinates, it is cut out by **homogeneous real linear equations**. Moreover, any closed \(GL(2,\mathbb R)\)-invariant subset of a stratum is a finite union of such affine invariant submanifolds.

**How it relates to your query.**  
A **rational billiard polygon** unfolds to a translation surface; the \(SL(2,\mathbb R)\) (or \(GL^+\)) orbit encodes all linear deformations of the billiard (renormalization). EMM tells you that every orbit closure is “linear/algebraic” in period coordinates, which is the foundational structure theorem behind modern “orbit + arithmetic” questions.

**Reference (arXiv):**

### Theorem (Closed orbit ⇔ Veech surface)
A translation surface \((X,\omega)\) is a **Veech surface** (i.e. its Veech group \(\Gamma(X,\omega)\subset SL(2,\mathbb R)\) is a lattice) **if and only if** its \(GL(2,\mathbb R)\)-orbit is **closed** (equivalently it projects to a **Teichmüller curve** in moduli).

**How it relates.**  
For rational billiards, “special” polygons (like those giving Veech surfaces) have exceptionally rigid dynamics; the corresponding Teichmüller disc descends to an algebraic curve (Teichmüller curve). This is exactly the “Teichmüller transfer surface / polygon / orbit” bridge.

(For orbit-closedness equivalences and lattice property; the dichotomy below is in the same circle of results.)

## 3) Dynamics on Veech surfaces: Veech dichotomy (periodic vs uniquely ergodic)

### Theorem (Veech Dichotomy)
If \((X,\omega)\) has **lattice Veech group** (i.e. is a Veech surface), then for every direction \(\theta\):
- either the straight-line flow in direction \(\theta\) is **completely periodic** (surface decomposes into finitely many cylinders in direction \(\theta\), with commensurable moduli),
- or the flow is **uniquely ergodic** (in particular minimal).

**How it relates.**  
This is the key payoff for billiards: for rational polygons whose unfolding is Veech, the billiard flow in every direction is “as simple as possible” (periodic or uniquely ergodic).

**Theorem_search matches:**

**Primary reference:**

### Theorem (KMS: a.e. direction uniquely ergodic)
For any translation surface, the directional flow is **uniquely ergodic for Lebesgue-a.e. direction**. In particular, for any **rational billiard table**, the billiard flow is uniquely ergodic for almost every direction (on the unfolded invariant surface).

**How it relates.**  
Even without the lattice/Veech property, rational billiards still have strong “generic direction” unique ergodicity.

**References:**

A translation surface is **square-tiled** (an **origami**, i.e. a branched cover of the flat torus ramified over at most one point) **if and only if** its Veech group is **commensurable with \(SL(2,\mathbb Z)\)** (equivalently, it shares a finite-index subgroup with \(SL(2,\mathbb Z)\)).

This is the standard “arithmeticity” criterion in this subject: square-tiled surfaces are exactly the “arithmetic” Veech surfaces, and they correspond to especially arithmetic Teichmüller curves (defined over number fields, often over \(\mathbb Q\) in suitable senses).

Below are several core results that (in practice) form the “theorem toolkit” for Teichmüller theory of **surfaces of topologically infinite type**. I’ve focused on the aspects that are genuinely different from the finite-type setting: (i) dependence on a base hyperbolic/conformal structure, (ii) inequivalence of natural metrics and the strict inclusions between the resulting Teichmüller spaces, and (iii) infinite-dimensional (Banach/Finsler) features.

Throughout, let \(S\) be a connected, orientable surface of **infinite topological type**, and fix a base hyperbolic (or conformal) structure \(H_0\) when required.

---

## 1) Completeness of the length-spectrum metric (infinite type)

### Theorem (Completeness of \(d_{ls}\))
On the length-spectrum Teichmüller space \(\mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)\) (defined via the length-spectrum distortion with respect to \(H_0\)), the **length-spectrum metric** \(d_{ls}\) is **complete** for surfaces of infinite topological type. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2851))

**How it relates.** In finite type, completeness is classical for several metrics, but in infinite type one first has to decide which “Teichmüller space” one means. This theorem says that once you build Teichmüller space using length-spectrum control, the resulting metric space is complete—an important foundational property for doing geometry/dynamics with \(d_{ls}\).

**Reference (arXiv + journal).**
- Daniele Alessandrini, Lixin Liu, Athanase Papadopoulos, Weixu Su, *On various Teichmüller spaces of a surface of infinite topological type*, Proc. AMS 140 (2012), 561–574.
- arXiv:1008.2851 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2851))

---

## 2) Quasiconformal vs length-spectrum Teichmüller space: strictness / nowhere denseness

### Theorem (QC inclusion can be nowhere dense in LS)
Assume the base hyperbolic surface \(H_0\) is **upper-bounded** and **admits short interior curves** (a standard hypothesis in this circle of work). Then the natural inclusion
\[
\iota:\ \mathcal T_{qc}(H_0)\hookrightarrow \mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)
\]
has image that is **nowhere dense** in \(\mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.6030))

A key corollary in the same work is an **explicit Fenchel–Nielsen coordinate description** of \(\mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)\) (under the same hypotheses) and **path-connectedness** of \(\mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.6030))

**How it relates.** For finite type surfaces, the “classical” Teichmüller space can be defined equivalently via quasiconformal maps, Fenchel–Nielsen parameters, extremal length, etc. In infinite type, these viewpoints can yield **different spaces and topologies**; this theorem is one of the clearest “separation” statements: the quasiconformal Teichmüller space can be very small inside the length-spectrum one.

**Reference.**
- Daniele Alessandrini, Lixin Liu, Athanase Papadopoulos, Weixu Su, *On the inclusion of the quasiconformal Teichmüller space into the length-spectrum Teichmüller space*, Monatshefte Math. 179 (2016), 165–189.
- arXiv:1201.6030 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.6030))

---

## 3) “Many Teichmüller spaces” and non-equivalence of natural metrics (infinite type)

### Theorem package (non-equivalence / basepoint dependence)
For infinite-type surfaces, Teichmüller spaces built from different control conditions—e.g.
- quasiconformal,
- length-spectrum,
- bi-Lipschitz,
- Fenchel–Nielsen,

are generally **not equivalent** (and can define different topologies / different subspaces), and the resulting spaces can depend on the **choice of base structure** \(H_0\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00289))

**How it relates.** This is the main conceptual shift compared to finite type: there is no single “the” Teichmüller space unless you specify the model (qc/ls/FN/BL) and the basepoint hypotheses.

**Key references.**
- Alessandrini–Liu–Papadopoulos–Su, arXiv:1008.2851 (comparisons between \(\mathcal T_{ls}\), \(\mathcal T_{qc}\), \(\mathcal T_{FN}\), etc.) ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2851))
- Fırat Yaşar, *Infinite-dimensional Teichmüller spaces*, arXiv:2104.00289 (systematic discussion of multiple metrics/spaces; basepoint dependence) ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00289))

---

## 4) Dense finitely-supported subspaces; contractibility phenomena

### Theorem (density of finitely supported Teichmüller space)
Yaşar defines a **finitely supported Teichmüller space** \( \mathcal T^{fs}(H_0)\) (roughly: deformations supported on finite-type subsurfaces, expressed via Fenchel–Nielsen data) and proves it is **dense** in a natural “asymptotically isometric” length-spectrum subspace \( \mathcal T^{0}_{ls}(H_0)\), both viewed inside \( \mathcal T_{ls}(H_0)\). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00289))

### Theorem (contractibility)
The **asymptotically length-spectrum bounded** Teichmüller space \(AT_{ls}(H_0)\) is **contractible**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00289))

**How it relates.** For infinite-type \(S\), it’s often useful to approximate by finite-type subsurfaces. “Finitely supported” subspaces formalize this approximation and give density statements. Contractibility results are important if you want to treat these as classifying spaces, or to compare with mapping class group actions.

**Reference.**
- Fırat Yaşar, *Infinite-dimensional Teichmüller spaces*, arXiv:2104.00289. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00289))

---

## 5) Banach-space models in infinite-dimensional Teichmüller theory (asymptotic Teichmüller space)

### Theorem (little Bers space \(Q_0(M)\cong c_0\); consequences for \(AT(M)\))
For a hyperbolic Riemann surface \(M\) of **infinite analytic type**, the **little Bers space** \(Q_0(M)\) is isomorphic (as a Banach space) to \(c_0\). As a consequence, the **asymptotic Teichmüller space** \(AT(M)\) is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to a bounded open subset of \( \ell^\infty / c_0\). ([ams.org](https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/2010-362-05/S0002-9947-09-04944-7/?utm_source=openai))

**How it relates.** This is a prototypical “infinite-dimensional” phenomenon: Teichmüller theory naturally lands in Banach spaces, and the quotient \( \ell^\infty/c_0\) is a standard hallmark of large-scale/infinite-dimensional behavior. This connects the geometric deformation theory to functional-analytic structure.

F:T(M)\to T(N)

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(T(M)) \cong \mathrm{MCG}(M)

**How it relates:** This is one of the main “organizing” results: even though \(T(M)\) is infinite-dimensional, its complex geometry is still rigid enough that holomorphic automorphisms come from the underlying surface.

## 2) Properness of mapping class group actions (in infinite type)

There are several inequivalent Teichmüller-type spaces for infinite-type surfaces (quasiconformal, length-spectrum, Fenchel–Nielsen, WP-subspaces, etc.), and the mapping class group may behave differently on each. In the “classical” quasiconformal Teichmüller space, one still has properness results (with appropriate topology/metric).

The mapping class group \(\pi_0(\mathrm{Diff}(S))\) acts **properly** on the Teichmüller space \(\mathcal T_S\).

A cornerstone in infinite-dimensional Teichmüller theory is that \(T(M)\) is modeled on Banach spaces of quadratic differentials / Beltrami differentials, via the Bers embedding.

There is a biholomorphic embedding (Bers embedding)

\beta: T(M)\hookrightarrow Q(M)

into a Banach space \(Q(M)\) of holomorphic quadratic differentials; the tangent/cotangent spaces can be described in terms of preduals such as the Bergman space \(A^1(M)\). \]
so \(x_i\) are Steklov eigenfunctions with eigenvalue \(\sigma=1\). (In particular, \(\sigma=1\) lies in the Steklov spectrum.)

**Why this matters for your query.** This is the basic geometric bridge: free boundary minimality produces Steklov eigenfunctions, and on **compact** \(\Sigma\) the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator is elliptic self-adjoint on \(\partial\Sigma\), hence the Steklov spectrum is discrete.

Let \((M,g)\) be a **smooth compact** Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary \(\partial M\). The Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) operator \(\Lambda_g\) (a.k.a. \[
0=\sigma_0 < \sigma_1 \le \sigma_2 \le \cdots \nearrow +\infty
\]
with finite multiplicities.

A precise theorem statement you can cite (from arXiv theorem database):

This is the mathematical reason why essentially all of the classical Steklov/free-boundary-minimal-surface literature assumes **compact** surfaces.

---

### (B) Non-compact case: discreteness generally fails without extra hypotheses
If \(M\) is **non-compact** (even if \(\partial M\) is compact), discreteness of the Steklov spectrum is **not automatic**. Intuitively: the harmonic extension problem interacts with “escape to infinity” in the interior, and one typically expects **essential/continuous spectrum** unless the geometry at infinity forces compactness of the relevant solution operator (equivalently compactness of the DtN resolvent on \(\partial M\)).

A useful general principle is:

So for a **non-compact minimal surface with free boundary**, *unless the surface is compact*, you should expect that the Steklov spectrum is **not purely discrete in general**, and you need additional assumptions to recover discreteness.

For a **compact** free boundary minimal surface \(\Sigma\subset B^n\), one has the classical relationship: coordinate functions restrict to Steklov eigenfunctions when the immersion is by first Steklov eigenfunctions (this is central in Fraser–Schoen and subsequent work). Below are the standard rigorous results behind the slogan

> “(planar) Couette flow is stable under small **Gevrey** perturbations”

together with the (equally standard) complementary result that **Gevrey-2 is essentially critical**.

---

## 1) 2D Euler near Couette on \(\mathbb T_x\times\mathbb R_y\): nonlinear asymptotic stability in Gevrey \(<2\)

### Theorem (Bedrossian–Masmoudi: nonlinear inviscid damping / asymptotic stability for Gevrey \(<2\))
Consider the 2D incompressible Euler equations on \(\mathbb T\times\mathbb R\), written as vorticity transport
\[
\partial_t\omega + u\cdot\nabla\omega = 0,\qquad u=\nabla^\perp\psi,\quad \Delta\psi=\omega,
\]
and perturbations of the Couette shear \((y,0)\) (equivalently perturbations of the Couette vorticity).

If the initial perturbation is sufficiently small in a Gevrey class of index strictly **better than Gevrey-2** (often written “Gevrey-\(1/s\)” with \(s>1/2\), corresponding to Gevrey class \(<2\)), then the solution exists globally and is **asymptotically stable**: the velocity converges (strongly, e.g. in \(L^2\)) to a limiting shear flow, and the nonzero \(x\)-modes undergo **inviscid damping** (decay), while the vorticity is mixed to small scales and converges only weakly.

This is the first fully nonlinear confirmation of Orr/Kelvin inviscid damping around Couette under a perturbative hypothesis. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.5028))

**Paper / arXiv**
- Jacob Bedrossian, Nader Masmoudi, *Inviscid damping and the asymptotic stability of planar shear flows in the 2D Euler equations*.  
  arXiv:1306.5028 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.5028))

**Relation to your query.** This is the flagship theorem that (precisely interpreted) proves: *Couette is nonlinearly stable under sufficiently small Gevrey perturbations*, with the Gevrey index required to be strictly better than 2.

---

## 2) 2D Euler near Couette in a finite channel: Gevrey asymptotic stability / inviscid damping

### Theorem (Ionescu–Jia: nonlinear inviscid damping in a channel, Gevrey regularity)
For 2D Euler on the channel \(\mathbb T\times[0,1]\), for sufficiently small perturbations of Couette in a suitable **Gevrey** class (plus technical assumptions, e.g. interior support of vorticity to manage boundary effects), solutions are global and exhibit **asymptotic stability** and **inviscid damping**: the velocity converges strongly to a nearby shear and the vorticity is mixed to high frequencies / converges weakly (modulo the shear component). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04026))

**Paper / arXiv**
- Alexandru Ionescu, Hao Jia, *Inviscid damping near the Couette flow in a channel*.  
  arXiv:1808.04026 ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04026))

**Relation to your query.** This shows the Gevrey-stability phenomenon persists in bounded geometries (with boundary-induced complications), again for small Gevrey perturbations.

---

## 3) Sharpness / criticality: instability below Gevrey-2

### Theorem (Deng–Masmoudi: long time instability in “low Gevrey”; Gevrey-2 critical)
There exist small perturbations of Couette that are *less regular than Gevrey class 2* for which the Couette flow is **nonlinearly unstable** on long time scales, via a fully nonlinear energy-cascade/echo-type mechanism. In particular, this demonstrates that **Gevrey-2 is (essentially) the critical regularity threshold** separating the known stable regime (Gevrey \(<2\)) from an unstable regime (Gevrey \(>2\) / rougher). ### Theorem (Bedrossian–Germain–Masmoudi: below-threshold stability, enhanced dissipation)
For 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes near plane Couette at large \(\mathrm{Re}\), sufficiently regular perturbations with size \(\epsilon \lesssim \mathrm{Re}^{-1}\) are global, remain close to Couette, and relax back to Couette as \(t\to\infty\); nonzero streamwise modes are rapidly damped after times \(t\gtrsim \mathrm{Re}^{1/3}\) via mixing-enhanced dissipation.
